lead: On the day the world keeps as Labour Day the Church remembers St Joseph, the working man of Nazareth, and today’s four readings form a short theology of work. Genesis tells how work, which God gave to the first man as a share in tending his garden, became toil and sweat after sin. In Wisdom, Solomon asks God to send wisdom to labour at his side, so that his work may please God. Colossians tells the baptized to do everything, in word or deed, in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks. In Matthew the people of Nazareth stumble over a carpenter’s son who teaches with wisdom. The words to watch are work, wisdom and name: the work that sin made heavy is lifted again when it is done with God’s wisdom and in the name of Jesus, as it was in the workshop of Joseph.

r.h: By the sweat of your face
set: Genesis 2–3 tells, in the language of story, the truth about where human beings stand before God. The man is formed from the dust of the ground and placed in the garden of Eden “to till it and keep it” (2:15). Work belongs to the good creation, before any sin. Then the man and the woman eat from the one tree God had forbidden, and in 3:14–19 God speaks to the serpent, to the woman and to the man in turn.

Today’s verses give the word to the man and then his sending out from the garden. The reading skips vv. 20–22: the naming of Eve, the garments of skin God makes for the couple, and God’s words about the tree of life. The garments matter: even in judgment God clothes those he must send away.
str: v. 17: the ground is cursed because of the man; he will eat of it in toil.
v. 18: thorns and thistles; the plants of the field.
v. 19: sweat until the return to dust.
v. 23: the man sent out to till the ground from which he was taken.
v. 24: the cherubim and the flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life. ¶ The man is not cursed; the ground is. The task of tilling remains, but now it is hard, and death sets its limit.
kw: The man (’ādām) is taken from the ground (’ădāmâ), and the two words sound alike in Hebrew. The man and the soil belong together: he is made from it, he lives from it, he returns to it.
The same noun is used in 3:16 for the woman’s pain in childbearing and in 3:17 for the man’s toil. Both of the great tasks of human life, giving life and sustaining it, now carry sorrow.

Heavenly guardians. Their images later stand over the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:18–22) and are woven into the curtain of the tabernacle. The way back to God’s presence is guarded, but it is not abolished.
vv: cursed is the ground because of you; in toil you shall eat of it all the days of your life;
Sin breaks the harmony between the man and the earth. Work does not become evil, but the earth no longer answers him easily.
By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the ground,
Bread is still given. The verse that pronounces judgment also promises that the man will eat; God does not abandon him to hunger.
you are dust, and to dust you shall return.
The words spoken to Christians at the start of the Great Fast in many Churches. They humble, but they do not end the story: the dust is the same dust into which God first breathed life (2:7).
therefore the Lord God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he was taken.
He leaves with a task. Outside Eden the man still works the ground; the vocation given in 2:15 continues in a harder place.
and a sword flaming and turning to guard the way to the tree of life.

The way to the tree of life is guarded, not destroyed. The Fathers saw it reopened by Christ: the Cross is the new tree of life, and the Book of Revelation ends with the tree of life given to the redeemed (Revelation 22:2).
ch: The Catechism teaches that in the garden “work is not yet a burden”, but the collaboration of man and woman with God in perfecting the visible creation (CCC 378), and that after the Fall the harmony between the human being and creation is broken (CCC 400). The Church therefore never treats work as a punishment in itself. St John Paul II, in his encyclical Laborem Exercens (1981), reads Genesis as the first “gospel of work”: the toil and sweat are real, yet work remains a good thing for the human person, through which he becomes more human. The Catechism adds that by enduring the hardship of work in union with Jesus, the carpenter of Nazareth and the Crucified, a person collaborates with the Son of God in his work of redemption (CCC 2427).

r.h: Send wisdom to labour at my side
set: The Book of Wisdom was written in Greek, most likely by a Jewish teacher in Alexandria in Egypt in the last century or so before Christ. The writer speaks in the person of Solomon, the king famed for wisdom. The Catholic Church receives the book as Scripture; Jews and most Protestants do not include it in their canon.

Chapter 9 is Solomon’s prayer for wisdom, a meditative retelling of his prayer at Gibeon (1 Kings 3:6–9). He confesses that even the most gifted person is nothing without the wisdom that comes from God (9:6). Today’s verses ask God to send wisdom from his throne, and then reflect on how little mortals can know without her.
str: v. 10: the petition: send her, that she may labour at my side.
vv. 11–12: what wisdom will do: guide, guard, make my works acceptable.
vv. 13–16: the limits of human reason: the body weighs down the soul; even earthly things are found with labour.
vv. 17–18: only God’s gift of wisdom and holy spirit sets human paths right.
kw: In this book wisdom is pictured as a person, a woman who sits beside God’s throne (9:4) and is sent out to dwell with human beings. The New Testament uses this language of Christ, “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).

Solomon asks that wisdom may “labor at my side” (9:10). He does not ask to be spared work, but to have a companion in it. A different word, ponos (toil), stands in v. 16: what is at hand “we find with labor”.

The body is called an “earthy tent” (9:15), a dwelling that can be folded up. St Paul uses the same image: “if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God” (2 Corinthians 5:1).
vv: Send her forth from the holy heavens, and from the throne of your glory send her, that she may labor at my side,
The prayer of every worker who wants his work to be more than effort. Wisdom here is not cleverness but the gift that makes work please God.
Then my works will be acceptable,
Solomon’s “works” include his judging and building. Work becomes acceptable to God not by its size but by the wisdom that guides it.
for a perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthy tent burdens the thoughtful mind.
The writer uses the language of Greek thought, but he does not despise the body. He is describing how hard it is for creatures of dust to know heavenly things.
Who has learned your counsel, unless you have given wisdom and sent your holy spirit from on high?

Wisdom and the holy spirit stand side by side. Christians hear in this verse a first light on the Spirit whom the Father sends, and in this season of Resurrection the Church is already looking toward Pentecost.
ch: St Joseph is the model of the worker who asked for wisdom. The Gospels never record a word he spoke; they record what he did, quickly and exactly, each time God made his will known (Matthew 1:24; 2:14, 21). St John Paul II, in Redemptoris Custos (1989), presents Joseph’s work as the daily means by which he served the mystery of the Incarnation, and says that human work was taken up into that mystery in the house of Nazareth. The Catechism counts wisdom first among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1831).

r.h: Do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus
set: The letter is written in the name of Paul to the Church at Colossae in Asia Minor. Many scholars think a disciple of Paul wrote it after his death; others hold that Paul wrote it, perhaps with the help of a co-worker such as Timothy, who is named with him in the opening (1:1). The Church receives it as part of the apostolic witness.

Just before this reading the baptized are told to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, meekness and patience (3:12). Today’s verses put the last garment on top of all the others: love. Then the passage turns to peace, to the word of Christ, to song, and finally to everything we do.
str: v. 14: above all, love, which binds everything together.
v. 15: the peace of Christ as the umpire in the heart; be thankful.
v. 16: the word of Christ dwelling richly; teaching and singing.
v. 17: whatever you do, in word or deed, in the name of the Lord Jesus, with thanks. ¶ Thanksgiving appears in each of vv. 15, 16 and 17.
kw: Love is the belt or ligament that holds the other virtues together “in perfect harmony”. Without it they fall apart.
The word for the judge at the games who awards the prize. The peace of Christ is to decide disputes in the heart and in the community.
From the family of words that gives us “Eucharist”. A Christian life is a life of thanksgiving, and its centre is the great Thanksgiving of the Holy Qurbana.
vv: Above all, clothe yourselves with love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
Love is not one virtue among the others but the one that makes the others whole.
And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in the one body.
Peace is not only a private calm. It is given to “the one body”, the Church.
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly;
The verb means to make one’s home. The word is to live in the community as in its own house, through reading, teaching and song.
And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
Nothing is left out: the carpenter’s bench, the kitchen, the office and the field. Work done in the name of Jesus becomes an offering.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the daily work of lay people, carried out in the Spirit, becomes a spiritual sacrifice acceptable to God through Jesus Christ, offered with the Lord’s Body in the Eucharist (Lumen Gentium 34). The Catechism takes up this teaching (CCC 901). St Joseph is the plainest example of a holy life made of ordinary work: the Church does not honour him for great deeds in public, but for faithful labour done for Jesus and Mary.

r.h: Is not this the carpenter’s son?
set: Matthew 13 gathers seven parables of the kingdom. When Jesus has finished them he goes to his “hometown”, Nazareth in Galilee, a small village where everyone knew his family. Matthew follows Mark’s account (Mark 6:1–6) but tells it more briefly and gently.

In Mark the people ask, “Is not this the carpenter?” (Mark 6:3). Matthew writes “the carpenter’s son”. Both are true: Jesus learned his trade from Joseph and worked at it himself. St Justin Martyr, in the second century, says that Jesus made ploughs and yokes.
str: vv. 53–54a: Jesus comes to his hometown and teaches in the synagogue.
vv. 54b–56: the people’s questions: where did he get this wisdom? Is he not one of us?
v. 57: they take offence; the saying about a prophet in his own country.
v. 58: few deeds of power because of their unbelief.
kw: A worker in wood, and often in stone as well: a builder. In a Galilean village he would make doors, beams, tools and furniture. The Son of God spent most of his years on earth at this work.
The place of one’s father. The familiar can become a barrier: they think they know him already.
The word for a stumbling block. They trip over the very ordinariness through which God had come close.
vv: Where did this man get this wisdom and these deeds of power?
They admit the wisdom and the power. Their difficulty is not the evidence but the source: he is too familiar to be from God.
Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary?
Joseph is not named here but described by his work. He is remembered in his own village as a craftsman, and Jesus as his son.
And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?
In Hebrew and Aramaic “brother” can mean a close relative. The Church teaches that these are not other children of Mary: James and Joseph are sons of another Mary (compare Matthew 27:56; CCC 500).
And he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.
Mark says he “could do no deed of power there” (Mark 6:5). Matthew’s wording makes clear that the limit is not in Jesus’ power but in their refusal to receive it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that during the greater part of his life Jesus shared the condition of the vast majority of human beings: a daily life spent without evident greatness, a life of manual labour (CCC 531), and that the hidden life at Nazareth allows everyone to enter into fellowship with Jesus by the most ordinary events of daily life (CCC 533). Pope Pius XII instituted the feast of St Joseph the Worker in 1955, so that the first of May, a day of labour across the world, would also be kept as a day to honour the dignity of work in the light of Nazareth. Pope Francis, in Patris Corde (2020), calls Joseph a working father who teaches the value, dignity and joy of earning one’s bread.

qa: Is work a punishment for sin?

No. Before any sin the man is placed in the garden “to till it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Sin did not create work; it made work hard, uncertain and mixed with pain (CCC 378, 400). In Christ even the hardship of work can be joined to his own offering and become a share in redemption (CCC 2427).
Did Jesus have brothers and sisters?

The Gospels speak of his “brothers and sisters”, but in the Bible these words are used for cousins and close relatives as well (for example, in the Hebrew of Genesis 13:8 Lot, Abraham’s nephew, is called his brother; NRSV kindred). The Church has always confessed that Mary remained a virgin, and the Catechism notes that James and Joseph, named here among Jesus’ “brothers”, are the sons of another Mary (CCC 499–500).
Why did the people of Nazareth reject him?

Not because the signs were lacking. They saw his wisdom and heard of his power. They could not accept that God would come so close, in a neighbour, a worker, a man whose family they knew. The Gospel warns every believer: familiarity with holy things can become a reason not to receive them.
rite: St Joseph, whom our tradition calls Mar Yausep, is dear to Syro-Malabar families, and many of our parishes bear his name. His feast as patron of workers falls today on the Saturday of the Fifth Week of Resurrection, so the joy of Easter surrounds it. In a land where many work in fields, in fishing, in building, and far from home in the Gulf and beyond, the feast is a reminder that the Church honours the work of every person and asks for just wages and humane conditions.

Pope Leo XIII, in Rerum Novarum (1891), began the modern social teaching of the Church on work and the rights of workers. Today is a good day to pray for those without work, for migrant workers and their families, and for employers who must decide justly, entrusting all of them to the protection of Mar Yausep.
study: Genesis says work became hard after sin. Where in my work do I feel the “thorns and thistles”, and how could I offer that hardship with Christ?
Solomon asked for wisdom to labour at his side. Do I pray before my work, and what would change if I did?
Colossians says “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.” Which part of my daily work have I kept apart from him?
The people of Nazareth could not see God in a familiar carpenter. Whom do I fail to respect because I think I already know them?

lead: This Sunday’s readings are about walls coming down and a people made one. Isaiah sees a messenger running over the mountains with good news for the ruins of Jerusalem: “Your God reigns.” In Acts, Peter on a rooftop in Joppa is told in a vision, “What God has made clean, you must not call profane,” and the way opens for the first Gentiles to be baptized. Ephesians says that Christ is our peace, who has broken down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile and made them one household of God. In John, on the night before he dies, Jesus prays for all who will believe through the apostles’ word: “that they may all be one.” The words to watch are peace, near and one. The Risen Lord does not gather a crowd of individuals; he builds one body, and he asks his Father that its unity may be a sign to the world.

r.h: How beautiful are the feet of the messenger
set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the people of Judah in exile in Babylon in the sixth century before Christ. Many scholars think they come from a prophet of the exile who stands in the tradition of Isaiah of Jerusalem. The great promise of these chapters is a new exodus: God himself will lead his people home.

Jerusalem lies in ruins, and watchmen stand on what is left of its walls. Today’s poem imagines the moment when a runner appears on the hills with the news that the exile is over. It comes just before the fourth Servant song (52:13–53:12), and the Church has always read the two together.
str: v. 7: the messenger on the mountains: peace, good news, salvation, “Your God reigns.”
v. 8: the sentinels sing: they see the Lord returning to Zion.
vv. 9–10: the ruins are told to sing; the Lord bares his holy arm before the nations.
vv. 11–12: the command to go out from Babylon, purified, carrying the vessels of the Lord; not in haste, for the Lord goes before and behind.
kw: One who brings glad tidings. The Greek translation uses the verb euangelizomai, from which comes the word “gospel”. St Paul quotes this verse for the preachers of Christ (Romans 10:15).
The heart of the message: not a new king of Judah, but God himself as king. Jesus begins his preaching with the same news: “The kingdom of God has come near” (Mark 1:15).
Not only the end of war but wholeness, all things set right. The messenger announces peace before he announces salvation; Ephesians today will say that Christ himself is that peace.
vv: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news,
The feet are dusty from the road, yet they are called beautiful because of the message they carry. The Church sees here every preacher of the Gospel, beginning with the apostles.
for in plain sight they see the return of the Lord to Zion.
Literally “eye to eye”. The watchmen do not hear a rumour; they see. The apostles will later say, “we have seen with our eyes” (1 John 1:1).
The Lord has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations;
A warrior rolls back his sleeve to act. Isaiah 53:1 asks, “to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”, and the answer there is the suffering Servant.
For you shall not go out in haste,
The first exodus was in haste (Exodus 12:11). This one will be in peace, with God as guard before and behind, like the pillar of cloud.
ch: St Paul quotes v. 7 when he asks how anyone will believe unless preachers are sent (Romans 10:15), and the Church has always applied it to the apostles and to all who bring the Gospel. The Catechism explains that the word “Gospel” means good news, the news that God has sent his Son (CCC 422). Read beside today’s Gospel, the messenger’s cry “Your God reigns” is fulfilled when the Risen Lord sends his disciples into the world with the news of his victory.

r.h: What God has made clean
set: Acts 10–11 is the longest story in Acts, and Luke tells the main event twice: here and in Peter’s report at Jerusalem (11:4–17). It concerns Cornelius, a Roman centurion at Caesarea, a Gentile who feared God, prayed and gave alms. An angel has told him to send for Peter, and his messengers are on the road.

Peter is staying at Joppa, on the coast, in the house of Simon, a tanner (9:43). For Jewish believers, the food laws of Leviticus 11 were part of their faithfulness to the covenant, marking Israel as a people set apart for God. Peter, a faithful Jew, has kept them all his life. The vision is not about lunch alone: it prepares him to enter a Gentile’s house.
str: vv. 9–10: noon, the rooftop, prayer, hunger, a trance.
vv. 11–12: the heaven opened; a sheet with every kind of creature.
vv. 13–14: “Get up, Peter; kill and eat.” “By no means, Lord.”
vv. 15–16: “What God has made clean, you must not call profane.” Three times; the sheet taken up.
kw: Literally “common”, that is, not set apart for God. Peter uses it for food. He will soon learn to apply the lesson to people: “God has shown me that I should not call anyone profane or unclean” (10:28).
A state in which a person is taken out of ordinary awareness to receive a vision. Peter falls into it while praying, as Paul later did in the Temple (22:17).
An aorist verb: God has already done it. Peter is not asked to decide what is clean, but to accept what God has decided.
vv: Peter went up on the roof to pray.
Flat roofs were used for rest and prayer. The vision comes to a man at prayer, as Cornelius too received his message while praying (10:30).
But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is profane or unclean.”
Peter calls the voice “Lord” and still refuses. His refusal is not stubbornness but loyalty to what he had always understood as God’s will.
“What God has made clean, you must not call profane.”
The decisive word. Mark’s Gospel already notes that Jesus “declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19).
This happened three times,
Three times, as Peter had denied the Lord three times and was three times asked, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). A lesson that cuts so deep must be given more than once.
ch: The Church reads this vision as a turning point in the mission: the Gospel crosses the boundary between Jew and Gentile, and the Council of Jerusalem later confirms that Gentile believers need not take on the whole Mosaic law (Acts 15:7–11). The lesson is not that God’s gifts to Israel were bad: the law was holy and given by God (Romans 7:12). It is that in Christ God now gathers all nations into one people without asking them first to become Jews. The Catechism speaks of the Church as the new People of God, made up of Jews and Gentiles, called together in Christ (CCC 781), and the Second Vatican Council teaches that God’s call to the Jewish people is irrevocable (Nostra Aetate 4).

r.h: He is our peace
set: Ephesians is written in the name of Paul, from prison (3:1; 4:1). Many scholars think it was composed by a disciple of Paul who gathered his teaching into a great letter for several Churches; others hold that Paul wrote it himself. The Church reads it as part of the apostolic witness. Its theme is the Church as the one body of Christ.

The readers are Gentile Christians. In the first half of chapter 2 the letter has told them that they were dead in sin and have been made alive by grace (2:1–10). Now it reminds them what they were in relation to Israel: outsiders to the covenants. Many scholars think the “dividing wall” recalls the barrier in the Jerusalem Temple beyond which Gentiles could not go; an inscription from it, warning foreigners not to pass, has been found.
str: vv. 11–12: remember what you were: far from Christ, outside Israel, without hope.
v. 13: but now, brought near by the blood of Christ.
vv. 14–16: he is our peace: the wall broken down, one new humanity, one body reconciled through the Cross.
vv. 17–18: peace proclaimed to far and near; access in one Spirit to the Father.
vv. 19–22: no longer strangers: fellow citizens, household, a temple built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone.
kw: The wall between two groups. The letter names it at once: “the hostility between us”. Christ has not destroyed Israel; he has destroyed the hostility.

The right of entry, used of being brought into the presence of a king. Through Christ both Jew and Gentile have access to the Father in one Spirit: a verse in which Father, Son and Spirit are named together.
The stone at the corner, or perhaps the keystone, which holds the whole building in line. Christ is the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22).
vv: being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise,
The Gentiles’ poverty is described by what Israel had: citizenship, covenants, hope. The promises belong first to Israel; the Gentiles are brought into them.
But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.
“Far” and “near” are the words of Isaiah 57:19, which v. 17 will quote. The blood of the Cross closes the distance.
For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
Not “he brings peace” but “he is our peace”. Peace is a person.
He has abolished the law with its commandments and ordinances,

This must be read with care. Paul elsewhere says the law is holy (Romans 7:12) and that faith upholds the law (Romans 3:31). What is ended is the law as a wall that kept the nations apart; Gentiles enter God’s people through Christ, not by first keeping the commandments that marked Israel off.
So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
The Gentiles do not form a second people beside Israel. They are made fellow citizens with the saints, joined to the people God had first chosen.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this passage where it speaks of the Jewish people: the Church believes that by his Cross Christ, our peace, reconciled Jews and Gentiles, making both one in himself (Nostra Aetate 4). The same document says that the Church draws sustenance from the root of that good olive tree onto which the wild branches of the Gentiles have been grafted (Romans 11:17–24). The Catechism uses this passage for the Church as the temple of God built on the apostles, with Christ as cornerstone (CCC 756). The Church is not built in place of Israel but on Israel’s promises, opened to every nation.

r.h: That they may all be one
set: John 17 is the prayer of Jesus at the end of the Last Supper, often called his “priestly prayer”. He has washed the disciples’ feet, given the new commandment, and spoken of his going to the Father. Now he lifts his eyes to heaven and prays: first for his own glorification (17:1–5), then for the disciples (17:6–19), and in today’s verses for all who will believe through their word.

In other words, Jesus prays here for us. Every believer since the apostles is included in “those who will believe in me through their word”. Here Jesus says plainly that he is praying for believers not yet born.
str: vv. 20–21: for all future believers: that they may be one, as Father and Son are one, so that the world may believe.
vv. 22–23: the glory given, so that they may be completely one, so that the world may know.
v. 24: “I desire that those also … may be with me where I am, to see my glory.”
vv. 25–26: the world has not known the Father; Jesus has made his name known, so that the Father’s love may be in them.
kw: “One” is neuter in Greek: not one person, but one thing, one communion. The model is the unity of the Father and the Son, and the means is being “in us”.
In John, glory is the radiance of God’s love, shown above all on the Cross. Jesus has given this glory to his disciples: the share in his life that makes them one.
Before anything was made, the Father loved the Son. The disciples are drawn into a love older than creation.
vv: “I ask not only on behalf of these, but also on behalf of those who will believe in me through their word,
Faith comes through the apostles’ word. The Church is apostolic: we believe because they preached.
that they may all be one. As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.
Unity is not only a good for the Church; it is a witness to the world. Division among Christians makes it harder for the world to believe.
The glory that you have given me I have given them, so that they may be one, as we are one,
The unity of Christians is not achieved by agreement alone. It is a gift of the glory of Christ, received in the Spirit.
Father, I desire that those also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory,
The prayer looks beyond this life. The final goal of unity is to be with Christ and see his glory.
so that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.”
The last words of the prayer. Its goal is love: the Father’s love for the Son dwelling in the disciples.
ch: The Second Vatican Council begins its decree on ecumenism by citing this prayer and teaches that division among Christians openly contradicts the will of Christ and is a scandal to the world (Unitatis Redintegratio 1–2). St John Paul II took the title of his encyclical on ecumenism, Ut Unum Sint (1995), from v. 21. The Catechism teaches that Christ always gives his Church the gift of unity, but the Church must always pray and work to maintain, reinforce and perfect it (CCC 820). St Cyril of Alexandria, commenting on this chapter, teaches that believers are made one body with Christ and with one another through sharing in his holy flesh in the Eucharist (in substance).

qa: Does Ephesians 2:15 mean that the law of Moses was bad?

No. The law was given by God and is “holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). The letter means that the law, as a wall separating Jews from Gentiles, no longer decides who belongs to God’s people. In Christ the Gentiles are brought near without first becoming Jews. The Church teaches that God’s gifts and call to the Jewish people are irrevocable (Romans 11:29; CCC 839).
Do Catholics still keep food laws?

The Church does not bind Christians to the food laws of Leviticus, following Acts 10 and the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15). Christians do keep fasts and abstinence, not because foods are unclean, but as acts of penance and love. All food is a gift of God to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4).
If Jesus prayed for unity, why are Christians still divided?

Jesus’ prayer has not failed: the Church is one in Christ, and the Catholic Church believes this unity subsists in her (CCC 820). But Christians have sinned against unity, on many sides, over many centuries (CCC 817). The Council teaches that there can be no true ecumenism without conversion of heart, and it calls prayer for unity the soul of the whole ecumenical movement (Unitatis Redintegratio 7–8).
rite: The Sixth Sunday of Resurrection falls in the last stretch of the season before the Ascension, and the Church’s prayer turns toward the gift of the Spirit who makes the Church one. For the St Thomas Christians of India this Gospel has a special weight. The one community that received the faith from Mar Thoma is now found in several Churches, Catholic and Orthodox and others. The Lord’s prayer “that they may all be one” makes our reunion a matter of prayer, patience and love, not of blame.

In the Holy Qurbana the priest prays for the peace and unity of the Church, and as the anaphora begins the people give one another the peace. That sign is a small answer to today’s readings: those who were far and near give peace to one another before they approach the one altar of the Lord.
study: Isaiah calls the messenger’s dusty feet beautiful. Who brought the Gospel to me, and how can I carry it to someone else this week?
Peter needed three times to hear “What God has made clean, you must not call profane.” Whom do I treat as unclean or beneath me?
Ephesians says Christ is our peace, who broke down the dividing wall. What wall in my family or parish needs to come down?
Jesus prayed for us “that they may all be one.” What can I do, in prayer and in action, for unity among Christians?

lead: Today the Church keeps the feast of two apostles, Philip and James, and the readings trace the road of an apostle from deliverance to mission. Israel on the far shore of the sea sings, “I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously.” Wisdom pictures the righteous, once mocked, standing with great confidence before those who despised them. Paul says, “woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel,” and tells how he became all things to all people. In John, Jesus comforts his disciples on the night before his death and answers Thomas: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” The words to watch are song, confidence and way. The apostles sang of a victory that was not theirs, endured the scorn of the world, and spent their lives showing others the way that is a person.

r.h: I will sing to the Lord
set: Exodus 14 tells how Israel, pursued by Pharaoh’s army, passed through the sea on dry ground while the waters returned upon the Egyptians. Chapter 15 answers that deliverance with song. Many scholars consider this “Song of the Sea” one of the oldest poems in the Bible. A short refrain sung by Miriam and the women with tambourines closes the chapter (15:20–21).
Israel did nothing to win this victory: they were told to “stand firm” and “keep still” (14:13–14). The song is therefore pure praise. It is a song about God, not about the singers.
str: v. 1: the opening cry: I will sing; horse and rider thrown into the sea.
vv. 2–3: who the Lord is: my strength, my salvation, my God, my father’s God; a warrior, whose name is the Lord.
vv. 4–5: what he has done: chariots and army sunk like a stone.
v. 6: the right hand of the Lord, glorious in power.
kw: Literally “he has risen up high”, a Hebrew doubling for emphasis. God is exalted above every power that set itself against him.
“He has become my salvation” (v. 2). The noun comes from the same root as the name Yehoshua, Joshua, Jesus: “the Lord saves”.
Literally “a man of war”. The image is of God fighting for those who cannot fight for themselves. The Lord’s war ends in a song, not in boasting.
vv: “I will sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.
The first song of the redeemed in the Bible. The Book of Revelation shows those who have conquered singing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3).
The Lord is my strength and my might, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father’s God,
Personal and ancestral at once: “my God” and “my father’s God”. The faith received from the fathers becomes the singer’s own.
The Lord is a warrior; the Lord is his name.
The verse joins power and name. The name revealed to Moses at the bush (3:14–15) is now known by what God has done.
your right hand, O Lord, shattered the enemy.
The right hand is the hand of strength and action. Christians confess that the Risen Christ is seated at the right hand of the Father.
ch: In the Easter Vigil of the Roman rite this song follows the reading of the crossing of the sea, because the exodus is the great figure of Christ’s passage from death to life and of our passage through the waters of Baptism. The Catechism teaches that the crossing of the Red Sea, a true liberation of Israel, announces the liberation wrought by Baptism (CCC 1221). The apostles were the first to sing the new song: the enemy overthrown was not an army but death itself.

r.h: The righteous will stand with great confidence
set: The Book of Wisdom was written in Greek, most likely in Alexandria, in the century or so before Christ. Chapter 2 gave the speech of the ungodly, who plot against the righteous man because his life rebukes theirs: “let us test what will happen at the end of his life; for if the righteous man is God’s child, he will help him” (2:17–18). The Church has always heard in those words the mockery at the foot of the Cross (Matthew 27:43).

Chapter 5 shows the reversal at the judgment. The same scoffers now see the righteous standing with confidence, and they confess their mistake. This is one of the clearest Old Testament witnesses to the hope that God will vindicate the just beyond death.
str: vv. 1–2: the righteous stands with confidence; the unrighteous are shaken at his unexpected salvation.
vv. 3–5: their confession: we mocked him; why is he counted among the children of God?
vv. 6–7: we strayed from the way of truth; we never knew the way of the Lord.
kw: Boldness, openness of speech, the frankness of one who has nothing to hide. The righteous, once silenced, now stands before his accusers without fear. In Acts the apostles preach “with all boldness” (Acts 4:29, 31).
The scoffers had denied that the righteous man was God’s child (2:18); now they see him numbered among the children of God. Jesus calls the peacemakers “children of God” (Matthew 5:9).
The scoffers confess that they did not know “the way of the Lord” (v. 7). Today’s Gospel answers them: Jesus is the way.
vv: Then the righteous will stand with great confidence in the presence of those who have oppressed them
To “stand” is the posture of one acquitted at the judgment. The apostles, once flogged and scorned, stand now in glory.
they will be amazed at the unexpected salvation of the righteous.
Unexpected to the scoffers, not to God. They had thought that the end of the righteous was dishonour.
We thought that their lives were madness and that their end was without honor.
The world often judges the saints this way. St Paul writes, “We are fools for the sake of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4:10).
So it was we who strayed from the way of truth,
The confession comes too late for those who refused, but it is written for us while there is time.
ch: The Church reads this passage on the feasts of martyrs and apostles because it describes their story: rejected in this world, vindicated by God. The apostles, says the Catechism, were chosen as witnesses of the Resurrection and became the foundation stones of the Church (CCC 642). Ancient tradition holds that both Philip and James gave their lives for Christ. Their confidence was not in their own strength but in the God who raised Jesus, the Righteous One.

r.h: Woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel
set: Paul founded the Church at Corinth around the year 50 and wrote this letter a few years later from Ephesus. In chapters 8–10 he deals with food offered to idols, and urges the “strong” to give up their rights for the sake of the weak. Chapter 9 is his own example: as an apostle he had the right to be supported by the community, but he gave it up so as not to hinder the Gospel.

Today’s verses explain why. Preaching is not a career Paul chose; it is a charge laid on him. His only “reward” is to offer the Gospel without charge, and to become all things to all people for its sake.
str: vv. 16–17: an obligation is laid on me; woe to me if I do not preach.
v. 18: my reward: to preach without charge.
v. 19: a slave to all, to win more.
vv. 20–22: to the Jews as a Jew; to those outside the law as one outside it; to the weak, weak.
v. 23: all for the sake of the gospel, to share in its blessings.
kw: A compulsion laid on him from outside. Paul did not volunteer; the Risen Lord seized him (Philippians 3:12).
The charge of a steward who manages his master’s house. Paul is a steward of the mysteries of God (4:1), not the owner of the Gospel.
The word of the merchant who makes a profit, used five times in vv. 19–22. The profit Paul seeks is people won for Christ.
vv: woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel!
The apostle cannot keep silent. The prophets felt the same: Jeremiah says the word was like a fire shut up in his bones (Jeremiah 20:9).
but if not of my own will, I am entrusted with a commission.
A steward does not own what he hands out. Paul’s only reward (v. 18) is to give the Gospel without payment, as it was given to him.
I have made myself a slave to all, so that I might win more of them.
He describes his mission in the words of the Lord, who came “not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45).
am under Christ’s law
Paul’s flexibility is not lawlessness. He is bound by the law of Christ, which is love (Galatians 6:2).
I have become all things to all people, that I might by all means save some.
Not changing the Gospel to please people, but changing himself to reach them.
ch: St Augustine, writing to St Jerome, explains that Paul became all things to all not with the cunning of a deceiver but with the love of one who feels with others (in substance). The Second Vatican Council quotes Paul’s “woe to me” when it teaches that the Church is missionary by her very nature (Ad Gentes 1–2), and St Paul VI in Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975) says that the Church exists in order to evangelize (no. 14). Philip, who brought Nathanael to Jesus (John 1:45–46) and brought the Greeks who wished to see him (12:20–22), is an apostle of this kind: one who leads others to the Lord.

r.h: I am the way, and the truth, and the life
set: The scene is the Last Supper. Jesus has washed his disciples’ feet, Judas has gone out into the night, and Jesus has said that he is going where they cannot follow now, and that Peter will deny him (13:36–38). The disciples are afraid. Today’s words begin the long farewell discourse of John 14–17.

Two apostles speak in this chapter. Thomas asks about the way (14:5), and just after our reading Philip says, “Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied” (14:8). Today’s feast of St Philip and the Gospel’s question from Thomas, our father in faith, meet in the same conversation.
str: v. 1: do not let your hearts be troubled; believe in God and in me.
vv. 2–3: many dwelling places in the Father’s house; I go to prepare a place and will come again.
v. 4: you know the way.
v. 5: Thomas: we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?
v. 6: I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me.
kw: The same verb is used of Jesus himself, troubled in spirit before Lazarus’s tomb (11:33) and at the betrayal (13:21). He who was troubled for us tells us not to be troubled.
From the verb menō, “to remain, abide”, one of John’s key words. The Father’s house is not a place of temporary lodging but of abiding.
Thomas asks for a road; Jesus gives himself. The first Christians called their faith “the Way” (Acts 9:2).
vv: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me.
Faith in Jesus is placed beside faith in God. The comfort Jesus gives is not a promise that nothing hard will happen, but trust in a person.
In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.
There is room. No one who comes to the Father through Christ is turned away for lack of space.
I will come again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, there you may be also.
The goal of the Christian life is not a place but being with Christ.
Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”
Thomas speaks for every honest disciple. His question draws out one of the greatest sayings in the Gospel. The same Thomas will later confess, “My Lord and my God!” (20:28).
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
He is the way because he is the truth, God’s faithful revelation, and the life, God’s own life shared with us.
ch: St Augustine summarizes this verse: as God, Christ is the homeland we are going to; as man, he is the way by which we go (in substance). The Catechism opens its section on life in Christ by saying that the first and last point of reference of catechesis will always be Jesus Christ himself, “the way, and the truth, and the life” (CCC 1698). The Church teaches that Christ is the one mediator and way of salvation, and also that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know him may be saved by his grace working in ways known to God (CCC 846–848).

qa: Which James is this?

The Roman tradition identifies today’s apostle as James the son of Alphaeus (Matthew 10:3), often called James the Less, and has also identified him with James “the brother of the Lord”, leader of the Church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19). Many Eastern traditions and many modern scholars distinguish the two. The Church does not require one view. He is not James the son of Zebedee, the brother of John.
Why are Philip and James celebrated together?

In the Roman tradition their relics were placed together in the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles in Rome in the sixth century, and so they came to share a feast. Many calendars, ours among them, keep them together.
Does “No one comes to the Father except through me” mean that non-Christians cannot be saved?

Jesus is the one way to the Father, and all who are saved are saved through him. But the Church teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ or his Church, yet seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will as their conscience shows it, may attain salvation by his grace (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). This does not lessen the Church’s duty to proclaim Christ, as Paul says today: “woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel!”
rite: For the Syro-Malabar Church, today’s Gospel is a family conversation. Thomas, whom we call our father in faith, asks the question, and the Lord answers with the words that sum up the Gospel. The ancient name of our tradition, Mar Thoma Margam, the Way or Law of Thomas, recalls that the faith we received is not a set of ideas but a road walked behind Christ.

The feast of apostles reminds us that we are an apostolic Church. Philip and James, like Thomas, left everything, carried the Gospel far from home, and, as ancient tradition holds, gave their lives for it. In this season of Resurrection we pray that the Church in India may proclaim Christ with the same confidence and love.
study: Israel sang after a victory they did nothing to win. When did I last thank God for a deliverance that was entirely his gift?
Wisdom describes the righteous mocked as fools. Am I ready to be thought foolish for Christ?
Paul says, “woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel!” How do I share my faith with those around me?
Thomas asked, “How can we know the way?” What is my honest question to the Lord today, and do I trust him to answer?

lead: Both readings look to the end. Second Peter says that the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and that we wait for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home. In Mark, Jesus says that no one knows the day or the hour, and gives one command three times: keep awake. In these last days before the Ascension, the Church remembers that the Lord who goes up to heaven will come again, and that the time between is a time for watchful, holy living.

r.h: New heavens and a new earth
set: Second Peter is written in the name of the apostle Peter as his last testament (1:14). Many scholars think it was written by a disciple in Peter’s name some decades after his death, drawing on the Letter of Jude; others defend Petrine authorship. The Church has received it as Scripture since the fourth century, though some early writers were hesitant. In chapter 3 the writer answers scoffers who say, “Where is the promise of his coming?” (3:4). His answer: God is not slow but patient, “not wanting any to perish” (3:9).
str: v. 10: the day of the Lord comes like a thief; the heavens pass away; the earth is laid bare.
vv. 11–12: what sort of people ought you to be? Holy and godly, waiting for and hastening the day.
v. 13: according to his promise, new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.
kw: Jesus’ own image for his unexpected coming (Matthew 24:43), used also by Paul (1 Thessalonians 5:2). The point is not menace but surprise: be ready at every hour.
A bold word: Christians can “hasten” the day by holy lives, prayer and repentance. The early Church prayed Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22).
vv: the earth and everything that is done on it will be disclosed.

Textual note: the Greek manuscripts differ here. The oldest read “will be found” (that is, laid bare before God), which the NRSV renders “disclosed”; many later manuscripts read “will be burned up”, which the POC follows. Either way, nothing will remain hidden from God.
what sort of persons ought you to be in leading lives of holiness and godliness,
The teaching about the end is never for idle speculation. It leads at once to a question about how we live now.
But, in accordance with his promise, we wait for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.
The promise is Isaiah’s (65:17; 66:22). The end is not destruction for its own sake but renewal: a world where justice finally dwells.
ch: The Catechism cites this verse when it teaches that at the end of time the visible universe itself will be transformed, so that the world itself, restored to its original state, may be at the service of the just (CCC 1043, 1047). The Second Vatican Council adds that the expectation of a new earth must not weaken but rather stimulate our concern for cultivating this one (Gaudium et Spes 39). The Christian waits for the end by working for justice now.

r.h: Keep awake
set: Mark 13 is Jesus’ last long discourse before his Passion, spoken on the Mount of Olives opposite the Temple. He has foretold the Temple’s destruction and spoken of trials, false messiahs, and the coming of the Son of Man. Today’s verses end the discourse. After many signs, the final word is not a timetable but a command: keep awake.
str: v. 32: no one knows the day or hour, not even the Son, but only the Father.
v. 33: beware, keep alert.
v. 34: the parable of the man on a journey, the servants with their work, the doorkeeper.
vv. 35–37: keep awake: evening, midnight, cockcrow, dawn; what I say to you I say to all.
kw: Literally “do not sleep”, to stay wakeful through the night.
Used three times in vv. 34–37. In Gethsemane Jesus will ask Peter, James and John to “keep awake” with the same verb, and will find them sleeping (14:34–37).
vv: But about that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
A verse the Church has always taken seriously (see the question below). It forbids every attempt to calculate the date of the end.
each with his work,
Watching is not idleness. The servants keep watch by doing the work each has been given.
in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or at dawn,

The four watches of the night in the Roman reckoning. Mark’s Passion story moves through the same hours: the supper in the evening (14:17), Gethsemane in the night, Peter’s denial at cockcrow (14:72), and the handing over to Pilate at dawn (15:1).
And what I say to you I say to all: Keep awake.”
The command is not only for the four disciples on the mountain but for the whole Church in every age.
ch: The Catechism explains that Christ’s human knowledge, united to the divine wisdom of the Word, enjoyed the fullness of understanding of the eternal plans he had come to reveal; what he said he did not know in this matter, he elsewhere declared he was not sent to reveal (CCC 474). The Church therefore never sets dates for the end, but lives each day in watchful hope (CCC 673).

qa: How can the Son not know the day or the hour?

The Church teaches that Jesus has a true human mind as well as his divine nature. Some Fathers explain the verse by his human knowledge; others say he did not know it as something he had come to reveal. The Catechism teaches that in his human knowledge, joined to the divine wisdom, Christ knew the eternal plans fully, and that what he said he did not know, he was not sent to reveal (CCC 474). The verse teaches us humility: the date belongs to the Father.
study: Second Peter asks, “what sort of persons ought you to be?” What would I change in my life if I took the Lord’s coming seriously today?
In the parable each servant keeps watch by doing his own work. What work has the Lord given me to do while I wait for him?

lead: Both readings speak of love that imitates God. Ephesians tells the baptized to be imitators of God, as beloved children, and to live in love as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us. In John, Jesus gives his commandment, “love one another as I have loved you,” and calls his disciples no longer servants but friends. On the eve of the Ascension the Lord leaves his friends one law to keep until he comes again: the law of his own love.

r.h: Imitators of God, as beloved children
set: Ephesians is written in the name of Paul. Many scholars think a disciple of Paul composed it; others hold that Paul wrote it himself. The Church reads it as part of the apostolic witness. Chapters 4–6 draw out the way of life that follows from being one body in Christ. Just before this reading the letter says, “be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ has forgiven you” (4:32). Today’s verses continue: forgiven children should resemble their Father.
str: vv. 1–2: imitate God; live in love as Christ loved us, a fragrant offering.
vv. 3–4: what has no place among saints: impurity, greed, vulgar talk; instead, thanksgiving.
v. 5: no inheritance in the kingdom for the impure and the greedy, who are idolaters.
kw: From the word that gives us “mimic”. Children copy their parents. Here believers are called imitators of God himself; elsewhere in the New Testament they are told to imitate Christ and the apostles.
The language of Old Testament sacrifice, whose smoke was a “pleasing odour” to the Lord (Exodus 29:18). Christ’s self-giving on the Cross is the true sacrifice, pleasing to the Father.
vv: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children,
The command is possible only because we are already beloved. We do not earn God’s love by imitating him; we imitate him because we are loved.
and live in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
“Live” is literally “walk”: love is a daily road. Its measure is the Cross.
but instead, let there be thanksgiving.
The remedy for an unclean tongue is not silence but thanksgiving. The Greek word is eucharistia.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the moral life of Christians is rooted in their dignity as children of God, called to imitate the Father’s holiness (CCC 1694, quoting this verse). The sacrifice of Christ, the “fragrant offering”, is made present in every Holy Qurbana, and the Church offers herself with it (CCC 1368).

r.h: I have called you friends
set: These words belong to the Last Supper discourse, just after the image of the vine and the branches (15:1–10). Jesus has told the disciples to abide in him as branches abide in the vine. Now he explains what abiding means: keeping his commandment, which is love. The passage begins and ends with the command “love one another” (vv. 12, 17).
str: v. 11: my joy in you, your joy complete.
vv. 12–13: my commandment: love one another as I have loved you; no greater love than to lay down one’s life.
vv. 14–15: you are my friends; no longer servants.
vv. 16–17: I chose you to bear fruit that lasts; love one another.
kw: In the Old Testament Abraham is called the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8), and the Lord spoke to Moses “as one speaks to a friend” (Exodus 33:11). Jesus gives this title to all his disciples.
The initiative is the Lord’s. Disciples in Jesus’ time usually chose their rabbi; here the Master chooses his disciples.
vv: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
The measure is new: not “as yourself” but “as I have loved you”.
No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
Spoken a few hours before the Cross. Jesus does not only teach this love; he is about to show it.
but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.
Friendship is shown by sharing secrets. The disciples are friends because Jesus has opened to them the heart of the Father.
fruit that will last,
The fruit is love, and love that comes from Christ does not pass away (1 Corinthians 13:8).
ch: The Catechism cites this commandment when it teaches that Jesus makes charity the new commandment, loving his own “to the end” and so making manifest the Father’s love (CCC 1823). It also teaches that chastity blossoms in friendship, and cites “I have called you friends” (CCC 2347).

study: Ephesians calls me to imitate God “as beloved children”. Do I live as someone already loved, or as someone trying to earn love?
Jesus calls his disciples friends. What would change in my prayer if I spoke to him as a friend?

lead: On the Thursday of the sixth week of Resurrection our Church keeps the Ascension of the Lord, and the four readings show a master taken up and disciples sent out. In Second Kings, Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, and Elisha, who would not leave him, receives a double share of his spirit. In Acts, the Lord is lifted up before the apostles’ eyes, a cloud takes him from their sight, and two men in white tell them that he will come again. First Timothy calls the Church to pray for everyone, because there is one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave himself for all. In Luke, the Risen Lord opens the disciples’ minds to the Scriptures, lifts his hands to bless them, and is carried up into heaven, and they return to Jerusalem with great joy. The words to watch are taken up, witness and bless. The Ascension is not an absence: the Lord goes ahead of us as our high priest, and his disciples are left with a promise, a mission and a blessing.

r.h: Elijah is taken up to heaven
set: Elijah the prophet of Tishbe stood alone for the Lord against the worship of Baal in the days of King Ahab, in the ninth century before Christ. At Horeb God told him to anoint Elisha as prophet in his place (1 Kings 19:16), and Elisha left his oxen and followed him (19:19–21). Now Elijah’s work is done.

The chapter is a journey: from Gilgal to Bethel, to Jericho, to the Jordan, and across it, retracing in reverse the road by which Joshua led Israel into the land. Three times Elijah tells Elisha to stay behind, and three times Elisha refuses. Groups of prophets, the “sons of the prophets”, know what is about to happen, but Elisha silences them.
str: vv. 1–6: the journey and Elisha’s threefold refusal: “I will not leave you.”
vv. 7–8: at the Jordan Elijah strikes the water with his mantle; the two cross on dry ground.
vv. 9–10: “Let me inherit a double share of your spirit”; the sign: if you see me taken.

vv. 11–12: the chariot of fire; Elijah ascends in a whirlwind; Elisha cries out and tears his clothes. ¶ In the verses that follow (2:13–15), Elisha takes up the fallen mantle, parts the Jordan himself, and the prophets say, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.”
kw: A storm wind, the sign of God’s presence. God answered Job “out of the whirlwind” (Job 38:1). Elijah does not climb to heaven; he is taken.
Literally “a mouth of two”, the portion of the firstborn son, who inherited twice as much as his brothers (Deuteronomy 21:17). Elisha is not asking to be greater than Elijah but to be his true heir.
The prophet’s cloak. Elijah threw it over Elisha when he called him (1 Kings 19:19); now it falls to him. The mantle is the sign of the mission handed on.
vv: “As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.”
Said three times (vv. 2, 4, 6). Faithfulness to the master to the very end is the condition for receiving his spirit.
Elisha said, “Please let me inherit a double share of your spirit.”
He asks for nothing for himself but the spirit for the mission. The Church hears in this the apostles waiting for the Spirit promised by the ascending Lord.
if you see me as I am being taken from you, it will be granted you;
Seeing the ascension is the condition for receiving the spirit. Luke stresses the same: the apostles saw him go (Acts 1:9–11), and then they received the Spirit.
a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them, and Elijah ascended in a whirlwind into heaven.

Elijah did not die in the ordinary way. Jewish tradition came to expect his return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5), and the Gospels see that hope fulfilled in John the Baptist (Matthew 17:12–13).
“Father, father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!”
Elisha calls Elijah the true strength of Israel, worth more than chariots and horses. The same words will be spoken over Elisha at his death (13:14).
ch: St Gregory the Great compares the two ascensions: Elijah was carried up in a chariot, as a servant needing help; the Redeemer ascended by his own power, needing no chariot (in substance, Homilies on the Gospels 29). Elijah went up into the sky; Christ entered heaven itself, the Father’s glory. Yet the pattern of the story shapes Luke’s telling: a master taken up while the disciple watches, and the spirit given to the one who saw. The Catechism teaches that Christ’s Ascension is his definitive entrance with his humanity into God’s heavenly domain (CCC 665).

r.h: As they were watching, he was lifted up
set: Acts is the second volume of Luke’s work, addressed like the Gospel to Theophilus (1:1). It opens by recalling that after his suffering Jesus presented himself alive to the apostles, “appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God” (1:3). He told them to wait in Jerusalem for the promise of the Father, the baptism with the Holy Spirit (1:4–5).

Today’s verses tell the Ascension itself, on the Mount of Olives (1:12). The scene closes the time of the appearances and opens the time of the Church: from now on the Lord will act through the Spirit and through his witnesses.
str: v. 6: the apostles’ question: is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?
vv. 7–8: not the times, but power: the Holy Spirit; witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.
v. 9: he is lifted up; a cloud takes him from their sight.
vv. 10–11: two men in white: why do you stand looking up? He will come in the same way.
kw: Those who have seen and testify. The word later came to mean those who bore witness with their blood: the martyrs. Verse 8 is the plan of the whole book of Acts, from Jerusalem to Rome.

In the Old Testament the cloud is the sign of God’s glory and presence, over Sinai and the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34). Daniel sees one like a son of man coming “with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13). The cloud does not hide Jesus in the sky; it receives him into the glory of God.
A passive verb: he was taken up by God. The same Jesus who was lifted up on the Cross is now lifted into glory.
vv: “Lord, is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?”

An honest question from faithful Jews who longed for God’s promises to Israel. Jesus does not mock the hope; he redirects it. The kingdom will come through the Spirit and through witness to all nations.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”
The last words of Jesus on earth in Luke’s writings are a mission. “The ends of the earth” reached India too, as our Church remembers with gratitude.
When he had said this, as they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight.
Luke stresses that they saw. The Ascension is not an idea about Jesus but an event witnessed by those who were with him.
“Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven?
A gentle rebuke. The disciples must not stand gazing at the sky; they have work to do on earth until he returns.
This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.”
“This Jesus”: the same Lord, in the same humanity. The Ascension already contains the promise of the Second Coming.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the cloud and heaven into which Christ is taken signify that his humanity has entered once for all into God’s glory (CCC 659), and that Christ, the head of the Church, precedes us into the Father’s glorious kingdom so that we, the members of his body, may live in the hope of one day being with him for ever (CCC 666). Since the Ascension, it adds, the coming of Christ in glory has been imminent, even though it is not for us to know the times (CCC 673). Pope St Leo the Great preached that what was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments (in substance, Sermon 74): the Lord who is no longer seen in the flesh meets us now in the mysteries of the Church.

r.h: One mediator between God and humankind
set: First Timothy is one of the three “Pastoral Letters”, written in the name of Paul to his co-worker Timothy, who leads the Church at Ephesus. Many scholars think they were written by a disciple of Paul after his death, to carry his teaching into a new generation; others defend Paul’s authorship. The Church receives them as part of the apostolic witness.

Chapter 2 begins the instructions for the Church’s worship. The first concern is prayer for everyone, including rulers, at a time when Christians were a small and often suspected minority in the Roman Empire.
str: vv. 1–2: pray for everyone, for kings and all in authority, so that we may live a quiet and peaceable life.
vv. 3–4: God our Saviour desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
vv. 5–6: one God, one mediator, Christ Jesus, himself human, who gave himself a ransom for all.
v. 7: Paul appointed herald, apostle and teacher of the Gentiles.
kw: One who stands between two parties to bring them together. Christ can do this because he is both: God from God, and “himself human”. He is the one mediator; any other mediation in the Church depends wholly on his.
The price paid to set a captive at liberty. The word echoes Jesus’ own saying that the Son of Man came to give his life “a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Here it is “for all”.
Petitions made on behalf of others. The Church’s prayer is not only for her own members but for the whole world.
vv: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for everyone,
“First of all”: prayer for others comes first in the Church’s worship. Four words for prayer, and one object: everyone.
for kings and all who are in high positions,
The Christians prayed for rulers who did not share their faith and sometimes persecuted them. Prayer for those in authority is a Christian duty in every age.
who desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
God’s will to save is universal. That is why the Church’s prayer must be universal too.
For there is one God; there is also one mediator between God and humankind, Christ Jesus, himself human,
“Himself human”: even now, ascended, Christ remains man. He has taken our nature into heaven and intercedes for us there (Hebrews 7:25).
who gave himself a ransom for all
No one is excluded from the price he paid. To pray for all is to pray in the direction of the Cross.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 4 when it teaches that God desires all to be saved and so wills that Christ be proclaimed to all (CCC 74, 851), and v. 5 when it calls the Cross the unique sacrifice of Christ, the one mediator between God and men (CCC 618). The Second Vatican Council teaches that Mary’s role in the Church in no way obscures or diminishes this unique mediation of Christ, but shows its power (Lumen Gentium 60). The reading fits the Ascension: the one mediator, who has gone up to the Father in our human nature, “always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25; CCC 667).

r.h: While he was blessing them, he was carried up into heaven
set: These are the last verses of Luke’s Gospel. On Easter Sunday evening the Risen Lord has appeared to the eleven and those with them in Jerusalem, shown them his hands and feet, and eaten a piece of broiled fish before them (24:36–43). Now he teaches them and leads them out to Bethany, on the Mount of Olives.

Read on its own, Luke’s Gospel seems to place the Ascension on the evening of Easter, while Acts speaks of appearances over a longer period (Acts 1:3). The same author wrote both. In the Gospel he gathers the Easter mysteries into one great day; in Acts he gives the longer story (see the question below).
str: v. 44: everything written about me in the law, the prophets and the psalms must be fulfilled.
vv. 45–47: he opens their minds: the Messiah suffers and rises; repentance and forgiveness are proclaimed to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
vv. 48–49: you are witnesses; wait in the city for power from on high.
vv. 50–51: at Bethany he lifts his hands, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven.
vv. 52–53: they worship him, return with great joy, and bless God in the Temple.
kw: The same verb is used of the eyes of the disciples at Emmaus, opened in the breaking of the bread (24:31), and of the Scriptures opened on the road (24:32). The Risen Lord opens both the book and the mind.

Luke’s Gospel opened in the Temple with the priest Zechariah, who came out and could not speak to bless the people (1:21–22). It closes with Jesus lifting his hands in blessing, as the high priest blessed the people (Sirach 50:20–21), and with the disciples blessing God in the Temple.
The worship given to God alone. The disciples now give it to the Risen Lord.
vv: Then he opened their minds to understand the scriptures,

The whole Old Testament becomes clear in the light of Christ’s death and Resurrection. This is why, on Sundays and feasts such as today, the Holy Qurbana sets readings from the Law and the Prophets beside the Apostle and the Gospel; in this season one of these lessons is from Acts.
and that repentance and forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
The mission that Acts 1:8 describes is already given here: from Jerusalem to all nations.
so stay here in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high.”
The image of clothing recalls Elisha taking up the mantle of Elijah. The disciples will be clothed with the Spirit at Pentecost.
Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them.
The last gesture of Jesus on earth is a blessing. He leaves with hands raised over his Church, and the blessing has not ended.
While he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.

Textual note: the words “and was carried up into heaven” are missing in a few ancient manuscripts, and “they worshiped him” in v. 52 likewise. Most manuscripts have them, and modern translations, including the NRSV and the POC, keep them.
and they were continually in the temple blessing God.
The Gospel ends where it began, in the Temple, with praise. The Ascension leaves the disciples not in grief but in great joy.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ Ascension marks the definitive entrance of his humanity into God’s heavenly domain, from where he will come again, and that this humanity is meanwhile hidden from our eyes (CCC 665). Lifted up from the earth, he draws all to himself (John 12:32), and as the one priest of the new and everlasting covenant he intercedes constantly for us (CCC 662). St Augustine preached on the Ascension that Christ, though he ascended alone, is not separated from us: the head is in heaven, and he is with us still in his body (in substance).

qa: Did the Ascension happen on Easter day or later?

Luke wrote both accounts. In his Gospel he tells the events of Easter as one connected whole, ending with the Ascension; in Acts he says that Jesus appeared to the apostles over a longer period (Acts 1:3) before he was taken up. The Church follows Acts in her calendar, keeping the Ascension on the Thursday of the sixth week of Resurrection, and reads both texts as one witness: the Risen Lord truly appeared, taught, and was taken up into glory.
Is heaven a place above the sky?

The Bible uses the language of “up”, the cloud and the sky, because heaven is above us in dignity, not because it can be reached by travel. The Catechism explains that “heaven” here means the Father’s glory, into which Christ entered with his body (CCC 659–665). The Ascension is not a journey into space but the entrance of a human being, Jesus, into the life of God.
If Jesus has gone to heaven, how is he still with us?

He promised, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). He is with us through the Holy Spirit whom he sends, in his word, in the poor, and above all in the Holy Qurbana. The Catechism says that Christ, now in glory, is present in his Church in many ways, and most especially under the Eucharistic species (CCC 1373).
rite: The Syro-Malabar Church keeps the Ascension on the Thursday of the sixth week of the Season of Resurrection, following the reckoning of Acts 1:3. In the East Syriac tradition the feast is called Sulaqa, “the going up”. Latin dioceses in India keep the solemnity this year on the following Sunday, 9 May, so neighbours of the two traditions may celebrate it on different days: the mystery is the same.

The Season of Resurrection continues after the Ascension until Pentecost, and the Church prays during these days, as the apostles did with Mary in the upper room, for the coming of the Spirit. The readings of the Holy Qurbana today give a model for that prayer: Elisha’s plea for a double share of the spirit, the Church’s prayer for all people, and the disciples’ joy as they return to bless God.
study: Elisha would not leave his master and asked for a double share of his spirit. What do I ask of the Lord for my own mission?
The angels ask, “why do you stand looking up toward heaven?” Where am I gazing upward when I should be at work as a witness?
First Timothy says to pray for everyone, including those in authority. Whom do I leave out of my prayers?
Jesus’ last act on earth was to bless his disciples. How can I be a blessing to others this week?

lead: The Lord has ascended, and the Church begins nine days of waiting for the Holy Spirit. Both readings lift our eyes upward. Paul, in chains, says he has not yet reached the goal and presses on toward “the heavenly call of God”, literally the call from above. In John, the one who comes from above is above all, speaks the words of God and gives the Spirit without measure. The Christian life is a race toward the One who has gone ahead of us, and he has promised to send us his Spirit for the running.

r.h: Pressing on toward the goal
set: Paul writes to the Philippians from imprisonment (1:7, 13). Where he was held is debated: Rome, Ephesus and Caesarea have all been proposed. Just before this reading he has warned against those who urged Gentile believers to be circumcised (3:2–3), and he has listed his own advantages: born of Israel, a Hebrew, a Pharisee, so zealous that he persecuted the church (3:5–6). All this he now counts as loss compared with knowing Christ (3:7–8).
Then comes a careful word. Knowing Christ is not a finished achievement. Some in Philippi may have thought they were already perfect; Paul, the great apostle, says that he himself has not arrived.
str: v. 12: not yet obtained, not yet at the goal; I press on, because Christ has made me his own.
vv. 13–14: one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind, straining forward, running for the prize.
v. 15: the mature think this way; where you think differently, God will make it clear.
kw: The same verb Paul used six verses earlier for himself as “a persecutor of the church” (3:6). Once he pursued Christians; now he pursues Christ. The energy is the same; the direction has been turned around.

Paul plays on the word: he strives to grasp, because he has already been grasped. “Christ Jesus has made me his own.” Our effort answers a hold that Christ laid on us first, on the road to Damascus and at our Baptism.

A runner leaning his whole body toward the line. St Gregory of Nyssa built on this word his teaching that the soul’s growth in God never ends: whoever finds God is drawn to seek him still more (in substance, Life of Moses).
vv: but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own.
Grace comes first, and it does not make us idle. Paul never says, “Christ has seized me, so I may rest.” He says, “so I run.”
forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead,

Paul does not forget the mercy shown to him; he speaks of it often. What he leaves behind is both his old pride and the weight of his old sin. The persecutor could have been crushed by his past. Forgiven, he looks forward.
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the heavenly call of God in Christ Jesus.
The Greek speaks of the “upward call” (anō klēsis). In the week of the Ascension the picture is clear: the One who called us has gone up, and the prize is to be where he is.
ch: The Church teaches that the grace of final perseverance is a gift to be asked for, and that her children rightly hope for it (CCC 2016). Paul’s words guard against two errors: the despair that says the race is too long, and the pride that says the race is already won. The novena to the Holy Spirit, which many begin today, is the Church running this race on her knees, asking for the strength only the Spirit gives.

r.h: The one who comes from above is above all
set: These verses follow the last witness of John the Baptist in this Gospel: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30). Ancient manuscripts had no quotation marks, and it is not clear whether vv. 31–36 continue the Baptist’s words or are the evangelist’s own reflection; many scholars think the latter. They gather up themes from the conversation with Nicodemus earlier in the chapter (3:11–13): heaven and earth, testimony, belief and life.
str: v. 31: the one from above and the one from the earth.
vv. 32–33: his testimony refused, and accepted.
v. 34: the one sent speaks God’s words and gives the Spirit without measure.
vv. 35–36: the Father has given all to the Son; faith brings life, refusal remains under wrath.
kw: The same word Jesus used to Nicodemus: no one can see the kingdom without being born anōthen, “from above” or “anew” (3:3). The one who comes from above makes it possible for us to be born from above.
Literally “to set one’s seal”. Whoever accepts the Son’s testimony puts his own seal to the statement that God is true. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it is our signature under God’s word.

The Greek does not say plainly who gives. It may mean that God gives the Spirit to the Son without measure, or that the Son gives the Spirit without measure. John’s Gospel teaches both: the Spirit rests on Jesus (1:32–33), and the risen Jesus breathes the Spirit on his disciples (20:22).
vv: The one who comes from above is above all;
Repeated at the end of the verse, this sentence frames the whole passage. The Ascension shows it in action: he who came down from heaven has gone back above all.
He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.
The prophets received the Spirit for a task and a time. The Son has the fullness, and from that fullness he gives (1:16).
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life;

Not “will have” but “has”. Eternal life begins now, in faith, and is completed in glory. The word for God’s “wrath” (orgē) appears only here in this Gospel. It is not a temper but the sad result of turning away from the only source of life.
ch: St Augustine explains that the Spirit was given to the Son without measure, but to us by measure, each according to the gift he receives (in substance, Tractates on John 14). On the day of Pentecost Peter will say of the ascended Lord: “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you both see and hear” (Acts 2:33). This Gospel prepares us for that gift.

qa: Does “God’s wrath” mean that God loses his temper?
