No. God has no passions as we do. Scripture speaks of his wrath to show that he is not indifferent to evil and that refusing him has real consequences. In John the contrast is between life and its absence: the Son offers life, and the one who refuses him stays where he was, outside it. God’s will is that all should be saved (1 Timothy 2:4).
rite: Today is the First Friday. Many Syro-Malabar families keep it with confession, the Holy Qurbana and devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. The Gospel fits the day: “The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands” (3:35). The heart that loves us is the heart of the Son into whose hands everything has been given.
study: What lies behind me that I need to leave behind, whether old pride or old guilt, so that I can run forward?
Where do I see the Spirit given to me “by measure” in my daily life, and what gift do I ask for in this novena?

lead: Both readings ask for an undivided heart. Paul wants the Corinthians to serve the Lord without distraction, whether in marriage or in a life given wholly to God. John the Baptist tells those who come to the Jordan that repentance must bear fruit, and he promises one who will baptize “with the Holy Spirit and fire”. Pentecost is eight days away. The Spirit who is coming will make our hearts whole and set them on fire.

r.h: Unhindered devotion to the Lord
set: In chapter 7 Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him (7:1). Some there seem to have thought that married life was unworthy of a spiritual person. Paul defends marriage firmly (7:2–5) and calls it a gift, as celibacy is a gift (7:7). On the question of the unmarried he says he has “no command of the Lord” but gives his own opinion (7:25).

He writes with “the impending crisis” in view (7:26) and the sense that “the appointed time has grown short” (7:29). Whatever the timing, the point holds for every age: this world in its present form is passing away (7:31), and every Christian life must be lived toward the Lord who is coming.
str: v. 32a: I want you without anxieties.
vv. 32b–34: the unmarried and the married: one set of cares, and divided interests.
v. 35: not a restraint, but good order and undivided devotion to the Lord.
kw: From merimna, anxiety. Jesus used the related verb: “do not worry about your life” (Matthew 6:25). Paul’s concern is pastoral: he wants hearts at peace.
Literally “has been divided into parts” (v. 34). Paul is not blaming married people. He is describing honestly that a husband or wife has two sets of real duties, both holy.

Translated “unhindered” (v. 35). A related verb describes Martha, who “was distracted by her many tasks” (Luke 10:40). Paul wants every Christian, married or not, to have something of Mary’s place at the Lord’s feet.
vv: I want you to be free from anxieties.
Before he speaks of states of life, Paul speaks of the heart. The goal is not a particular way of life for its own sake, but a heart given to the Lord.
and his interests are divided.

This is realism, not complaint. Earlier in the same chapter Paul has praised married love and asked couples not to deprive one another (7:3–5). A married person serves the Lord through spouse and children; that service has its own cares.
I say this for your own benefit, not to put any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and unhindered devotion to the Lord.
The word translated “restraint” is literally a noose or halter (brochos). Paul refuses to tie anyone. A vocation is an invitation, never a trap.
ch: The Church honours both callings. “Both the sacrament of Matrimony and virginity for the Kingdom of God come from the Lord himself” (CCC 1620). St John Paul II taught that virginity for the Kingdom does not contradict the dignity of marriage but presupposes and confirms it (Familiaris Consortio 16). Consecrated life is a sign of the world to come; Christian marriage is a sign of Christ’s love for his Church. Each needs the other.

r.h: He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire
set: John the Baptist preaches in the wilderness of Judea, and people come to him from Jerusalem, all Judea and the region of the Jordan (3:1, 5). Matthew names Pharisees and Sadducees among them, two groups who disagreed on much, for example on the resurrection (Acts 23:8). In Luke the same warning is spoken to the crowds in general (Luke 3:7).
John speaks as the prophets of Israel spoke, calling his own people to conversion. His words are strong because the time is urgent: the one he has been sent to announce is near.
str: vv. 7–8: the warning, and the call to bear fruit.
v. 9: do not rely on descent from Abraham.
v. 10: the ax at the root.
vv. 11–12: the one who is coming: Spirit and fire, the winnowing fork.
kw: A change of mind and heart, a turning around of the whole person. John asks that it be visible: repentance has fruit.
with the Holy Spirit and fire
Fire both purifies and judges. Christians hear in these words the day of Pentecost, when “divided tongues, as of fire” rested on each disciple (Acts 2:3).
The tool for throwing threshed grain into the wind, so that the light chaff blows away and the grain falls. The coming one sorts what is real from what is empty.
vv: Bear fruit worthy of repentance.
Tears alone are not enough, and words alone are not enough. Conversion shows in changed lives: in Luke, John goes on to tell people to share, to be honest and not to extort (Luke 3:10–14).
God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham.

Many scholars hear a play on words in Hebrew and Aramaic, between “stones” (’ăbānîm) and “children” (bānîm). Being Abraham’s child is a gift of God, never a possession. Paul says that God’s calling of Israel is irrevocable (Romans 11:29); John’s warning is against presumption, and it reaches every Christian who trusts in a name rather than a life.
He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.
John’s baptism prepares; the baptism Jesus gives makes new. The one who seemed too great even to have his sandals carried will come down into the water himself (3:13–17).
ch: The Catechism explains that while water signifies birth and fruitfulness in the Spirit, fire symbolizes the transforming energy of the Holy Spirit’s actions, and it cites the Baptist’s words (CCC 696). In the Sacraments of Initiation the Church gives both: the water of Baptism and the anointing of the Spirit. This second day of the novena is a good time to ask that the fire be kindled again in us.

qa: Is John the Baptist condemning the Pharisees and Sadducees as a group?

John speaks to those in front of him, as a prophet calls his own people to conversion. The Gospels themselves show Pharisees who were open to Jesus, such as Nicodemus (John 3:1) and Gamaliel (Acts 5:34–39), and Paul was proud to have been a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). The Church teaches that the Jewish people may not be presented as rejected or accursed (Nostra Aetate 4). The warning against empty religion is meant for us.
study: What distracts me most from the Lord in my present state of life, and what “good order” would help me?
What fruit of repentance can others see in my life this week?

lead: The Lord ascended on Thursday, and next Sunday the Spirit will come at Pentecost. This Sunday stands in between, and its four readings are about being sent. In the Temple Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned, is purified by a burning coal and answers, “Here am I; send me!” In the upper room, while the disciples wait in prayer with Mary, Peter leads the community in choosing Matthias, so that the Twelve are complete before the Spirit comes. Paul sings of Christ who emptied himself and was highly exalted, so that every tongue should confess him Lord. In Mark the risen Lord sends the eleven into all the world, is taken up into heaven, and goes on working with them. The words to watch are send, witness and Lord. Today is the third day of the novena to the Holy Spirit.

r.h: Isaiah is purified and sent
set: King Uzziah of Judah (also called Azariah) reigned for many years, and his reign was strong and prosperous. He died about 740 before Christ, as the power of Assyria was rising in the north. Chronicles remembers that late in life he presumed to burn incense in the Temple and was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). In the year of an earthly king’s death, Isaiah sees the true King.

Many scholars think this vision is Isaiah’s call, placed here at the head of a section that opens in the first person (chapters 6–8). The scene is the Temple in Jerusalem, but the throne is God’s heavenly throne: the Temple can hold only the hem of his robe.
str: vv. 1–4: the vision: the Lord enthroned, the seraphs, the cry “Holy”, the shaking and the smoke.
v. 5: “Woe is me!”: the prophet sees himself before the King.
vv. 6–7: the burning coal from the altar touches his lips; guilt removed.
v. 8: “Whom shall I send?” “Here am I; send me!”
vv. 9–10: a hard commission: the people will hear and not understand.
vv. 11–13: “How long?” Until the land is emptied; yet a stump remains, a holy seed.
kw: Probably from śārap, to burn: “burning ones”. They cover their faces before God’s glory and their feet in humility. Even the purest creatures cannot look on God directly.
Hebrew has no simple word for “most”, so it repeats: “holy, holy, holy” means holiness beyond all measure. Holiness here is God’s utter otherness and purity, which fills the whole earth with glory.
The answer of Abraham (Genesis 22:1), of Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:4) and of the boy Samuel (1 Samuel 3:4). It is not an offer of skills but of oneself: “I am here, available.”
vv: I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lofty; and the hem of his robe filled the temple.
John’s Gospel says of this vision: “Isaiah said this because he saw his glory and spoke about him” (John 12:41). The Church reads Isaiah’s sight of the King as a glimpse of the glory of the Son.
Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.
The song of heaven, which the Book of Revelation hears again around the throne (Revelation 4:8). The Church has made it the song of every Eucharist.
Woe is me! I am lost, for I am a man of unclean lips,
Close to God, Isaiah does not feel proud but unclean, as Peter fell at Jesus’ knees and called himself a sinful man (Luke 5:8). The nearer we come to the light, the more we see our own shadows.
your guilt has departed and your sin is blotted out.
The coal comes “from the altar”. Purification is God’s work, not Isaiah’s; the prophet is cleansed before he is sent.
“Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And I said, “Here am I; send me!”

The “us” may be God speaking with the heavenly court around him. Many Fathers heard in it a hint of the Trinity. God asks; he does not force. Isaiah volunteers before he knows how hard the mission will be.
The holy seed is its stump.

Textual note: this last clause is not found in the ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, but it is in the Hebrew text and in the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran. The tree is cut down, but life remains in the stump. Isaiah will later say, “A shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse” (11:1).
ch: The Catechism quotes Isaiah’s cry, “Woe is me! I am lost”, to show that before the glory of the thrice-holy God we discover our own smallness and sin (CCC 208). The hard words of vv. 9–10 are taken up by Jesus to explain why many do not understand his parables (Matthew 13:14–15) and by Paul at the end of Acts (28:26–27). They describe a mystery of hardening that Paul says is partial and not final (Romans 11:25–26); they are never a curse on Israel.

St Ephrem, the harp of the Spirit, loved this coal. The seraph, he says, did not touch the fire with his fingers but took it with tongs, while we take the Fire into our mouths in the Bread (in substance, Hymns on Faith 10). The Syriac tradition speaks of the Holy Mysteries as the living coal, and every Holy Qurbana joins the song of the seraphs: “Holy, holy, holy”.

r.h: Matthias is added to the eleven apostles
set: The Lord has been taken up (1:9–11), and the disciples have gone back to the upper room in Jerusalem. Luke names the eleven and says that they “were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus, as well as his brothers” (1:13–14). The Spirit has not yet come. In this waiting time Peter, whom Jesus had told to strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32), stands up to lead.

Matthew tells the death of Judas differently: he hanged himself, and the chief priests bought a potter’s field with the money (Matthew 27:3–10). Both accounts agree that the money bought a field that came to be called the Field of Blood. Luke’s point is not to describe Judas in detail but to say that his place among the Twelve must be filled.
str: v. 15: Peter stands among about a hundred and twenty.
vv. 16–17: the Scripture about Judas had to be fulfilled; he had a share in this ministry.
vv. 18–19: an aside on Judas’s end and the Field of Blood.
v. 20: two verses from the Psalms.
vv. 21–22: the condition: a witness from the baptism of John to the Ascension.
vv. 23–26: two names, a prayer, the lot; Matthias is added to the eleven.
kw: The apostle is first of all a witness to the Resurrection (v. 22), one who has been with Jesus and can say what he saw. In later Christian use the word came to mean a martyr, one whose witness is sealed with his blood.

The word in v. 20, from Psalm 109:8 in its Greek form. In the later Church it became the word for the office of a bishop (episkopos, overseer). Here it names the apostolic charge that Judas abandoned.

The word frames the story: Judas “was allotted his share” in this ministry (v. 17), and the disciples “cast lots” (v. 26). Through Latin, this word gave the Church the word “clergy”: those who have received a share in the ministry.
vv: In those days Peter stood up among the believers (together the crowd numbered about one hundred twenty persons) and said,
Before Pentecost, before any sermon, Peter already acts as the one who strengthens his brothers. He does not decide alone; he puts the question before the community.
one of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection.

The Twelve recall the twelve tribes of Israel; Jesus had promised that they would sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Luke 22:30). Their number had to be whole when the Spirit came upon the renewed people of God.
Lord, you know everyone’s heart. Show us which one of these two you have chosen
“Lord” here most likely means Jesus, who chose the apostles in the beginning (1:2). The community proposes; the Lord chooses.
and the lot fell on Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles.

Casting lots was an ancient way of leaving the choice to God (Proverbs 16:33). This is the last time the New Testament mentions it. After Pentecost the Church decides with the Spirit’s guidance: “it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28).
ch: The Church sees in this choice the beginning of apostolic succession. The apostles took care to appoint others to continue their mission, and the bishops have succeeded them (CCC 861–862). St Clement of Rome, writing at the end of the first century, already says that the apostles appointed men and gave instructions that others should succeed them (in substance, 1 Clement 42–44). St John Chrysostom admires that Peter, the first of the apostles, did nothing on his own authority but acted with the whole company (in substance, Homilies on Acts 3). Authority in the Church is service, exercised in communion.

r.h: Every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord
set: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, and its church was the first Paul founded in Europe (Acts 16:11–40). The community was dear to him, but it was not without rivalries: later he begs two women, Euodia and Syntyche, to be of the same mind in the Lord (4:2). So Paul asks for unity and gives the deepest reason for it: the mind of Christ.

Verses 6–11 have the rhythm of a hymn. Many scholars think it was sung by Christians before Paul quoted it; others think Paul composed it himself. Either way it is one of the oldest witnesses to the faith that Jesus, who was in the form of God, became man and is now Lord.
str: vv. 1–4: if there is any encouragement in Christ, be of one mind; humility; look to the interests of others.
v. 5: let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus.
vv. 6–8: the way down: form of God, emptied, form of a slave, obedient to death on a cross.

vv. 9–11: the way up: highly exalted, the name above every name, every knee, every tongue: Jesus Christ is Lord. ¶ The hymn moves like a great V: down to the Cross, then up to the throne. The Ascension we have just celebrated is the top of the second stroke.
kw: Not a mere appearance but the real way of being. Christ was “in the form of God”, truly God, and took “the form of a slave”, truly a man. The same word is used for both, so that both natures are equally real.

A rare word, and its exact sense is debated: something to be grasped, or something to be clung to for one’s own advantage. Either way the sense is clear: Christ did not use his equality with God for himself.

From this verb comes the word kenosis. Christ did not cease to be God. As the ancient liturgy sings, he remained what he was and took up what he was not. He emptied himself by taking on our poverty, not by losing his divinity.

The Greek Bible used this word for the divine name of the God of Israel. Paul takes the words of Isaiah, where God says, “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear” (Isaiah 45:23), and applies them to Jesus. To confess Jesus as Lord is to confess him as God.
vv: Let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus,
The great hymn is introduced for a very practical reason: a quarrelling parish. Doctrine and daily life are not separate; the mystery of Christ is the pattern for how we treat one another.
who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be exploited,
Adam grasped at being like God (Genesis 3:5) and fell. Christ, who truly was equal with God, did not grasp, and he raised us up.
but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being born in human likeness.
The Son did not merely look human; “being born” is literally “becoming”. He became what we are.
even death on a cross.

Crucifixion was the death of slaves and rebels. In a Roman colony like Philippi, where citizens were proud that the law protected them from it, these words were shocking. The lowest point of the hymn is the place of our salvation.
Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name,
The verb is a strong one, “super-exalted”. The Ascension is the Father’s answer to the Son’s obedience. The humanity that was humbled is the humanity that is now enthroned.
every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
The confession of Christ does not take glory away from the Father; it gives glory to him. To kneel at the name of Jesus is to worship the one God.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 5–8 when it teaches the Incarnation: the Son of God assumed a human nature in order to accomplish our salvation in it (CCC 461). The Councils of the Church, from Nicaea onward, read this hymn as a witness that the Son is truly God and truly man. St Augustine gave a rule for reading the Gospels: some things are said of Christ according to the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, and some according to the form of a slave, in which the Father is greater (in substance, On the Trinity 1). Both are true of the one Lord.

r.h: Go into all the world and proclaim the good news
set: Today’s Gospel comes from what is called the longer ending of Mark (16:9–20). The two oldest complete Greek manuscripts of the New Testament, Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, end the Gospel at 16:8, and many scholars think these verses were added early by another hand, gathering up appearances told in the other Gospels and Acts. They are found in the great majority of manuscripts, and St Irenaeus already quotes them late in the second century. The Council of Trent received the sacred books “with all their parts” as they were read in the Church, and the Church accepts these verses as inspired Scripture.
Earlier in this ending the disciples refused to believe Mary Magdalene (16:11) and the two who had met him on the road (16:13). Now he appears to the eleven themselves at table.
str: v. 14: he appears to the eleven at table and rebukes their unbelief.
vv. 15–16: the mission: all the world, the whole creation; faith and Baptism.
vv. 17–18: the signs that will accompany those who believe.
v. 19: he is taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God.
v. 20: they go out everywhere; the Lord works with them.
kw: “The whole creation” (v. 15). The good news is not for one people only, nor even for human beings alone: Paul says that the creation itself waits for its release from decay, to share the glory of the children of God (Romans 8:19–21).
The same verb Luke uses for the Ascension (Acts 1:2, 11). The Lord is not simply gone; he has been received into the glory of the Father.
“The Lord worked with them” (v. 20), literally “working together with”. The Ascension does not leave the Church alone; it begins a new kind of presence in which the Lord acts through his disciples.
vv: he upbraided them for their lack of faith and stubbornness,
The founders of the Church were not heroes of faith from the first. The Lord sends men he has just had to rebuke. The mission rests on his choice, not on their merit.
Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.
Our Church remembers that one of the eleven at that table, the apostle Thomas, went as far as India.
The one who believes and is baptized will be saved;

Faith and Baptism belong together. The Catechism cites this verse in teaching that Baptism is necessary for salvation for those to whom the Gospel has been proclaimed and who have had the possibility of asking for it (CCC 1257). The verse does not add “and is not baptized” to the second half: what condemns is the refusal to believe.
they will pick up snakes in their hands, and if they drink any deadly thing, it will not hurt them;

Acts tells how Paul, bitten by a viper on Malta, shook it off and suffered no harm (Acts 28:3–6). These are promises of protection in the mission, not tests to perform. Jesus himself refused to put God to the test (Matthew 4:7; Deuteronomy 6:16).
was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.
The words of Psalm 110:1, “Sit at my right hand”. To sit at God’s right hand is to share his rule. The man Jesus, with his wounded and risen body, now reigns.
And they went out and proclaimed the good news everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by the signs that accompanied it.
The Gospel of Mark ends not with the disciples standing and looking up, but with them going out. The Lord in heaven and the disciples on earth work together.
ch: The Catechism opens its teaching on the Ascension with v. 19 (CCC 659). It teaches that the Ascension marks the definitive entrance of Jesus’ humanity into God’s heavenly domain, from where he will come again, and that he precedes us there so that we, his members, may live in the hope of being with him forever (CCC 665–666). St Leo the Great, preaching on this feast, said that what was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments (in substance, Sermon 74). The Lord who has gone up still touches us, in the Word and the Holy Mysteries.

qa: If the oldest manuscripts end Mark at 16:8, is today’s Gospel really Scripture?

Yes. Whether or not Mark himself wrote these verses, the Church has received them from very early times as part of the inspired Gospel, and they are read in her liturgy. Inspiration does not depend on our knowing which hand held the pen. The Church distinguishes the scholarly question of authorship from the question of canonicity, and on the second she is clear.
Why did the apostles replace Judas, but not James when he was killed (Acts 12:2)?

Judas left his place by betrayal; James kept his to the end and died a faithful witness. The Twelve were complete when the Spirit came at Pentecost, as the foundation of the renewed people of God, and the Book of Revelation sees the twelve names of the apostles on the foundations of the holy city (Revelation 21:14). After that the apostles’ mission continued through those they appointed, not by refilling the number of the Twelve.
When Christ “emptied himself”, did he stop being God?

No. The Church teaches that the Son remained fully God when he became fully man, without confusion and without separation (Council of Chalcedon, 451). He “emptied himself” by taking the form of a slave, hiding his glory and accepting our weakness and death. The God who cannot suffer chose to suffer in the flesh he made his own.
rite: In the Syro-Malabar calendar the Ascension of our Lord was kept on Thursday, 6 May, the fortieth day of the Resurrection season. This Sunday is the last of that season. Next Sunday, with Pentecost, the Church begins the Season of the Apostles, which remembers how the Spirit sent the apostles to the ends of the earth. Our Church carries in its very name the memory of that sending: the faith brought to India by Mar Thoma, one of the eleven at the table in today’s Gospel.

These days between Ascension and Pentecost are the Church’s first novena: the disciples in prayer with Mary, waiting. Many of our families and parishes pray the novena to the Holy Spirit through this week. In every Holy Qurbana we sing with Isaiah’s seraphs, “Holy, holy, holy”, and receive from the altar the living coal that cleanses lips and hearts. Each Qurbana ends with a sending; this Sunday reminds us that we, too, are sent.
study: Isaiah says “Here am I; send me!” before he knows the cost. Where is God asking me to say yes today?
The disciples prayed together with Mary while they waited for the Spirit. How will my family keep this week of waiting before Pentecost?
Paul gives the hymn of Christ’s humility to settle quarrels. Where in my parish or home is the mind of Christ most needed?
The Lord “worked with them”. In what ordinary work of mine can I ask him to work with me?

lead: Both readings speak of gifts that come before we ask. Paul thanks God, who chose the Thessalonians and called them through the Gospel, and he tells them to hold fast to what they were taught. At Jacob’s well a tired Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, and then offers her living water. In the week before Pentecost we know what that water is: the Gospel itself says that Jesus spoke of the Spirit (John 7:39).

r.h: God chose you as the first fruits for salvation
set: Paul founded the church in Thessalonica, the chief city of Macedonia, in the face of strong opposition (Acts 17:1–9). This second letter answers a confusion: some were saying “that the day of the Lord is already here” (2:2), perhaps on the strength of a letter falsely said to be from Paul. Many scholars think the letter itself was written by a disciple in Paul’s name; others hold that it comes from Paul, who signs it with his own hand (3:17).
Just before this reading Paul has warned of a lawless one who will deceive many before the end (2:3–12). Now the tone changes completely, from warning to thanksgiving.
str: vv. 13–14: thanksgiving: God chose you, sanctified you by the Spirit, called you through the Gospel, for glory.
v. 15: so stand firm and hold fast to the traditions.
vv. 16–17: a prayer: may the Lord and the Father comfort and strengthen you.
kw: The first part of the harvest, given to God as a sign that all belongs to him. Textual note: some manuscripts read ap’ archēs, “from the beginning”. In Greek the two readings differ by a single letter. The NRSV prints “first fruits” and gives “from the beginning” in its note; either way, the choice was God’s before it was theirs.
Literally “what is handed on”. Paul names two ways: “by word of mouth or by our letter”. The faith reached the Thessalonians as living teaching before any of it was written.
The word is related to Paraklētos, the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit in John’s Gospel (14:16, 26). God’s comfort is not only a feeling; it is strength “in every good work and word”.
vv: God chose you as the first fruits for salvation through sanctification by the Spirit and through belief in the truth.
The whole Trinity is at work: the Father chooses, the Spirit makes holy, and the call leads to “the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2:14). Our faith is our answer, but the first word is God’s.
stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by our letter.
Against a false message, Paul does not invent something new. He sends his readers back to what they already received. Faith is guarded by faithfulness to the apostles’ teaching.
who loved us and through grace gave us eternal comfort and good hope,
Hope is a gift “through grace”. In the end it is not our strength that keeps us standing, but the love of the Father and the Son.
ch: The Second Vatican Council cites v. 15 when it teaches that the apostles handed on what they had received, and warned the faithful to hold fast to the traditions they had learned by word of mouth or by letter (Dei Verbum 8). Sacred Tradition and Sacred Scripture flow from the same divine wellspring and move toward the same goal (Dei Verbum 9; CCC 80). They are not two rival sources but one living Word of God, entrusted to the Church.

r.h: Jesus gives living water
set: Jesus leaves Judea for Galilee, and “he had to go through Samaria”. Samaria lay on the direct road north, but in John “had to” often points to God’s plan as well. The Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim, near Shechem, and accepted only the five books of Moses as Scripture. Between them and the Jews there was a long history of mutual distrust, with wrongs remembered on both sides.

Sychar was near the field Jacob bought and gave to Joseph (Genesis 33:19; 48:22; Joshua 24:32). A well called Jacob’s Well is still shown there today. It is noon, the heat of the day. The disciples have gone to buy food, and Jesus sits alone by the well.
str: vv. 3–6: the journey, the well, Jesus tired at noon.
vv. 7–9: “Give me a drink”; the woman’s surprise.
v. 10: “If you knew the gift of God”: living water.
vv. 11–12: she misunderstands: no bucket, a deep well, our father Jacob.
vv. 13–15: water that ends thirst; “Sir, give me this water”.
kw: In everyday speech it meant running water from a spring, fresher than water stored in a cistern. The woman hears it so. Jesus means more: later he cries out that rivers of living water will flow from the believer’s heart, and John adds, “he said this about the Spirit” (7:38–39).
“The gift of God” (v. 10). In Acts the same noun is used for the Holy Spirit: “you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).
Jacob’s well is called a “spring” in v. 6 and a “well” or cistern (phrear) in vv. 11–12. Jesus promises a pēgē (v. 14): not water drawn up with effort, but a spring rising inside the one who drinks.
vv: Jesus, tired out by his journey, was sitting by the well.

St Augustine says that Jesus was tired for our sake: by his strength he created us, and by his weakness he came to seek us (in substance, Tractates on John 15). The Son of God knew a long road and a hot day.
Give me a drink.
The one who will give living water begins by asking. On the Cross he will say again, “I am thirsty” (19:28). He comes to us first as one in need, so that we may discover our own need.
If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.
Two things she does not yet know: the gift, and the giver. The rest of the chapter is her slow discovery of both, until her whole town says, “this is truly the Savior of the world” (4:42).
The water that I will give will become in them a spring of water gushing up to eternal life.
The verb “gushing up” is used elsewhere for leaping. The Spirit is not stagnant in us; he rises, moves, and carries us toward eternal life.
ch: The Catechism begins its teaching on prayer at this well. Jesus thirsts; his asking arises from the depths of God’s desire for us. Whether we realize it or not, prayer is the meeting of God’s thirst with ours; God thirsts that we may thirst for him (CCC 2560, drawing on St Augustine). The Catechism also teaches that the Spirit is the living water welling up from Christ crucified as its source and welling up in us to eternal life (CCC 694). Every Baptism is this well, and every Pentecost novena is the woman’s prayer: “Sir, give me this water.”

qa: Why does the Gospel say that Jews and Samaritans did not share things in common?

John explains the woman’s surprise for readers who did not know the region. Jews and Samaritans had been divided for centuries over the place of worship and over the Scriptures, and each side had grievances. Jesus crosses that line, as he crosses the line between a Jewish teacher and an unknown woman. He does not deny the difference; he will say that “salvation is from the Jews” (4:22). But he speaks with her as one to be given the gift of God.
study: What tradition of faith did I receive “by word of mouth” from my parents or grandparents, and how am I handing it on?
Jesus first asks the woman for a drink. When has someone’s need become, for me, the place where I met the Lord?

lead: Two things that can turn us in on ourselves: knowledge and possessions. In Corinth some Christians knew that idols are nothing and used that knowledge without caring for weaker believers; Paul says that love must govern what we know. In Luke a man asks Jesus to settle an inheritance, and Jesus tells of a rich man who spoke only to himself and forgot God. In both readings the question is the same: whom do my gifts serve?

r.h: Do not become a stumbling block to the weak
set: In a city like Corinth much of the meat sold in the market came from animals sacrificed in pagan temples, and temples had dining rooms where people held family and social meals. The Corinthians had asked Paul about this food (8:1). Some reasoned that, since “no idol in the world really exists” (8:4), they could eat anything anywhere.

Paul agrees that the idols are nothing. But he begins with a warning: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (8:1). Later he will forbid taking part in sacrificial meals as such (10:20–21). Here his concern is the brother or sister whose faith is still fragile.
str: v. 8: food does not bring us closer to God, or take us further away.
v. 9: take care that your liberty does not trip up the weak.
v. 10: an example: someone sees you eating in an idol’s temple.
vv. 11–12: the weak destroyed by your knowledge; to sin against them is to sin against Christ.
v. 13: Paul’s own resolve: I will never eat meat if it makes one fall.
kw: Literally a right or an authority. The Corinthians were proud of their right. Paul does not deny it, but in the next chapter he shows how he himself gave up his rights for the sake of the Gospel (9:12).
The inner judgment by which a person knows right and wrong. A weak conscience is not a wicked one; it is one not yet fully formed, and it can be wounded.

In v. 10 the Greek says literally that the weak conscience will be “built up” to eat idol food. Paul turns the Corinthians’ own word against them: your example will “build up” your brother, all the way to his ruin.
vv: But take care that this liberty of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.
A stumbling block is a stone on the path that makes someone fall. What is harmless for me may be the stone my brother trips over.
So by your knowledge those weak believers for whom Christ died are destroyed.
Paul measures the worth of a weak believer by the price paid for him: the death of Christ. No Christian is unimportant.
Therefore, if food is a cause of their falling, I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause one of them to fall.
Just before, Paul says that to sin against them is to “sin against Christ” (8:12). It is the lesson Paul learned on the Damascus road: Christ and his members are one.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 12 among the rules that guide conscience: charity always proceeds by way of respect for one’s neighbour and his conscience (CCC 1789). Paul gives the same teaching in Romans: “Do not let what you eat cause the ruin of one for whom Christ died” (Romans 14:15). The principle reaches beyond food: to drink, to speech, to what we post and share. Liberty is a gift of Christ, and love decides how it is used.

r.h: The parable of the rich fool
set: Jesus is on his long journey to Jerusalem (9:51), and the crowd has gathered “by the thousands” (12:1). He has just been speaking of fearless witness and of God’s care for those who trust him (12:4–12). A man interrupts with a family quarrel.

Teachers of the law were sometimes asked to settle such disputes, and the law of Moses gave rules for inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17). The man is not asking Jesus to judge fairly; he has already decided what Jesus should say.
str: v. 13: the request about the inheritance.
v. 14: Jesus refuses to be made a judge.
v. 15: the warning against all kinds of greed.
vv. 16–19: the parable: a great harvest, bigger barns, a conversation with his own soul.
v. 20: God speaks: “You fool!”
v. 21: the lesson: rich toward God.
kw: Literally “having more”, the desire for more and more. The Letter to the Colossians calls greed idolatry (Colossians 3:5): what we cannot stop wanting has become our god.

In the Bible a fool is not a person without intelligence; this man is clever with his crops. The fool is the one who lives as if God did not exist: “Fools say in their hearts, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 14:1).

The rich man speaks to his own psychē, “Soul, you have ample goods”. That night his psychē, his life, is demanded of him. The same word frames the story: he planned everything for his soul except the soul itself.
vv: for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.
Jesus does not say that possessions are evil. He says that life is not made of them. We are more than what we own.
And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.

He speaks only to himself. In his speech there is no God, no neighbour, no family: only “I”, “my” and “my soul”. Sirach describes the same man, who says, “I have found rest, and now I shall feast on my goods!” and does not know how soon he will die (Sirach 11:19).
You fool! This very night your life is being demanded of you. And the things you have prepared, whose will they be?
The Greek says literally “they are demanding your soul”, an indirect way of speaking of God’s action. The man worried about room for his crops; he never asked where his soul would go.
ch: St Basil the Great preached on this parable to the rich of his city: the bread you keep belongs to the hungry, and the coat in your chest to the one who has none (in substance, Homily on “I will pull down my barns”). The Catechism teaches that the tenth commandment forbids greed and the desire to amass earthly goods without limit (CCC 2536). To be “rich toward God” is to store up treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:20), and the way to heaven passes through the hands of the poor.

qa: Is it wrong to save money or plan for the future?

No. Prudence is a virtue, and Scripture praises Joseph, who stored grain in Egypt so that the land would not perish in the famine (Genesis 41:36). The rich man’s fault is not planning but planning only for himself, as if he were the owner of his life and of his goods. The question Jesus asks is not “Do you save?” but “For whom, and toward whom, do you live?”
study: Is there something I have a right to do that might cause a weaker brother or sister to stumble? How would love change my choice?
If my life were demanded of me tonight, what would I be “rich toward God” in?

lead: No one has ever seen God, says John, but when we love one another God lives in us, and he has given us of his Spirit. In the Gospel Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven at the hour of his glory and says what eternal life is: to know the Father and the One he has sent. In this week between the Ascension and Pentecost the two readings belong together. The Son has returned to the glory he had before the world began, and the Spirit he sends teaches us to know God by loving.

r.h: God is love; he has given us of his Spirit
set: The First Letter of John comes from the same circle as the Fourth Gospel. Tradition links it with the apostle John; many scholars think it was written by an elder of the community that treasured his teaching. It is written to churches shaken by a division: some had left (2:19), denying that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (4:2).
Against them the letter holds together three things: right faith in Jesus, love for one another, and the gift of the Spirit. Today’s passage weaves all three.
str: v. 12: no one has seen God; if we love, God lives in us.
vv. 13–16: how we know we abide in him: the Spirit, the confession of Jesus, love. “God is love.”
vv. 17–18: love made perfect gives boldness; perfect love casts out fear.
vv. 19–21: we love because he first loved us; no love for God without love for the brother or sister.
kw: The great word of John’s writings, used again and again in this passage. To abide is to stay, to make one’s home. God makes his home in us, and we in him.
“God is love” (vv. 8, 16). John does not say only that God loves, but that love is what God is. Love here is not first our feeling but God’s self-giving, seen in the sending of the Son (4:9–10).

The fear John speaks of “has to do with punishment”, the fear of a slave before a master. It is not the holy fear of God that Scripture praises as the beginning of wisdom. The more we love, the less we cower.
vv: No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God lives in us, and his love is perfected in us.
The same words open the Gospel’s statement that the only Son has made the Father known (John 1:18). The God no one has seen becomes visible, in a way, in a community that loves.
God is love, and those who abide in love abide in God, and God abides in them.
Perhaps the most famous sentence in the letter. It does not make love into God; it says that the God revealed in Jesus is love, and that whoever truly loves is living in him.
We love because he first loved us.

Textual note: some later manuscripts add an object, “we love him” or “we love God”. The shorter reading, followed by the NRSV, is wider: every true love in us, for God and for our neighbour, is an answer to his love.
ch: Pope Benedict XVI began his first encyclical with v. 16: “God is love, and those who abide in love abide in God, and God abides in them”; these words, he wrote, express with remarkable clarity the heart of the Christian faith (Deus Caritas Est 1). The Catechism teaches that God’s very being is love (CCC 221). St Augustine, preaching on this letter, gave his short rule, “Love, and do what you will”: when the root within is love, nothing but good can come from it (in substance, Homilies on the First Letter of John 7).

r.h: This is eternal life: that they may know you
set: The long discourse at the Last Supper (chapters 13–16) ends, and Jesus turns from his disciples to his Father. He prays aloud, first for himself (17:1–5), then for his disciples (17:6–19), then for all who will believe through their word (17:20–26). Christian tradition calls this the “priestly” prayer of Jesus (CCC 2747).

Throughout John’s Gospel the “hour” has been awaited. At Cana Jesus said, “My hour has not yet come” (2:4). Now he says, “the hour has come”. It is the hour of the Cross, which John sees as the hour of glory.
str: v. 1: Jesus looks up: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son.”
v. 2: authority over all people, to give eternal life.
v. 3: what eternal life is.
v. 4: the work on earth finished.
v. 5: the glory he had before the world existed.
kw: Not a clock hour, but the appointed time of the Father’s plan: the Passion, death, Resurrection and return to the Father, seen as one movement.
In the Old Testament God’s glory (kābôd) is his weighty, shining presence. In John the Cross is the place where that glory is most fully seen, because there love goes to the end (13:1).
Biblical knowing is not only information but personal communion. Eternal life is not a reward added after we know God; knowing him is eternal life, already begun.
vv: he looked up to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you,
The Son does not seek his own glory; he asks to be glorified so that he may glorify the Father. Their glory is one.
And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

Some in the fourth century used this verse to deny that the Son is truly God. St Augustine answered that we should read it as one confession: that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, as the only true God (in substance, Tractates on John 105). The Son is named with the Father as the one whom to know is life.
So now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had in your presence before the world existed.
The Son existed before the world, as the Prologue says (1:1). He asks to return to that glory, now as the Word made flesh. In the Ascension our human nature enters the glory of God with him.
ch: The Catechism teaches that when “his hour” came, Jesus prayed to the Father, and that this prayer of the hour fills the end times and carries them toward their consummation (CCC 2746–2749). Last Thursday we kept the Ascension; on Sunday the Spirit will come. Between them the Church prays with the Son’s own prayer: that we may know the Father, and so live.

study: John says that the God no one has seen becomes visible in our love for one another. Where can others see God in my family this week?
Jesus says eternal life is to know the Father. Am I growing in knowing God, or only in knowing about him?

lead: The two readings stand at the two ends of discipleship. John begins his letter with the joy of witnesses who heard, saw and touched the Word of life, and who share that life so that others may have fellowship with the Father and the Son. In Luke, Jesus turns to the crowds walking with him and tells them honestly what following him costs: the cross, the first place in the heart, all one has. The fellowship is a gift; the cost is the way to keep it. In this last week of the Resurrection season, both readings ask whether we have truly met the Risen One, and whether we will follow him all the way.

r.h: What we have seen and touched
set: The First Letter of John comes from the same circle as the Fourth Gospel, near the end of the first century. Tradition names the apostle John as its author; many scholars think it was written by an elder of the community that treasured his witness. The letter does not name its readers, but it is plain that some had left the community (2:19) and were denying that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh (4:2). These opening verses answer them before the letter has even greeted anyone: the life of God was not an idea; it was seen and touched.
str: v. 1: what was from the beginning, heard, seen, looked at, touched: the word of life.
v. 2: an aside: this life was revealed, and we testify to it.
v. 3: the purpose: that you may share our fellowship, which is with the Father and his Son Jesus Christ.
¶ The Greek sentence is long and breathless, and the main verb, “we declare”, arrives only in verse 3. The writer seems to stumble over his own wonder.
kw: The words recall the first line of the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), and the first line of Genesis. What the disciples touched in Galilee was the eternal Word.
A physical word: to feel with the hands. Luke uses the same verb when the Risen Lord says, “Touch me and see” (Luke 24:39). Faith rests on a real body, not on a vision.
A sharing in something held in common. It is the word for the life of the first community in Jerusalem (Acts 2:42) and for our share in the body and blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16).
vv: what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and touched with our hands, concerning the word of life
Four verbs climb from hearing to touching. The writer speaks for the apostolic witnesses, and the Church still speaks with that “we” whenever she proclaims the Gospel.
this life was revealed, and we have seen it and testify to it, and declare to you the eternal life that was with the Father
“With the Father” echoes John 1:1, “the Word was with God.” The life that appeared in time was with the Father before all time.
so that you also may have fellowship with us; and truly our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
There is no private road to the Father. We enter communion with God by entering the communion of those who saw and believed: the apostolic Church.
ch: The Second Vatican Council opens its Constitution on Divine Revelation with these very verses (Dei Verbum 1), because they say what revelation is: God showing himself so that we may share his life. The Catechism uses them to describe the joy of handing on the faith: the first disciples burned to proclaim Christ and invite every age to share their communion with him (CCC 425). St Augustine, preaching on this letter, recalls that the Risen Lord let his disciples touch his hands and side, and says that the Word of life was handled so that we might believe (in substance).

r.h: Count the cost
set: Jesus is on his long journey to Jerusalem (9:51), and the crowds are growing. He has just told the parable of the great dinner, in which the host’s house must be filled (14:15–24). Now he turns round to the people walking behind him. Walking with him in a crowd is not yet the same as being his disciple, and he wants them to know the difference.
str: vv. 25–27: two conditions: to put him before every human bond, and to carry the cross.
vv. 28–30: the parable of the tower: sit down and estimate the cost.
vv. 31–32: the parable of the king going to war.
v. 33: the conclusion: give up all your possessions.
vv. 34–35: salt that has lost its taste.
kw: A Semitic way of speaking that sets two loves side by side: to love one less than the other. Matthew gives the sense: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me” (Matthew 10:37). Jesus does not cancel the commandment to honour parents; he asks for the first place.
In verse 33 the word means to take leave of, to say goodbye. The disciple does not despise what he has, but holds it loosely, ready to let it go for Christ.
Literally “to become foolish”, from the same root as mōros, fool. Salt that has lost its savour is like a disciple who has lost his wisdom: nothing remains to give flavour.
vv: Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
Luke’s hearers knew what it meant to see a condemned man carry his cross to execution. Jesus speaks this on the road to Jerusalem, where he will carry his own.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and estimate the cost
The parables do not ask us to be calculating with God. They ask us not to begin lightly. Discipleship begun in enthusiasm must be finished in faithfulness.
Salt is good; but if salt has lost its taste, how can its saltiness be restored?
Salt in the ancient world was often impure, and its true salt could wash out, leaving only grey dust. A disciple who keeps the name but loses the life is like that.
ch: St Gregory the Great asks how we can be told to hate those we are commanded to love, and answers that we love them rightly when we refuse to listen to them whenever they would lead us away from God (in substance, Homilies on the Gospels 37). The Catechism takes up verse 33 when it teaches poverty of heart: Jesus bids his disciples prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544). Each state of life lives this differently, but no Christian is excused from it.

qa: Does Jesus really want us to hate our families?

No. The word “hate” is a Semitic way of saying “love less, put second”, as Genesis says that Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah” and then calls Leah “unloved” (Genesis 29:30–31). Jesus himself commands honour for parents (Mark 7:10). He asks for the first place, and a heart that loves God first loves its family better, not less.
study: The Letter of John speaks of hearing, seeing and touching. Where do I meet the Risen Lord in a way that is real and not only an idea?
What would it mean for me to “sit down and estimate the cost” of following Christ this year, in my family, my work and my money?

lead: On the feast of Mar Mathias Shleeha the four readings tell one story: God chooses, and he does not choose as we would. In Bethlehem Samuel looks at the tallest of Jesse’s sons and is told that the Lord looks on the heart; the youngest, out with the sheep, is anointed. In the upper room the believers pray to the Lord who knows every heart, and the lot falls on Matthias, a faithful man of whom Scripture says nothing else. Paul reminds the Corinthians that God chose the weak and the low so that no one might boast. And Jesus thanks his Father for revealing the mysteries of the Kingdom to infants. The words to watch are chosen and heart. Two days before Pentecost, the Church is made ready by restoring the Twelve.

r.h: The Lord looks on the heart
set: King Saul has disobeyed the word of the Lord, and Samuel has been told that the kingdom will be given to another (15:26–28). Samuel grieves for Saul, but God sends him to Bethlehem, to the house of Jesse, with a horn of oil (16:1). The journey is dangerous, since anointing a new king while Saul lives could be taken as treason; so Samuel goes under the cover of offering a sacrifice (16:2–3).
Bethlehem is a small town of Judah. Jesse is the grandson of Ruth the Moabite (Ruth 4:17). From this house, and from this town, the Messiah will one day be born (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:6).
str: vv. 4–5: Samuel at Bethlehem; the elders tremble; the sacrifice prepared.
vv. 6–7: Eliab, and the Lord’s word: not by appearance, but by the heart.
vv. 8–10: seven sons pass by; none is chosen.
v. 11: “Are all your sons here?” The youngest is keeping the sheep.
vv. 12–13: David is brought in and anointed; the spirit of the Lord comes upon him.
kw: To pour oil on a person and set him apart for God. The one anointed is the māšîaḥ, the “anointed one”, which comes into Greek as Christos. Every time we say “Christ” or “Messiah” we remember this horn of oil.
In Hebrew the heart is not only feeling but the centre of the person: thought, will and decision. God sees the whole person from within.
Literally “the small one”. The youngest son, given the sheep to mind, is the least likely heir. Scripture again and again passes over the eldest: Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and now David.
vv: the Lord does not see as mortals see; they look on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.
This is the key verse of the reading, and of the feast. The believers in Acts will pray with the same faith: “Lord, you know everyone’s heart.”
“There remains yet the youngest, but he is keeping the sheep.”
Jesse did not even think to call him. The future shepherd of Israel is found among the flocks, and Christ, born in David’s town, will call himself the good shepherd (John 10:11).
for we will not sit down until he comes here.
The Hebrew speaks of sitting down, or gathering round, for the sacrificial meal; the POC renders it “we will not eat”. Nothing begins until the one God has chosen is present.
and the spirit of the Lord came mightily upon David from that day forward.
The anointing with oil is the outward sign; the gift of the Spirit is what it means. The same pattern returns at the Jordan, when the Spirit comes upon Jesus (Luke 3:22; 4:18).
ch: The Church reads David’s anointing as a figure of Christ, the Son of David, anointed with the Holy Spirit (Acts 10:38). The Catechism explains that “Christ” means anointed, and that in Israel those consecrated for a mission from God were anointed in his name: kings, priests and, at times, prophets (CCC 436). On this feast the reading also teaches about every call: God’s choice does not follow rank or appearance, and those who choose ministers in the Church must look, as far as human beings can, at the heart.

r.h: The lot fell on Matthias
set: The scene lies between the Ascension and Pentecost. The eleven apostles, with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus and his brothers, are in the upper room devoting themselves to prayer (1:13–14). Before the Spirit comes, Peter rises to fill the place left empty by Judas.

The number twelve matters. Jesus chose the Twelve as a sign of the twelve tribes of Israel (Luke 22:30), the whole people of God gathered again. The Church that will be born at Pentecost must stand on that full foundation. When the apostle James is later killed (12:2), no one is chosen to replace him: the Twelve had to be complete once, as witnesses, at the beginning.
str: vv. 15–17: Peter rises among about one hundred twenty believers; Scripture had to be fulfilled concerning Judas.
vv. 18–19: an aside by Luke on Judas’ death and the Field of Blood.
v. 20: two verses from the Psalms.
vv. 21–22: the condition: a witness from the baptism of John to the Ascension.
vv. 23–26: two are proposed; prayer; the lot falls on Matthias.
kw: Judas “was allotted his share” (v. 17), literally his lot, and at the end “the lot fell on Matthias” (v. 26). The same word frames the whole reading. From it comes our word “clergy”: those whose lot is the Lord’s service.
The word of Psalm 109:8 in its Greek form. It is related to episkopos, overseer, from which comes “bishop”. Luke sees in the apostolic office a charge of oversight that must be handed on.
“Lord, you know everyone’s heart” translates this single Greek word, found in the New Testament only here and in 15:8. It is the prayer of 1 Samuel 16:7 on Christian lips.
vv: In those days Peter stood up among the believers (together the crowd numbered about one hundred twenty persons)
Peter, who denied the Lord three times, now leads the community. The number one hundred twenty is ten times twelve: a small Israel gathered round the Twelve.
one of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection.

The first task of an apostle is to witness to the Resurrection. Matthias had walked with Jesus from the Jordan to the Mount of Olives, though the Gospels never once mention his name. Faithfulness unseen is not faithfulness unknown to God.
“Lord, you know everyone’s heart. Show us which one of these two you have chosen
They do not ask God to bless their choice; they ask him to show his. The prayer probably addresses the Lord Jesus, who chose the first Twelve (1:2).
And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles.

Casting lots was an old way of leaving a decision to God (Proverbs 16:33). After Pentecost the Church never uses it again in Acts; she will choose with prayer, laying on of hands and the guidance of the Spirit (6:6; 13:2–3).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Lord Jesus gave his community a structure, choosing the Twelve with Peter as their head; representing the twelve tribes of Israel, they are the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem (CCC 765). The Second Vatican Council sees in this election the beginning of apostolic succession: the apostles took care to appoint successors, so that the mission entrusted to them would continue to the end of the world (Lumen Gentium 20). St John Chrysostom notes that Peter, though first, acts together with all, and leaves the choice to God in prayer (in substance, Homilies on Acts 3). Of Matthias’ later life we know little for certain. Eusebius reports that he was said to be one of the seventy disciples (Luke 10:1); later traditions place his preaching in various lands.

r.h: God chose what is weak
set: The Christians of Corinth were divided into parties, each boasting of a favourite teacher (1:12), and some prized eloquence and human wisdom. Paul answers with the message of the Cross, which looks like foolishness to the world but is the power of God (1:18). Now he asks them to look at themselves: their own calling proves his point.
str: v. 26: consider your call: not many wise, powerful or of noble birth.
vv. 27–28: God chose the foolish, the weak, the low and despised, things that are not.
v. 29: the purpose: that no one might boast before God.
v. 30: all is from God in Christ Jesus, who became our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption.
kw: Not first a vocation to a work but God’s call into Christ. Paul uses the word for the whole community: each of them was called by name.

The verb is repeated three times in two verses: God chose, God chose, God chose. It is the language of Israel’s election (Deuteronomy 7:6–7), not because they were many but because the Lord loved them.
A key word in Paul’s letters. The boasting he forbids is self-reliance before God. In the next verse he quotes Jeremiah 9:24: let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.
vv: not many of you were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.

“Not many”, not “none”: there were people of standing at Corinth too, such as Erastus, the city treasurer (Romans 16:23). But most were ordinary people, labourers, freed slaves, households of small means.
God chose what is low and despised in the world, things that are not, to reduce to nothing things that are
“Things that are not” are people the world counts as nobodies. God creates from nothing, and in his Church he raises up from nothing.
He is the source of your life in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption
Christ is not only our teacher of wisdom; he is himself our wisdom. All four gifts come to us not as achievements but in union with him.
ch: This reading suits the feast of a little-known apostle. The Church did not choose the most famous of the hundred and twenty; she prayed, and God chose Matthias. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, marvels that the world was won not by philosophers or orators but by fishermen and tentmakers (in substance). The Second Vatican Council teaches that all in the Church are called to holiness (Lumen Gentium 39–40): God’s call is not reserved for the gifted, and every gift is his.

r.h: Revealed to infants
set: Chapter 11 is a chapter of mixed response. John the Baptist sends from prison to ask whether Jesus is the one to come (11:2–3); some call Jesus a glutton and drunkard (11:19); the towns of Galilee where most of his miracles were done do not repent (11:20–24). At this low point Jesus turns to his Father in thanksgiving. The welcome he did not find among the important he finds among the little ones.
str: vv. 25–26: thanksgiving: hidden from the wise, revealed to infants.
v. 27: the Father and the Son know each other; the Son reveals the Father.
vv. 28–30: the invitation: come to me, take my yoke, find rest.
kw: Little children, too young to speak well. Here it means the humble and simple, those without learning or standing, like the fishermen who followed him.
A strong form of the verb “to know”: full, intimate knowledge. Only the Son knows the Father in this way, and he shares that knowledge with whom he chooses.
Not idleness but the rest that God gives, like the Sabbath rest. Jesus’ words recall Jeremiah 6:16: “and find rest for your souls.”
vv: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants
Jesus does not despise learning; he rejoices that God’s gift does not depend on it. Pride closes the heart that learning ought to open.
and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.
Here Matthew sounds like John’s Gospel. The Son’s choice is the source of every apostolic call, Matthias’ included.
“Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.
Many hear an echo of Wisdom’s invitation in Sirach: “Draw near to me, you who are uneducated” (Sirach 51:23). Jesus speaks as Wisdom in person.
ch: The Catechism draws on this thanksgiving to describe Jesus’ prayer: his exclamation “Yes, Father!” reveals the depth of his heart, his adherence to the Father’s good pleasure (CCC 2603). St Augustine often contrasts the proud wise of this world with the little ones to whom Christ reveals himself, and says that God’s mysteries are open to the humble (in substance). On the feast of an apostle this Gospel says where every mission begins: not in our talent, but in the Son’s will to reveal the Father through those he chooses.

qa: Acts says Judas fell headlong and burst open; Matthew says he hanged himself. Which is right?

The two accounts differ, and the Church has never hidden it. Matthew tells that Judas hanged himself and that the priests bought a potter’s field with the silver (Matthew 27:3–10); Luke, in an aside, tells that a field was acquired with the reward and that Judas fell headlong (Acts 1:18). Since ancient times readers have suggested that both memories can be held together, and that both preserve the name “Field of Blood”. What both teach is the same: the betrayal ended in ruin, and the place Judas left had to be filled.
Why did the apostles use lots? Is that not leaving things to chance?

For them it was the opposite of chance. They first set the conditions, chose two worthy men and prayed; then they let God decide between them. “The lot is cast into the lap, but the decision is the Lord’s alone” (Proverbs 16:33). After Pentecost, with the Spirit given, Acts never again shows lots being cast.
Was Matthias a full apostle, or only a replacement?

A full apostle. Luke says he “was added to the eleven apostles”, and from the next chapter the Twelve stand together (2:14). The Church keeps his feast as an apostle. Paul was also called an apostle by the Risen Lord, but in another way, as the apostle to the nations; the Twelve were the witnesses from the beginning.
rite: Our tradition calls the apostles Shleeha, “the sent ones”, and the Syro-Malabar Church, proud of its descent from Mar Thoma Shleeha, honours every one of the Twelve as a father in faith. In the Creed of the Holy Qurbana we confess one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church. Mar Mathias reminds us that the apostolic Church is not only the famous apostles, but also the faithful man chosen in prayer, of whom only one scene is told.

The feast falls two days before Pentecost, which opens the Season of the Apostles. The Twelve are complete again, gathered with Mary in prayer, waiting for the Spirit. This is a good day to pray for our bishops and priests, for those discerning a vocation, and for those who choose and form them, that they may look at the heart as the Lord does.
study: Samuel almost anointed the wrong son because he looked at appearance. Where do I judge people by what I see rather than by their heart?
Matthias followed Jesus for years without being named. What faithful service in my parish goes unseen, and how can I honour it?
Paul says God chose the weak to shame the strong. How does that change the way I see my own weakness?
The apostles prayed, “Show us which one you have chosen.” How do I bring my own big decisions to God in prayer?

lead: On this last day of the Resurrection season the Church honours Mary as Protectress of Harvest, and the readings are full of fields, grain and a coming gift. Exodus commands Israel to keep the festival of harvest, the feast of first fruits that would later be called Pentecost, which the Church celebrates tomorrow. Joel promises threshing floors full of grain after the locusts, and then something greater: God will pour out his spirit on all flesh. Paul looks at the great harvest of the nations and of Israel and declares that God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable. In Matthew the Father’s will is that not one little one be lost. The words to watch are harvest, pour out and mercy. Mary, who waited in prayer for the Spirit with the apostles, stands at the threshold of the feast.

r.h: The festival of harvest
set: These verses belong to the Book of the Covenant (Exodus 20:22–23:33), the first collection of laws given at Sinai. They set Israel’s year round three great pilgrim festivals, each tied to the farmer’s calendar and each turned into a memory of what God had done.

In the land of Israel barley ripens in spring and wheat some weeks later; grapes, olives and summer fruit are gathered in autumn. Israel was to bring the work of its hands before the Lord at each turning of the year. Later texts call the harvest festival the Feast of Weeks, kept seven weeks after the barley (Leviticus 23:15–16; Deuteronomy 16:9–10). In Greek it was called Pentecost, “the fiftieth day”.
str: v. 14: three times a year a festival for the Lord.
v. 15: Unleavened Bread in the month of Abib, the month of the Exodus; no one empty-handed.
v. 16: Harvest, the first fruits; and Ingathering at the end of the year.
kw: A pilgrim feast, from a root that may mean to go round or to dance. These were days when the people went up together to the Lord’s sanctuary.
“Ears of grain”: the month when the barley is in the ear, in spring. Israel’s new year of freedom began with the new grain.
The first and best of the crop, given back to God before the rest is used. The first fruits declare that the whole harvest is a gift.
vv: Three times in the year you shall hold a festival for me.
The year itself becomes a path of worship. Israel’s calendar teaches that time belongs to God.
No one shall appear before me empty-handed.
Not a tax but a thanksgiving. Those who have received from God come before him with something of what he gave.
You shall observe the festival of harvest, of the first fruits of your labor, of what you sow in the field.
This harvest feast is the one the New Testament calls Pentecost (Acts 2:1). On that day God gathered his own first fruits: about three thousand persons (Acts 2:41).
ch: The Church reads Israel’s feasts as fulfilled in Christ without being emptied. Paul calls the Risen Christ “the first fruits of those who have died” (1 Corinthians 15:20), and James says that God gave us birth by the word of truth “so that we would become a kind of first fruits of his creatures” (James 1:18). The Catechism teaches that on the day of Pentecost, when the seven weeks of Easter had come to an end, Christ’s Passover is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit (CCC 731). On a Marian feast of the harvest it is fitting to remember that the Church calls Mary the most excellent fruit of the redemption (CCC 508): in her, first and most fully, Christ’s work bore its harvest.

r.h: I will pour out my spirit
set: The book of Joel cannot be dated with certainty; many scholars place it after the Exile, when the Temple stood again. It begins with a terrible plague of locusts, which the prophet sees as a sign of the Day of the Lord, and with a call to fasting and repentance: “rend your hearts and not your clothing” (2:13).

Then the tone changes: “the Lord became jealous for his land, and had pity on his people” (2:18). Today’s verses are God’s answer. The land, the animals and the children of Zion are told not to fear. In the Hebrew Bible verses 28–29 begin a new chapter (3:1–2).
str: vv. 21–24: do not fear, soil, animals, children of Zion: the rain, the grain, the wine and oil.
vv. 25–27: the lost years restored; God in the midst of Israel; no more shame.
vv. 28–29: afterward: the spirit poured out on all flesh, on sons and daughters, old and young, slaves male and female.
kw: The autumn rain that softens the ground for sowing. The same Hebrew word can also mean “teacher”, and some ancient translations, including the Latin Vulgate, read “the teacher of righteousness”. The NRSV reads “early rain”.
The verb for pouring water or oil in abundance. God’s spirit is not given drop by drop but poured like the rain of verse 23.
Every human being, in weakness and mortality. The gift is no longer only for a prophet or a king, as with Samuel and David, but for the whole people, without regard to sex, age or status.
vv: Do not fear, O soil; be glad and rejoice, for the Lord has done great things!
The earth itself is addressed. The land that the locusts stripped will rejoice. Mary will sing the same: “the Mighty One has done great things for me” (Luke 1:49).
The threshing floors shall be full of grain, the vats shall overflow with wine and oil.
Grain, wine and oil are the three great gifts of the land. Christians cannot hear them without thinking of the bread and wine of the Holy Qurbana and the oil of anointing.
I will repay you for the years that the swarming locust has eaten
A verse of deep comfort. God does not only stop the loss; he restores what was lost.
Then afterward I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy
Peter quotes these verses on the day of Pentecost to explain what the crowd is seeing (Acts 2:16–21). Joel’s “afterward” has become “in the last days”.
ch: The Church hears in Joel the promise fulfilled at Pentecost, as Peter himself proclaims (Acts 2:17). The Catechism, teaching on the Holy Spirit in the time of the promises, sees the prophets awaiting a new outpouring of the Spirit on the whole people (CCC 715). The fruitfulness of the land and the outpouring of the Spirit belong together: the God who sends rain on the fields sends his Spirit on hearts. This is why the Church blesses fields and seed and prays for good harvests: the Creator of the earth is the Giver of life.

r.h: The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable
set: In Romans 9–11 Paul wrestles with a grief that touches him personally: most of his own people, Israel, have not accepted Jesus as the Messiah (9:1–5). Has God’s word failed? Paul’s answer grows chapter by chapter. Just before this reading he compares Israel to a cultivated olive tree and the Gentile believers to wild branches grafted in, and warns the Gentiles not to boast (11:17–24).
Now he reveals a “mystery”, a part of God’s plan once hidden and now made known. These verses are among the most important in the New Testament for how Christians must think of the Jewish people.
str: v. 25: the mystery: a partial hardening on Israel until the full number of the Gentiles comes in.
vv. 26–27: and so all Israel will be saved, as the prophets foretold.
vv. 28–29: enemies as regards the gospel, beloved as regards election: God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable.
vv. 30–32: disobedience and mercy for Gentiles and for Israel alike: God will have mercy on all.
kw: In Paul not a riddle but God’s saving plan, now revealed. Even Israel’s “no” has a place in the plan of mercy.
Literally “not to be regretted”. God does not change his mind about the gifts he gave Israel: the covenants, the law, the worship, the promises (9:4). This word is the heart of the reading.
The word returns four times in three verses, and the passage ends on it. Mercy, not merit, is the last word for Gentiles and Jews alike.
vv: a hardening has come upon part of Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in.
Paul says “part”, not all, and “until”, not forever. He himself, and all the first apostles, were Israelites.
And so all Israel will be saved
Paul does not explain how or when. He leaves it in God’s hands, as the doxology that follows shows: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (11:33).
As regards the gospel they are enemies of God for your sake; but as regards election they are beloved, for the sake of their ancestors
The Greek says only “enemies”; the words “of God” are supplied by the translation. However one renders it, Paul’s point is that Israel remains beloved by God because of the patriarchs.
for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.
The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse when it speaks of the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; Lumen Gentium 16).
For God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all.
No one can stand before God by his own record. All, Gentile and Jew, receive mercy as a gift.
ch: The Church teaches that the Jews remain very dear to God, for the sake of the patriarchs, since God does not take back the gifts he bestowed or the choice he made (Nostra Aetate 4, quoting this passage). The Catechism adds that the Jewish faith, unlike other religions, is already a response to God’s revelation in the Old Covenant, and it quotes Romans 11:29 (CCC 839). It also teaches that Christ’s glorious coming is linked to the recognition of the Messiah by “all Israel” (CCC 674). In 2015 the Holy See’s Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews took the very words of verse 29 as the title of a document on Catholic and Jewish dialogue. The Church never speaks of Israel as replaced: she is grafted on to Israel’s root.

r.h: Not one of these little ones
set: Chapter 18 is Matthew’s discourse on life in the community of disciples. It begins when the disciples ask who is greatest, and Jesus places a child among them (18:1–5). He warns against causing a little one to stumble (18:6–9). Today’s verses follow: the little ones are not to be despised, and the one who strays must be sought. Then comes the teaching on correcting a brother and on forgiving seventy-seven times.
str: v. 10: do not despise the little ones; their angels see the Father’s face.
vv. 12–13: the parable of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine.
v. 14: the Father’s will: that not one be lost.
kw: In Matthew, both children and the humble, ordinary disciples, those easily overlooked or easily led astray.
To wander, to be led off the path. Luke’s parable speaks of a sheep that is “lost” (Luke 15:4); Matthew speaks of one that has strayed, a member of the community who has wandered.
“It is not the will of your Father”: the same word as in the Our Father, “your will be done” (6:10). The Father’s will is that none be lost.
vv: Take care that you do not despise one of these little ones; for, I tell you, in heaven their angels continually see the face of my Father in heaven.
The little ones may be unimportant to us, but they are so important to God that their angels stand always in his presence.
What do you think? If a shepherd has a hundred sheep, and one of them has gone astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go in search of the one that went astray?
Verse 11 is missing in the NRSV. A few manuscripts add “For the Son of Man came to save the lost”, probably taken from Luke 19:10; the oldest manuscripts do not have it.
So it is not the will of your Father in heaven that one of these little ones should be lost.
In Luke the parable ends with joy in heaven; in Matthew it ends with the Father’s will, as a charge to those who care for the community.
ch: The Catechism cites verse 10 for the Church’s faith in guardian angels: from its beginning until death human life is surrounded by their watchful care and intercession (CCC 336). The Fathers loved the shepherd who goes to the mountains as a picture of the Word who came down to seek lost humanity. In Matthew the parable is also a rule for pastors and for every Christian: no one in the community may be written off.

qa: Does Romans 11 mean that the Jewish people are enemies of God?
