No. Paul says that in relation to the gospel many have not yet accepted it, and that this has opened the door to the Gentiles; but in the same breath he says they are “beloved” and that God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable. The Church teaches that the Jews may not be presented as rejected or accursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598, 839). Christians are to approach the Jewish people with respect, gratitude and love.
Why does the Syro-Malabar Church keep a feast of Mary for the harvest?

The Church of the East has long kept days asking Mary’s protection over the work of the fields, and this commemoration in mid-May belongs to that tradition. It is not a nature festival placed beside the faith: it asks the Mother of the Lord, who bore the true Bread from heaven, to pray for those who sow and reap, and for a just sharing of the earth’s fruits.
Do we each have a guardian angel?

The Church teaches that from its beginning until death human life is surrounded by the watchful care and intercession of angels, and that beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd leading him to life (CCC 336, quoting St Basil). Matthew 18:10 is one of the texts on which this faith rests.
rite: In our tradition Mary is honoured at the turning points of the farmer’s year, and this commemoration falls in the season of the first harvests. It also falls on the eve of Pentecost, Israel’s feast of harvest, when God gathered the first fruits of the Church. Mary was in the upper room with the apostles, praying for the Spirit (Acts 1:14). The Catechism says that she aided the beginnings of the Church by her prayers, imploring the gift of the Spirit (CCC 965).

It is a good day for farming families to pray in the Holy Qurbana for the fields, for rain in its season, for those who work the land and those who go hungry, and for a just sharing of the harvest. Tomorrow the Resurrection season gives way to the Season of the Apostles, and the Church, like a field ready for the sickle, waits for the Spirit.
study: Israel was told not to come before God empty-handed. What first fruits of my time, work or money do I bring to God?
Joel promises that God will restore “the years that the swarming locust has eaten”. What lost years or losses in my life do I need to entrust to God?
How do I speak about the Jewish people, and how does Romans 11:29 call me to change?
Who are the “little ones” in my parish who are overlooked or have strayed, and what can I do to seek them?

lead: Pentecost opens the Season of the Apostles, and its four readings show how God makes a people his own. At Sinai, in the third month after the Exodus, God offers Israel a covenant: they will be his treasured possession, a priestly kingdom and a holy nation. In Jerusalem, on the feast that remembered the harvest and, for many Jews, the gift of the Law, the Spirit comes with wind and fire, and the apostles speak so that every nation hears in its own language. Paul tells the Corinthians that the one Spirit gives many gifts for the common good. In John, Jesus promises that the Spirit of truth will guide his disciples into all the truth. The words to watch are covenant, fire and truth. What began at Sinai with one people is opened to all.

r.h: A priestly kingdom and a holy nation
set: Israel has crossed the sea, been fed with manna and given water from the rock. Now, in the third month, they reach the mountain where God first spoke to Moses from the bush (3:12). Here the covenant will be made and the Law given (chapters 19–24).

Later Jewish tradition came to celebrate the giving of the Law at Sinai on the Feast of Weeks, the harvest festival kept fifty days after Passover. That is why this reading stands beside Acts 2 today: the Church’s Pentecost is the new Sinai, where the law is written not on stone but on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).
str: vv. 1–2: arrival at Sinai, in the third month; Israel camps before the mountain.
vv. 3–4: God calls Moses: “I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.”
vv. 5–6: the offer: if you keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession, a priestly kingdom, a holy nation.
vv. 7–8: Moses sets the words before the elders; the people answer as one.
v. 9: God will come in a dense cloud, so that the people may hear and believe.
kw: A king’s private treasure, the jewels he keeps for himself. The whole earth is God’s, but Israel is his own jewel, chosen not to be proud but to serve.
A people set between God and the nations, as priests stand between God and the people. Israel’s calling is for the sake of the world.
Holy means set apart for God. Israel is to be different from the nations so as to show them who God is.
vv: You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.

The covenant begins with grace, not with a command. God first reminds Israel of what he has done; only then does he ask for their answer. The goal of the Exodus is not a place but a person: “to myself”.
you shall be my treasured possession out of all the peoples. Indeed, the whole earth is mine
Election is not favouritism. The God of the whole earth chooses one people so that through them he may bless all (Genesis 12:3).
but you shall be for me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.

St Peter applies these words to the baptized: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people” (1 Peter 2:9). The Church does not take Israel’s place; she is brought into Israel’s calling.
The people all answered as one: “Everything that the Lord has spoken we will do.”
A single voice, a single answer. At Pentecost the many languages will again make one confession of faith.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the chosen people was constituted by God as “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation”, and that the whole Church, the new people of God, shares in Christ’s priesthood (CCC 1539, 1546). The Second Vatican Council quotes 1 Peter 2:9 when it teaches the common priesthood of the faithful, by which the baptized offer spiritual sacrifices and share in offering the Eucharist (Lumen Gentium 10). Many Fathers saw in Sinai, with its fire, cloud and voice, a figure of Pentecost: there the Law was given on tablets of stone; here the Spirit writes it in hearts (in substance, St Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter 17).

r.h: Tongues as of fire
set: The disciples have been waiting in Jerusalem, as the Risen Lord told them, for the promise of the Father (1:4–5). The Twelve are complete again (1:26). Now comes the Feast of Weeks, called in Greek Pentecost, one of the three pilgrim feasts when Jews came from far and wide to the Temple. That is why the city is full of “devout Jews from every nation under heaven”.

Luke tells the event with signs from Israel’s Scriptures. Wind and fire recall Sinai, where the Lord descended in fire and the whole mountain shook (Exodus 19:18). The many languages recall Babel, where human pride ended in confusion and scattering (Genesis 11:1–9).
str: v. 1: the day of Pentecost; all together in one place.
vv. 2–3: a sound like wind; tongues as of fire resting on each.
v. 4: filled with the Holy Spirit, they speak in other languages.
vv. 5–11: the crowd from every nation hears God’s deeds of power in its own language.
vv. 12–13: amazement and mockery: “What does this mean?” “They are filled with new wine.”
kw: Literally “was being fulfilled”. Luke uses the word for the coming of a promised time (as in Luke 9:51). The feast itself reaches its fulfilment.
Luke uses pnoē, a blast of wind, beside pneuma, Spirit. In Hebrew one word, rûaḥ, means both wind and spirit, as in the breath that moved over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2).
The word of verses 6 and 8, the language one learned at home. The Gospel does not erase the languages and cultures of the nations; it speaks in each of them.
vv: When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place.
“All together”: the one hundred twenty, with the apostles and Mary (1:14–15). The Spirit comes to a community at prayer.
Divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them.
One fire, divided so that each receives it. The Spirit is given to the Church and to each member personally.
Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and residents of Mesopotamia
The list begins in the east, beyond the Roman Empire, in the lands where the Church of the East would grow. Our own Church’s tradition traces its family to these very regions.
in our own languages we hear them speaking about God’s deeds of power.
The content of their speech is praise: the mighty works of God. Babel tried to make a name for itself (Genesis 11:4); Pentecost proclaims the name of God.
ch: The Catechism teaches that on the day of Pentecost, when the seven weeks of Easter had come to an end, Christ’s Passover is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and that on that day the Holy Trinity is fully revealed (CCC 731–732). The Church, it says, was made manifest to the world on the day of Pentecost by the outpouring of the Spirit (CCC 1076). St Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching on Pentecost, contrasts the confusion of tongues at Babel, which scattered the proud, with the gift of tongues at Pentecost, which gathers all into one (in substance, Oration 41).

r.h: The same Spirit
set: The Corinthians were rich in spiritual gifts and proud of them. Some prized speaking in tongues above all and looked down on those without it (see chapters 12–14). Paul does not reject the gifts; he puts them in order. They come from one Spirit, they serve the one body, and the greatest of all, as chapter 13 will show, is love.
str: vv. 1–3: the test of the Spirit: no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit.
vv. 4–6: varieties of gifts, services and activities; the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God.
v. 7: each gift is a manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
vv. 8–10: a list of nine gifts.
v. 11: one Spirit gives to each as he chooses.
kw: Gifts of grace, from charis, grace. A charism is not a reward for holiness but a gift for service.
Perhaps the oldest Christian creed, spoken at baptism (Romans 10:9). In the Greek Old Testament Kyrios stands for the divine name. To call Jesus Lord is to confess him as God.
What benefits all together. A gift kept for oneself has missed its purpose.
vv: no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit.
Faith itself is the first gift of the Spirit. Every Christian who confesses Christ already shows that the Spirit is at work.
Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of services, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God
Spirit, Lord, God: Paul’s pattern is already Trinitarian. The unity of the Church reflects the unity of the one God in three persons.
To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
“To each”: no one in the Church is without a gift, and no gift is for private glory.
All these are activated by one and the same Spirit, who allots to each one individually just as the Spirit chooses.
The Spirit chooses, as the Lord chose Matthias. We do not choose our gifts; we receive them and put them to use.
ch: The Catechism teaches that charisms, whether extraordinary or simple and humble, are graces of the Holy Spirit which directly or indirectly benefit the Church, ordered to her building up, to the good of all and to the needs of the world (CCC 799). Charity is the true measure of them (CCC 800), and discernment of charisms belongs to those who lead the Church, who must not extinguish the Spirit but test everything (CCC 801; Lumen Gentium 12).

r.h: He will guide you into all the truth
set: These words are spoken at the Last Supper, on the night before Jesus died (John 13–17). Jesus is preparing his friends for his departure. They are full of sorrow. He tells them that his going is for their good, because only then will the Advocate come. Here come the last two of the five sayings about the Spirit in the Supper discourse (14:16–17; 14:26; 15:26; 16:7–11; 16:13–15).
str: vv. 5–7: sorrow at his going; it is to your advantage, for the Advocate will come.
vv. 8–11: the Spirit will prove the world wrong about sin, righteousness and judgment.
vv. 12–13: the Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth.
vv. 14–15: he will glorify me; all that the Father has is mine.
kw: One called to stand beside another: a defender in court, a helper, a comforter. Jesus has been their Advocate; he will send “another” (14:16).
A word from the law court: to expose, to bring to the light. The Spirit reverses the world’s verdict on Jesus. The one it condemned is shown to be righteous.
To lead along a road, as a guide leads travellers. The Spirit does not give a new Gospel; he leads the disciples deeper into the truth that is Christ (14:6).
vv: Nevertheless I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you
The disciples wanted Jesus to stay as he was. He gives them something greater: his presence within them through the Spirit.
about sin, because they do not believe in me; about righteousness, because I am going to the Father
The deepest sin is unbelief, refusing the light. Jesus’ going to the Father, through the Cross and Resurrection, is the Father’s verdict that he is righteous.
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth; for he will not speak on his own, but will speak whatever he hears
The Spirit speaks what he hears, as the Son speaks what he hears from the Father (8:26). The Trinity is a communion of listening and giving.
All that the Father has is mine. For this reason I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you.
The Spirit’s work is to make Christ known. Wherever the Spirit is truly at work, Christ is glorified.
ch: The Catechism gathers these promises: the Spirit of truth, the other Paraclete, will teach the disciples everything, remind them of all that Christ said, bear witness to him, lead them into all truth, glorify Christ, and prove the world wrong about sin, righteousness and judgment (CCC 729). Pope St John Paul II devoted a large part of his encyclical on the Holy Spirit, Dominum et Vivificantem (1986), to the words “he will convince the world concerning sin”. The Second Vatican Council teaches that through the Spirit the understanding of the apostolic Tradition grows in the Church, as she advances towards the fullness of divine truth (Dei Verbum 8).

qa: Did the apostles speak foreign languages, or did the crowd hear a miracle?

Luke stresses both: they “began to speak in other languages” (2:4), and each one “heard them speaking in the native language of each” (2:6). Whether the wonder was in the speaking or in the hearing, the sign is the same: the Gospel is for every people, in its own tongue. This is different from the gift of tongues at Corinth, which needed an interpreter (1 Corinthians 14:27).
Does the Spirit bring new revelations beyond Christ?

No. Jesus says the Spirit “will take what is mine and declare it to you” (16:14). The Church teaches that the Christian economy will never pass away and that no new public revelation is to be expected before the glorious coming of Christ (Dei Verbum 4; CCC 66). The Spirit leads the Church deeper into what Christ has revealed, so that its meaning is grasped more fully over the centuries.
Why is Pentecost linked to Sinai?

In Exodus, Israel reaches Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt, about the time of the harvest festival. Later Jewish tradition remembered the giving of the Law on the Feast of Weeks. Luke tells the coming of the Spirit with signs of Sinai: a sound from heaven, fire, a people gathered. For Christians, the Spirit fulfils what Jeremiah promised, a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34).
rite: With Pentecost the Syro-Malabar Church begins the Season of the Apostles (Shleeha), which remembers the Church’s first mission under the Spirit. It suits our Church that the list of nations at Pentecost begins with “Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and residents of Mesopotamia”: the Church of the East grew in those lands, and from that Church our ancestors in Malabar received their liturgy and their bishops for many centuries, while they kept the faith first preached, by our tradition, by Mar Thoma Shleeha, who was in the upper room (Acts 1:13).

At every Holy Qurbana, in the Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, the priest asks that the Holy Spirit come and rest upon the offering, bless it and sanctify it, for the pardon of sins and the hope of resurrection. Pentecost is not only a memory; it happens again on our altars and in us. This is a good day to renew our confirmation, the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit, and to ask what gift the Spirit has given each of us for the common good.
study: God reminded Israel, “I bore you on eagles’ wings,” before asking for obedience. What has God done for me that I need to remember before I answer him?
At Pentecost each one heard the Gospel in his own language. How can my family and parish speak the faith in the language of young people, the poor and those far away?
Paul says each one is given a gift for the common good. What gift has the Spirit given me, and how am I using it?
Jesus said his going away was for his disciples’ good. Where in my life has a loss opened the way for the Spirit?

lead: On the day after Pentecost the Church honours Mary as Mother of the Church. Paul asks the Corinthians to let all their gifts serve the building up of the assembly, because God is a God of peace, not of disorder. In Matthew, Jesus invites the weary to learn from him, gentle and humble in heart. The Church born of the Spirit grows when gifts are shared in order and in humility, and Mary, the humble handmaid, is the first to have learned from the heart of her Son.

r.h: Let all things be done for building up
set: Paul is near the end of his long answer about spiritual gifts (chapters 12–14). He has said that love is the greatest gift (chapter 13) and that prophecy, which builds up the community, is more useful in the assembly than tongues without interpretation (14:1–5). Now he gives practical rules for the Corinthians’ gatherings for worship, which seem to have been lively and at times chaotic.
str: v. 26: each brings something; let all be for building up.
vv. 27–28: tongues: two or three, in turn, with an interpreter, or silence.
vv. 29–31: prophets: two or three, the others weigh what is said, one by one.
vv. 32–33: the spirits of prophets are subject to the prophets; God is a God of peace.
kw: Literally the building of a house. Paul uses it again and again in this chapter. The test of every gift in worship is whether it builds the house of God.
To sift and judge. Even true prophecy must be tested by the community; no one speaks beyond the Church’s judgment.
Confusion, unrest, even tumult. Its opposite is peace, eirēnē, the order that comes from God.
vv: When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.
A rare window into early Christian worship: hymns, teaching and prophecy shared by many members. Variety is welcome, but it must serve the whole.
For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged.
The Spirit does not compete with himself. Waiting one’s turn is itself a gift of the Spirit.
for God is a God not of disorder but of peace.

The NRSV places the next words, “As in all the churches of the saints”, with what follows; other translations end verse 33 with them. Either way, the order of worship reflects the God who is worshipped.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the judgment about the genuineness and proper use of charisms belongs to those who preside over the Church, whose special task is not to extinguish the Spirit but to test all things and hold fast to what is good (Lumen Gentium 12). The Church’s liturgy, with its fixed order, is not opposed to the Spirit. It is the house the Spirit has built over centuries, so that the whole people may pray with one voice.

r.h: Learn from me
set: Jesus has just thanked his Father for revealing his mysteries to infants (11:25–27). He now turns to the people. Many of them felt weighed down: by poverty, by sickness, and by the many interpretations of the Law laid on them by some teachers (compare 23:4). Jewish teachers spoke of taking up “the yoke of the kingdom of heaven”, meaning faithful obedience to God. Jesus offers his own yoke.
str: v. 28: come to me, you who are weary; I will give you rest.
v. 29: take my yoke, learn from me, gentle and humble in heart.
v. 30: my yoke is easy, my burden light.
kw: The wooden beam that joins two oxen to share a load. A yoke is not taken off; it is shared. Jesus does not promise a life without burden, but a burden carried with him.
Praus is the meek of the Beatitudes (5:5); tapeinos means lowly. In Luke, Mary sings that God “has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant” (Luke 1:48), using the related noun tapeinōsis.
More exactly “kind, good, well-fitting”, like a yoke made to fit the neck so that it does not chafe.
vv: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus describes his own heart. The lesson he gives is not first a doctrine but a way of being: gentleness and humility.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
The commandments of Christ are not lighter because they ask less, but because love carries them, and he carries them with us.
ch: The Church sees Mary as the first and best disciple of the gentle and humble heart of her Son. Pope St Paul VI proclaimed her “Mother of the Church” on 21 November 1964, at the Second Vatican Council, and in 2018 Pope Francis set her memorial on the Monday after Pentecost. The Council teaches that Mary, by her faith, love and obedience, cooperated in the birth of the faithful in the Church, and is for that reason a mother to us in the order of grace (Lumen Gentium 53, 61).

qa: Why is Mary called Mother of the Church if she is herself a member of the Church?

Both are true. Mary is a member of the Church, its most excellent member, redeemed by her Son. She is also its mother, because she gave birth to the Head and, at the Cross, received the beloved disciple as her son (John 19:26–27). The Council calls her “a preeminent and singular member of the Church” and also honours her “as a most beloved mother” (Lumen Gentium 53). In the upper room she prayed with the apostles for the Spirit (Acts 1:14), as a mother among her children.
rite: The Syro-Malabar Church, in the first days of the Season of the Apostles, keeps Mary in the midst of the apostles as their mother. In our East Syriac tradition Mary is above all Mother of Christ and Mother of God, honoured in every Holy Qurbana; today’s title adds that the Mother of the Head is also the mother of his body.
study: When I take part in the Holy Qurbana, do I help build up the assembly or think mostly of my own devotion?
Jesus says, “Learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart.” In what relationship do I most need to learn gentleness this week?

lead: Both readings are about faith that holds on. Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians, whose faith and love keep growing in the middle of persecution, and lifts their eyes to the day when the Lord Jesus will be revealed and glorified in his saints. In Matthew, two blind men by the road out of Jericho cry out to the Son of David, and the louder the crowd tells them to be quiet, the louder they cry. Jesus stops, has compassion, opens their eyes, and they follow him. In the Season of the Apostles the Church learns from both: to persevere, and to keep asking for sight.

r.h: Worthy of the kingdom
set: Paul founded the church at Thessalonica in Macedonia on his second journey, and had to leave in haste because of opposition (Acts 17:1–10). The young community continued to suffer. Many scholars think the Second Letter to the Thessalonians was written in Paul’s name by a disciple, because its style and its teaching on the end differ from the First Letter; others hold that Paul wrote it soon after 1 Thessalonians. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case.

The language of this passage is that of Jewish apocalyptic writing: angels, fire, the day of the Lord. Its purpose is not to frighten the faithful but to comfort them: their suffering is seen by God, and justice will be done.
str: vv. 3–4: thanksgiving for growing faith and love, and pride in their steadfastness.
vv. 5–10: God’s righteous judgment: relief for the afflicted, and the revealing of the Lord Jesus.
vv. 11–12: Paul’s prayer that God make them worthy and that Jesus be glorified in them.
kw: Endurance under a load; the strength to remain. It is the virtue of those who do not give way under trial.
Literally an unveiling. The Lord Jesus is already reigning; on the last day what is hidden will be made plain to all.
Not that we earn the kingdom by ourselves, but that God by his grace makes us fit for it. Paul prays for this; it is God’s work in us (v. 11).
vv: because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing.
Persecution has not shrunk this church; it has deepened it. Faith and love are not fixed amounts but living things that grow.
These will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might
The heart of the punishment is separation from the Lord. Judgment belongs to God alone; the persecuted are never told to take revenge (compare Romans 12:19).
so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.
An exchange of glory: Christ glorified in his people, his people glorified in him. All of it is “according to the grace” of God.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the chief punishment of hell is eternal separation from God, in whom alone we can have the life and happiness for which we were created, and that this state is a definitive self-exclusion from communion with God (CCC 1033, 1035). It also teaches that God predestines no one to go to hell (CCC 1037). The Church prays, as Paul does here, that all may be made worthy of their call. Today, in many lands, Christians still suffer for their faith; the Church prays for them and for those who wrong them.

r.h: Lord, let our eyes be opened
set: Jesus is on his last journey to Jerusalem. He has just foretold his passion for the third time (20:17–19), and the mother of James and John has asked for places of honour for her sons (20:20–28). Now, leaving Jericho, about fifteen miles from Jerusalem, he meets two blind men. The next scene is his entry into the city as the Son of David (21:1–11).

Mark tells of one blind beggar, Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46–52), and Luke of one blind man as Jesus approached Jericho (Luke 18:35–43). Matthew several times tells of two where others tell of one (as with the demoniacs in 8:28); perhaps two witnesses make the testimony sure.
str: v. 29: leaving Jericho, a large crowd following.
vv. 30–31: two blind men cry out; the crowd rebukes them; they cry louder.
vv. 32–33: Jesus stops: “What do you want me to do for you?”
v. 34: compassion, touch, sight, following.
kw: The cry of the blind men, Kyrie eleēson, “Lord, have mercy”, became one of the oldest prayers of the Church’s liturgy.
A title for the Messiah, the promised king from David’s line. The blind men see who Jesus is before their eyes are opened.
From splanchna, the inner organs: a compassion felt in the depths of one’s being. Matthew uses it of Jesus before he heals and feeds the crowds (9:36; 14:14; 15:32).
vv: The crowd sternly ordered them to be quiet; but they shouted even more loudly, “Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David!”
The crowd following Jesus becomes an obstacle to those who want to reach him. Their persistence is a lesson in prayer.
Jesus stood still and called them, saying, “What do you want me to do for you?”
A few verses earlier he asked the mother of James and John, “What do you want?” (20:21). She asked for places of glory for her sons; the blind men ask for sight.
Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes. Immediately they regained their sight and followed him.
They follow him on the road to Jerusalem, to the Cross. Sight is given so that we may follow.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus heard the prayer of faith during his ministry, and that the urgent cry of the blind men, “Have mercy on us, Son of David”, has been renewed in the traditional prayer to Jesus known as the Jesus Prayer (CCC 2616). St Augustine, preaching on this Gospel, says that the crowd which tried to silence the blind men stands for the noise of worldly habits, even among Christians, that hinders us from crying to Christ; we must cry the louder until he stops for us (in substance, Sermon 88).

qa: Does 2 Thessalonians teach that God takes revenge?

The passage speaks of God’s justice, in the strong language of the prophets. Its point is that suffering for the kingdom is not forgotten and that evil will not have the last word. Vengeance belongs to God, not to us (Romans 12:19), and the Christian answers persecution with prayer, even for persecutors (Matthew 5:44). The Church teaches that hell is a state of definitive self-exclusion from God, and that God wills all to be saved (CCC 1033, 1037).
study: Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians’ faith and love are growing. Where do I see faith and love growing in my family or parish, and do I thank God for it?
If Jesus asked me today, “What do you want me to do for you?”, what would I ask for? Is it glory, or sight?

lead: In the first week after Pentecost both readings are about small beginnings that God makes great. Paul closes his correction of the Corinthian assembly with a simple rule for the Lord’s Supper: judge yourselves, and wait for one another. In Matthew, Jesus speaks of a tiny mustard seed that becomes a tree and of a little yeast hidden in a great mass of flour. The Church of the apostles was small and divided, yet it carried the life of the whole Kingdom.

r.h: When you come together to eat, wait for one another
set: In 11:17–34 Paul corrects the way the Corinthians celebrate the Lord’s Supper. The Eucharist was then joined to a common meal in a private house. Those who had more arrived early and ate their own food, while the poor, who may have come late after work, were left hungry (11:21–22). Paul hands on what he received from the Lord, the words over the bread and the cup (11:23–26), and warns that whoever eats and drinks “without discerning the body” eats and drinks judgment (11:29). Today’s verses are his conclusion.
str: vv. 31–32: judge yourselves now; the Lord’s judgment is a father’s discipline, not condemnation.
vv. 33–34a: two practical rules: wait for one another, and satisfy hunger at home.
v. 34b: other matters will wait until Paul comes.
kw: The same verb stands behind “discerning the body” (v. 29) and “if we judged ourselves” (v. 31). To discern the body is to see Christ in the bread and also in the brothers and sisters at the table; to judge oneself is to look honestly at one’s own heart before coming.
The word for training a child. The Lord’s correction is meant to save, “so that we may not be condemned along with the world”.
To wait for, and so to receive one another. Some scholars think the word here also carries the sense of welcoming, sharing what one has with those who come later.
vv: But if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged.
Paul plays on the verbs for judging. An honest look at ourselves now spares us a harder judgment later.
we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.
Even the Lord’s correction is mercy. Paul has just said that some in the community are weak and ill (11:30); he does not explain this as anger but as a call to return.
So then, my brothers and sisters, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.
After the high teaching on the Body and Blood of the Lord comes a very plain rule. The Eucharist is never only a private devotion; it gathers a people, and no one may be left out.
ch: The Catechism quotes this chapter when it teaches that we must examine our conscience before receiving Holy Communion (CCC 1385), and it adds that the Eucharist commits us to the poor: to receive the Body and Blood of Christ in truth we must recognize Christ in the poorest, his brethren (CCC 1397). St John Chrysostom often reminded his people in substance that one cannot honour Christ at the altar and despise him in the poor at the church door.

r.h: The mustard seed and the yeast
set: Matthew 13 is the third of the five great discourses of Jesus in this Gospel, the chapter of parables. Jesus has told the parable of the sower and of the weeds among the wheat. Now come two short parables, one taken from a man’s work in the field and one from a woman’s work in the house. The evangelist then explains why Jesus speaks in parables, quoting Psalm 78:2.
str: vv. 31–32: the mustard seed, smallest of seeds, becomes a tree where birds nest.
v. 33: the yeast mixed into three measures of flour leavens it all.

vv. 34–35: Jesus speaks to the crowds in parables, fulfilling the word of the psalm. ¶ The two parables make a pair: one shows growth that can be seen from outside, the other a change that works hidden from within.
kw: The black mustard of Galilee has a very small seed, proverbial for smallness (17:20), yet the plant can grow to the height of a man. Matthew says it “becomes a tree”, a deliberate stretching of the image.
In the Bible leaven is often a sign of corruption (16:6; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Here, surprisingly, it is the image of the Kingdom. A little of it, hidden in the dough, changes everything.

The Greek says the woman “hid” the yeast in the flour; the NRSV renders it “mixed in”. Verse 35 then speaks of what “has been hidden from the foundation of the world”. The Kingdom works hidden before it is seen.
vv: it is the smallest of all the seeds, but when it has grown it is the greatest of shrubs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.

The birds nesting in the branches recall the great tree of Daniel 4:12 and the cedar of Ezekiel 17:23, images of a kingdom that gives shelter to the nations. The Kingdom of God begins small but has room for all peoples.
yeast that a woman took and mixed in with three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.

Three measures is a very large amount, enough bread for well over a hundred people. It is the amount Sarah prepared for the three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18:6). The woman’s small act at home feeds a feast.
I will open my mouth to speak in parables; I will proclaim what has been hidden from the foundation of the world.

Textual note: a few ancient manuscripts read “through the prophet Isaiah”, although the words come from Psalm 78:2. St Jerome already knew this reading. The psalm is ascribed to Asaph, whom Scripture calls a seer (2 Chronicles 29:30), so Matthew can call him a prophet.
ch: The Second Vatican Council asks the lay faithful to work for the sanctification of the world from within, like leaven (Lumen Gentium 31). The Catechism says that through his parables Jesus invites people to the feast of the Kingdom, but that a radical choice is also required: to gain the Kingdom one must give everything (CCC 546). St John Chrysostom, preaching on these parables, pointed to the apostles: few, poor and weak, yet the Gospel they carried filled the world (in substance, Homilies on Matthew). A Syro-Malabar reader may think of the faith brought by one apostle to our shore, which has grown into a tree with many branches.

qa: Is the mustard seed really the smallest of all seeds?

Jesus speaks as a teacher of his own land, where the mustard seed was the proverbial smallest seed people sowed. Scripture is not giving a lesson in botany; it uses common speech to teach a truth about the Kingdom. The Church teaches that Scripture teaches without error the truth God wished to put down for the sake of our salvation (Dei Verbum 11).
study: Paul says, “wait for one another.” Who in my parish or family is left out or left behind at our gatherings, and what could I do about it?
Where do I see the Kingdom working small and hidden, like yeast, in my home or workplace?

lead: Both readings speak of the place where God meets his people. Hebrews quotes Jeremiah’s promise of a new covenant, with God’s law written on the heart. In John, Jesus drives the traders from the Temple and speaks of the temple of his body, destroyed and raised in three days. The meeting place of God and humanity is now the risen body of Christ, and through the Spirit, the hearts of those who belong to him.

r.h: I will write my laws on their hearts
set: The Letter to the Hebrews does not name its author; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture. In chapters 7–10 it shows that Christ is the true high priest who serves in the true sanctuary. Just before this reading it calls him “the mediator of a better covenant” (8:6). To show that God himself promised such a covenant, the writer quotes Jeremiah 31:31–34 in full. It is the longest quotation of the Old Testament in the New.
str: v. 7: if the first covenant had been faultless, no second would be needed.
vv. 8–9: the promise of a new covenant, not like the one made at the Exodus.
vv. 10–12: its gifts: the law written on hearts, knowledge of the Lord for all, sins forgiven.
v. 13: the conclusion: the first has been made “old”.
kw: The Greek kainos means new in kind, not only recent. Diathēkē is also the word for a last will (9:16–17), so the Latin and our tradition speak of the New Testament. Jesus took up Jeremiah’s word at the Last Supper: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (1 Corinthians 11:25).
For the Bible the heart is not only feeling but the centre of thought and decision. The law that was written on stone tablets is now written within, by the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:3).
The writer means that the priesthood and sacrifices of the first covenant were a shadow pointing to Christ (8:5; 10:1). He does not say that God has rejected Israel.
vv: God finds fault with them when he says:

The fault is with the people who broke the covenant, not with God’s gift. Textual note: some manuscripts have a slightly different form of “them”, so the phrase can also be read “finding fault, he says to them”.
I will put my laws in their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
The heart of every covenant in the Bible: “I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” What is new is how it will be kept: from within.
for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.
In the Bible to “know” God is more than to know about him; it is a relationship of trust and love. The new covenant gives this knowledge to the small as well as the great.
and I will remember their sins no more.
Forgiveness stands at the base of the new covenant. In Hebrews it is given once for all through the blood of Christ (10:17–18).
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it teaches that the New Law, the law of the Gospel, is the work of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, and becomes the interior law of charity (CCC 1965–1966). The Church also teaches that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121; Romans 11:29). The Jewish people remain the people to whom God first spoke, and Christians read Jeremiah’s promise with them, confessing that it is fulfilled in Christ.

r.h: The temple of his body
set: John tells of Jesus driving the traders from the Temple near the beginning of his Gospel, at the first of three Passovers he mentions. Matthew, Mark and Luke place it in the last week, just before the Passion. The Temple of Jerusalem had been rebuilt and greatly enlarged by Herod the Great, from about 20 BC. In its outer court animals were sold for the sacrifices, and money changers turned the coins of pilgrims into the coinage accepted for the Temple tax.

In John “the Jews” who question Jesus here are the Temple authorities. Jesus himself, his disciples and the pilgrims around them are all Jews. The scene is a prophetic sign within Israel, not a rejection of Israel.
str: vv. 13–16: the Passover; the whip of cords; “Stop making my Father’s house a marketplace!”
v. 17: the disciples remember Psalm 69:9.
vv. 18–22: the demand for a sign; “Destroy this temple”; the temple of his body.
vv. 23–25: many believe because of signs, but Jesus knows what is in everyone.
kw: In vv. 14–15 John uses hieron, the whole Temple area with its courts. When Jesus says “Destroy this temple” he uses naos, the sanctuary itself, the dwelling of God. That is the word he applies to his body.
The words recall the last line of Zechariah: “there shall no longer be traders in the house of the Lord of hosts on that day” (Zechariah 14:21). Jesus acts as the one who brings that day.
The verb is used both for raising a building and for raising the dead. Jesus’ answer holds both meanings, and the authorities hear only the first.
vv: Stop making my Father’s house a marketplace!
Jesus calls the Temple “my Father’s house”. As a boy in Luke he had said the same (Luke 2:49). His zeal is the zeal of a Son for his Father’s honour.
Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.
At his trial false witnesses will twist these words (Mark 14:58). John explains them at once: Jesus spoke of his body.
But he was speaking of the temple of his body.
The place where God dwells among us is now the flesh of the Word (1:14). Through him the Church, too, becomes God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16).
After he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this; and they believed the scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
Easter memory: the disciples understood only after the Resurrection. The Holy Spirit, Jesus later promises, “will remind you of all that I have said to you” (14:26).
for he himself knew what was in everyone.
Faith that rests only on wonders is not yet the faith Jesus seeks. He knows the human heart, and still he gives himself for it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus was not hostile to the Temple, where he taught and which he loved; his words about destroying it point to his own death and to the new age in which his body would be the definitive Temple (CCC 583–586). St Augustine saw in the forty-six years a sign of the body Jesus took from the race of Adam, since the Greek letters of the name Adam add up to forty-six (in substance, Tractates on John 10). Every Syro-Malabar church, with its veiled sanctuary, the madbaha, is a sign of that body in which heaven and earth meet.

qa: Why does John place the cleansing of the Temple at the start, when the other Gospels place it at the end?

The Church has never required one answer. Some commentators think Jesus acted in the Temple twice. Many think John, who arranges his Gospel by signs and feasts, placed the scene at the start on purpose, so that the whole ministry is read in the light of the true Temple, the body of Jesus that will be destroyed and raised. The Gospels tell the truth about Jesus, but they do not always follow the same order (Dei Verbum 19).
study: What would change in my prayer if I believed that God’s law is written on my heart and not only in a book?
Is there anything in my life, or in our parish life, that makes the Father’s house look like a marketplace?

lead: The Friday of Gold, the first Friday after Pentecost, remembers the first sign the apostles worked after the Spirit came: the healing of the man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate. The four readings form one picture. Isaiah promises that when God comes the lame shall leap like a deer. In Acts it happens: Peter, with no silver or gold, raises the man in the name of Jesus, and he enters the Temple walking and leaping. Paul then shows the gold the Church truly holds, the love that never ends. In Luke, Jesus gives a widow’s son back to her at Nain and answers John the Baptist with the very signs Isaiah had promised. The words to watch are lame, name and love.

r.h: The lame shall leap like a deer
set: Isaiah 34 and 35 form a pair: judgment on Edom, then the blossoming of the desert and the return of the redeemed to Zion. Many scholars think chapter 35 is close in style and date to chapters 40–55, the prophecies of consolation spoken to the exiles in Babylon. The road home through the desert is a new exodus.

The verses just before this reading picture the wilderness bursting into flower and seeing “the glory of the Lord, the majesty of our God” (35:2). Today’s verses turn to the weak and fearful people who will walk that road.
str: vv. 3–4: strengthen the weak; say to the fearful: here is your God.
vv. 5–6a: the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap, the speechless sing.
vv. 6b–7: water breaks out in the desert.
vv. 8–9: the Holy Way, safe from beasts, for the redeemed.
v. 10: the ransomed return to Zion with everlasting joy.
kw: The lame man was among those who could feel shut out from the full life of the people. Isaiah promises that when God comes he will not just walk but leap. Acts 3:8 shows the healed man “walking and leaping”.
A road that belongs to God. Those who walk it are made holy by the one who leads them. The first Christians called their life “the Way” (Acts 9:2).
the redeemed / the ransomed of the Lord
Two words for release. The first comes from gō’ēl, the next of kin who buys back a relative from slavery. God acts as Israel’s next of kin.
vv: Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees.
Hebrews takes up this verse to encourage tired Christians: “lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees” (Hebrews 12:12). Encouraging the weak is the work of every believer.
Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped;
Jesus’ answer to John the Baptist in today’s Gospel echoes this verse. The signs of God’s coming are signs of healing.
then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the speechless sing for joy.
Healing ends in praise. The man at the Beautiful Gate does not go home quietly; he goes into the Temple praising God.
A highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Holy Way;
The way home is God’s own road, and even “fools” shall not go astray on it. Salvation does not depend on our cleverness.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the signs Jesus worked fulfil the prophecies and show that he is the Messiah, and that they deliver some people from earthly evils as a sign of a deeper liberation from sin (CCC 547–549). The Fathers read this chapter as a picture of the Church: the desert of the nations made fruitful by the waters of Baptism, and the weak made strong by the Spirit.

r.h: What I have I give you
set: After Pentecost the believers in Jerusalem kept going to the Temple daily (2:46). Peter and John go up at three in the afternoon, the hour of prayer when the evening sacrifice was offered. A man more than forty years old (4:22), lame from birth, is carried each day to a gate called Beautiful. Its exact place is uncertain; many think it was the great bronze gate on the east side of the inner courts.

The healing leads to Peter’s second speech in Acts, given in Solomon’s Portico, the colonnade on the east side of the Temple courts where Jesus had once walked (John 10:23). Peter speaks as a Jew to his own people, calling them “friends” and heirs of the covenant.
str: vv. 1–10: the healing at the Beautiful Gate.
vv. 11–16: Peter explains: not our power, but the name of Jesus, whom God glorified and raised.
vv. 17–21: “you acted in ignorance”; repent, that times of refreshing may come.
vv. 22–26: Moses and all the prophets foretold these days; the blessing promised to Abraham comes first to you.
kw: The word sounds through the chapter (vv. 6, 16) and the next. In the Bible the name is the person present and acting. Peter does not heal by his own power but by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth.
God “has glorified his servant Jesus” (v. 13) echoes the Greek of Isaiah 52:13, where the Servant “shall be exalted and lifted up”. The Servant who suffered is the one God has glorified.
Archēgos means founder, pioneer, the one who leads the way. Peter sets the contrast sharply: a murderer was released, and the Author of life was killed; but God raised him.
vv: Peter looked intently at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.”
Before the healing comes a look. The man was used to people passing by; now two people stop and meet his eyes.
But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.”
These words give the feast its name, as it is commonly explained. The apostles are poor, but they hold the greatest treasure: the name of Jesus and the power of his Spirit.
Jumping up, he stood and began to walk, and he entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
Isaiah 35:6 fulfilled. A man who had sat for years at the gate now goes in. Healing restores him to the worship of his people.
“And now, friends, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers.
After hard words, Peter offers an excuse and an open door. The Catechism cites this verse to teach that responsibility for the death of Jesus cannot be charged to the Jewish people as such (CCC 597).
You are the descendants of the prophets and of the covenant that God gave to your ancestors,
Peter ends with blessing, not condemnation. The promise to Abraham, that all families of the earth would be blessed, now goes out from Jerusalem to the nations.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the name of Jesus is at the heart of Christian prayer and that there is no other name by which we must be saved (CCC 432, 2666; Acts 4:12). A well-known story, perhaps legendary, tells that St Thomas Aquinas was shown the treasures of the papal court and was told, “The Church can no longer say, ‘I have no silver or gold.’” He answered, “Nor can she say, ‘Stand up and walk.’” The story has lasted because it says something true: the riches of the Church are the name of Jesus, the sacraments and charity.

r.h: A still more excellent way
set: The Corinthians prized spectacular gifts, above all speaking in tongues. In chapter 12 Paul has said that all gifts come from the one Spirit for the common good, and that the Church is one body with many members. Before he speaks of tongues and prophecy in chapter 14, he sets love at the centre. Chapter 13 is not a wedding poem first of all; it is a correction for a proud and divided community.
str: 12:31: strive for the greater gifts; a still more excellent way.
13:1–3: without love, tongues, prophecy, faith and even sacrifice are nothing.
13:4–7: what love does and does not do.
13:8–12: love never ends; our knowledge is partial, like a dim mirror.
13:13: faith, hope and love abide; the greatest is love.
kw: The word the New Testament chose for the love God has for us in Christ, and that the Spirit pours into our hearts (Romans 5:5). In 13:4–7 Paul describes it with verbs: love is something that acts.

Literally “in a riddle”. Ancient mirrors were of polished metal and gave a dim image; Corinth was known for its bronze work. God spoke to Moses “face to face… not in riddles” (Numbers 12:8); that clarity is promised to us at the end.
The three that Christian tradition calls the theological virtues, because they come from God and lead to God (CCC 1812–1813).
vv: If I speak in the tongues of mortals and of angels, but do not have love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.
Paul begins with the gift the Corinthians valued most. Without love even the speech of angels is only noise.
and if I hand over my body so that I may boast, but do not have love, I gain nothing.

Textual note: the manuscripts differ by one letter in Greek. Some read “so that I may boast” (followed by the NRSV), others “to be burned” (followed by our Malayalam translation). Either way, even the greatest sacrifice without love gains nothing.
It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
Not a naive love that ignores evil, for love “rejoices in the truth” (v. 6). It is a love that does not give up.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then we will see face to face.
The promise of the vision of God. Our present knowledge, even of faith, is true but partial.
And now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; and the greatest of these is love.
Faith will give way to sight and hope to possession; love alone remains, because God is love (1 John 4:8).
ch: The Catechism quotes this chapter to teach that charity is the greatest of the virtues and gives life to all the others (CCC 1826–1827), and it cites 13:12 for the vision of God face to face that faith already tastes in advance (CCC 163). St Thérèse of Lisieux tells how, searching for her place in the Church, she read 1 Corinthians 12 and 13 and understood that love is the heart of the Church: “in the heart of the Church, my mother, I shall be love.” On the Friday of Gold this is the gold the Church can always give.

r.h: Young man, I say to you, rise!
set: Nain was a small town in Galilee, south-east of Nazareth, on the slope of the hill of Moreh. Only Luke tells this miracle. Close by lay Shunem, where the prophet Elisha raised the son of a woman who had welcomed him (2 Kings 4). The scene also recalls Elijah, who raised the only son of a widow at Zarephath (1 Kings 17:17–24).

A widow who has lost her only son has lost not only her child but her support and her future. Jesus acts without being asked. Then John the Baptist, now in prison (Luke 3:20), sends two disciples with a question, and Jesus answers with what they have seen.
str: vv. 11–12: two crowds meet at the gate: one with Jesus, one with the dead.
vv. 13–15: compassion; “Do not weep”; he touches the bier; the young man rises.
vv. 16–17: fear and praise: a great prophet; God has visited his people.
vv. 18–20: John’s question: “Are you the one who is to come?”
vv. 21–23: the signs of Isaiah, and a blessing on those not offended.
kw: A strong word: to be moved in the depths of one’s being. In Luke it is used of Jesus here, of the Good Samaritan (10:33) and of the father of the prodigal son (15:20).
The same verb as in Zechariah’s song: God “has looked favorably on his people and redeemed them” (1:68). At Nain, God’s visit has a face.
Literally to trip over a stumbling block. John expected a Messiah of fire and judgment (3:16–17); Jesus brings healing and mercy first. Blessed are those who do not stumble over the way he comes.
vv: When the Lord saw her, he had compassion for her and said to her, “Do not weep.”
Here Luke the narrator calls Jesus “the Lord”, the title of God, at a moment of pure compassion. His first word is to the mother, not to the dead son.
Then he came forward and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still.
Contact with the dead made a person ritually unclean (Numbers 19:11). Jesus is not stopped by that fear; life flows from him into death.
The dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
The last words repeat almost exactly the Greek of 1 Kings 17:23, where Elijah gave the boy to his mother. A greater than Elijah is here.
the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news brought to them.
Jesus answers John with the words of Isaiah (35:5–6; 61:1). The list ends not with the dead raised but with the poor hearing good news.
And blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me.
A beatitude for John and for us: blessed are those who accept God’s way of saving, even when it is not the way we expected.
ch: The Catechism says that Christ’s compassion toward the sick and his many healings are a resplendent sign that “God has visited his people” (CCC 1503), quoting this Gospel. St Ambrose saw in the widow of Nain an image of Mother Church, who weeps for her children dead in sin and rejoices when Christ gives them back to her alive (in substance, Commentary on Luke). The Church still prays for the dead at every Holy Qurbana, trusting the Lord who said, “Young man, I say to you, rise!”

qa: Why is this day called the Friday of Gold?

The name is commonly explained from Peter’s words, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you” (Acts 3:6). The Churches of the Syriac tradition keep the first Friday after Pentecost as a feast of the first apostolic miracle. Its exact history is not certain, but its meaning is plain: the gift the apostles give is better than gold, the healing power of the name of Jesus.
In Acts 3 Peter tells the crowd “you killed the Author of life”. Does this blame the Jewish people?

No. Peter, a Jew, speaks to his fellow Jews in Jerusalem about what happened there weeks before, and at once adds, “I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers” (3:17). The Church teaches that the death of Christ cannot be charged against all Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today, and that all sinners were the authors of his Passion (CCC 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4). Peter’s speech ends with blessing for his people (3:26).
rite: In the Syro-Malabar calendar the Friday of Gold falls in the first week of the Season of the Apostles (Shleeha). The calendar notes that if only two readings are chosen it is proper to read from the Acts of the Apostles, so that the day keeps its memory of the Beautiful Gate. Throughout this season the Holy Qurbana is offered with the Anaphora of the Apostles Mar Addai and Mar Mari.

The day also has a lesson for our parishes and institutions. A Church rich in buildings must still be able to say, with Peter, “what I have I give you”: the name of Jesus, the sacraments, and hands that raise up the weak, the disabled and the elderly so that they too may enter the house of God praising him.
study: Peter and John stopped and looked at the man at the gate. Who sits at the “gate” of my life whom I usually pass by?
Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 and put your own name in place of “love”. Where do I fall short, and what do I ask of the Spirit?
Jesus acted at Nain before anyone asked him. Whose sorrow can I notice today without waiting to be asked?
John the Baptist was puzzled by the way Jesus worked. When have I been disappointed by how God acted, and what did I learn?

lead: On the eve of the feast of the Most Holy Trinity, both readings speak of unity that does not erase difference. Paul tells the Corinthians that the body is one and has many members, and that all were baptized in one Spirit into one body. In John, the crowd that ate the loaves comes looking for Jesus, and he turns them from bread that perishes to the work God asks: to believe in the one he has sent.

r.h: Many members, one body
set: In chapter 12 Paul answers the Corinthians’ questions about spiritual gifts. Some boasted of showy gifts; others felt they did not belong. He has just said that there are varieties of gifts but the same Spirit, given to each “for the common good” (12:4–7). Now he takes up an image well known in the ancient world, the body and its members, which writers used to call citizens to harmony. Paul gives it a new depth: the body is Christ’s.
str: v. 12: the body is one with many members; “so it is with Christ”.
v. 13: one Spirit, one Baptism, one body, across every division.
vv. 14–17: no member may say “I do not belong”; each is needed.
vv. 18–20: God arranged the members as he chose: many members, one body.
kw: Paul does not say “so it is with the Church” but “so it is with Christ”. The Church is not only like a body; it is the body of Christ (12:27).
A living part of a body, not a member of a club. Each limb has its own task and lives only by the life of the whole.

“We were all made to drink of one Spirit” (v. 13). The image is of water poured out or drunk. Many commentators hear Baptism and the outpouring of the Spirit; some also think of the Eucharistic cup (10:4, 16).
vv: For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.
The surprise is at the end of the sentence. Christ himself, head and members, is the one body.
Jews or Greeks, slaves or free
The deepest divisions of the ancient world, of birth and of social standing, do not divide the body. Paul says the same in Galatians 3:28.
If the foot would say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.
Paul answers those who feel unimportant. A sense of being less does not make one less a member.
But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose.
The variety in the Church is God’s design, not an accident to be smoothed out.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the unity of the body does not do away with the diversity of its members: in the building up of Christ’s body there is a diversity of members and functions, and one Spirit distributes his gifts for the welfare of the Church (CCC 791; Lumen Gentium 7). Pope Pius XII’s encyclical Mystici Corporis (1943) presents the Church as the Mystical Body of Christ. The image also speaks to the communion of the Churches: the Syro-Malabar, Latin, Syro-Malankara and other Churches are members of one Catholic body, each with its own gifts.

r.h: The work of God is to believe
set: Jesus has fed five thousand people with five barley loaves and two fish (6:1–15) and has walked on the sea to his disciples (6:16–21). The next day the crowd crosses the lake in boats and finds him at Capernaum (6:24, 59). There begins the long discourse on the Bread of Life. Today’s verses are its opening exchange.
str: v. 25: “Rabbi, when did you come here?”
v. 26: you seek me because you ate your fill, not because you saw signs.
v. 27: work for the food that endures; the Father has set his seal on the Son of Man.
vv. 28–29: “What must we do?” “Believe in him whom he has sent.”
kw: Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food that endures for eternal life. Later in the chapter he says plainly what that food is: “the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh” (6:51).
A seal marks ownership and guarantees what is genuine. The Father has marked the Son as his own. Many of the Fathers connected this seal with the Spirit, who rested on Jesus at his baptism (1:32–33).
The crowd asks about “works” in the plural. Jesus answers with one “work”: faith. It is called the work of God because God asks it and God makes it possible.
vv: you are looking for me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.
A sign points beyond itself. The crowd saw only full stomachs. Jesus is not scornful; he wants to lead them further.
Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures for eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you.
Notice the paradox: we are to work for a food that is given. Effort and gift belong together.
This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.
Faith is not a work by which we earn God’s favour. It is the work God does in us and asks of us, the trusting gift of ourselves to the One the Father has sent.
ch: The Catechism teaches that faith is a gift of God, a supernatural virtue infused by him, and at the same time an authentically human act (CCC 153–154). St Augustine, preaching on this verse, explained that to believe in him is more than to believe what he says: it is by believing to love him and to go into him and be made one with his members (in substance, Tractates on John). Faith of this kind does not stand against good works; by grace it brings them forth.

qa: Does John 6:29 mean that faith alone matters and works do not?

No. Jesus calls faith “the work of God” because it is the root of everything else. In Catholic teaching faith, hope and charity are given together by grace, and living faith “works through love” (Galatians 5:6). The good works done in grace are themselves God’s gift and truly ours (CCC 2008).
study: Which member of my parish or family do I treat as if they did not belong? What would change if I saw them as needed by the body?
Why do I seek Jesus: for what he gives, or for who he is?

lead: One week after Pentecost the Church turns from what God has done to who God is: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The four readings of the feast do not give a definition; they show God acting. At Mamre, the Lord comes to Abraham as three visitors and is welcomed at a meal. In Isaiah, the God who is “the first and the last” speaks, and a mysterious voice says, “the Lord God has sent me and his spirit.” Paul shows the three at work in our lives: peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, and God’s love poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. In John, Jesus says that the Spirit takes what is his, and that all the Father has is his. The words to watch are sent, poured and mine. The calendar also gives readings for the Second Sunday of the Apostles (Joel 2, Acts 4, 1 Corinthians 6, Luke 7); these notes follow the readings of the feast.

r.h: Three men by the oaks of Mamre
set: Abraham has settled by the oaks of Mamre near Hebron (13:18). God has promised him a son, but he and Sarah are old and still childless. In the heat of the day, when travel stopped, three men appear. The story continues after today’s reading with the promise that Sarah will have a son within a year (18:10), and in the next chapter two of the visitors, now called angels, go on to Sodom (19:1).

The narrator tells us at the start that it is “the Lord” who appears. Abraham sees three men. The text moves between singular and plural, and this has made the scene one of the most pondered pages of the Old Testament.
str: v. 1: the Lord appears at Mamre in the heat of the day.
v. 2: three men; Abraham runs to meet them and bows down.
vv. 3–5: he begs them to stay: water, rest, a little bread.
vv. 6–8: the great meal prepared in haste, and Abraham standing by them as they eat.
kw: In verse 3 Abraham speaks to one (“my lord… your servant”); in verses 4–5 he speaks to all three. The Jewish scribes who added vowels to the Hebrew text pointed the word as the divine title, Lord, showing that they understood Abraham to be speaking to God.
Abraham runs (vv. 2, 7) and hastens (vv. 6, 7) in the heat of the day, an old man serving strangers. Hospitality here is not a duty done slowly but love in a hurry.

Sarah kneads three measures of choice flour, far more than three guests could eat. Jesus’ parable of the yeast, read on Wednesday, uses the same measure (Matthew 13:33). God is welcomed with abundance.
vv: The Lord appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day.
God comes at an ordinary hour, to an ordinary tent. The Letter to the Hebrews remembers this scene: “by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2).
He looked up and saw three men standing near him.
One Lord, three men. The Old Testament does not reveal the Trinity, but the Church has always seen in this meeting a shadow of what would be revealed in Christ.
Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
Abraham offers “a little” and gives a feast. The washing of feet will return, in a greater way, when the Lord himself washes the feet of his disciples (John 13:5).
and he stood by them under the tree while they ate.
The host does not sit; he waits on his guests. The man to whom God made promises now serves God at table.
ch: Many Fathers saw in the three visitors a figure of the Trinity, and the Latin liturgy long sang a line often traced to St Ambrose: “He saw three, and worshipped one” (in substance). Others, such as St Justin Martyr, saw the Word of God with two angels. Both readings come from the same faith: the God who visits Abraham is the God who will make himself known as Father, Son and Spirit. The famous icon of St Andrei Rublev (early fifteenth century) shows the three at table with a cup in the centre. The Catechism sees in the hospitality at Mamre a prelude to the annunciation of the true Son of the promise (CCC 2571).

r.h: I am the first, and I am the last
set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the exiles in Babylon in the sixth century before Christ. God has raised up Cyrus, king of Persia, to release them. Chapter 48 closes the first half of these prophecies with a strong call to listen, and just after this reading comes the cry, “Go out from Babylon” (48:20).

In these verses God speaks as Creator and Lord of history. Then, in verse 16, a new voice is heard: someone sent by the Lord God, together with his spirit. Many scholars think it is the prophet himself, or the Servant of whom the next chapter speaks.
str: v. 12: “Listen to me”: I am He, the first and the last.
v. 13: the Creator of earth and heavens.
vv. 14–15: the one whom the Lord loves (Cyrus) will do his will against Babylon.
v. 16: “Draw near”; a voice: the Lord God has sent me and his spirit.
v. 17: the Redeemer who teaches and leads in the way.
kw: A short solemn formula in these chapters (41:4; 43:10). In the Greek Old Testament it is egō eimi, “I am”, which Jesus uses of himself in John’s Gospel (John 8:58).
God is before all things and remains after all. In the Book of Revelation the Risen Christ takes the same title: “I am the first and the last” (Revelation 1:17; 22:13).

In verse 16 the Hebrew can be read “the Lord God has sent me and his spirit”, with the spirit sent along with the speaker, or “has sent me, and his spirit has”. The phrase joins the Lord God, the one he sends, and his spirit.
vv: Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called: I am He; I am the first, and I am the last.
God’s self-naming begins with a relationship: “whom I called”. The God of all ages is the God of a people.
My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens;
The Creator of all is not far away. The same hand that spread the heavens will lead the exiles home.
And now the Lord God has sent me and his spirit.

Many Fathers read this verse in the light of the New Testament: the Father sends the Son, and with him the Spirit. The prophet did not know the doctrine of the Trinity, but his words are open to the fullness God would reveal.
I am the Lord your God, who teaches you for your own good, who leads you in the way you should go.
God teaches and leads. Jesus will promise a Spirit who “will guide you into all the truth” (John 16:13), today’s Gospel.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God’s inmost being as Holy Trinity is a mystery that cannot be reached by reason alone, nor even by the faith of Israel before the Incarnation of the Son and the sending of the Spirit (CCC 237). Yet Israel’s faith in the one God, “I am He; I am the first, and I am the last,” remains the foundation. The Church confesses not three gods but one God in three Persons (CCC 253).

r.h: God’s love poured into our hearts
set: In chapters 1–4 Paul has shown that all, Jews and Gentiles, need God’s saving justice, and that it is given through faith in Jesus Christ, as it was given to Abraham (chapter 4). Chapter 5 begins a new section: what life is like for those who have been justified. Paul writes to a Church he had not yet visited, in about AD 57.
str: vv. 1–2a: justified by faith, we have peace and access to grace through Christ.
v. 2b: we boast in hope of sharing God’s glory.
vv. 3–4: we boast even in sufferings: endurance, character, hope.

v. 5: hope does not disappoint, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Spirit. ¶ In five verses God, the Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit are named, each at work in the believer.
kw: The word for being brought into the presence of a king. Through Christ we are led into the grace in which we now stand.
Literally the quality of something that has been tested and proved, like metal through fire. Endurance produces a tried and true character.
The verb is used of the Spirit “poured out” at Pentecost (Acts 2:17, 33). The tense means poured once and remaining: the love of God is not a passing feeling but a gift that stays.
vv: Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,

Textual note: the manuscripts differ by one letter. Many ancient ones read “let us have peace”; others read “we have peace”, which the NRSV follows. Our Malayalam translation reads it as an invitation. Both are true: peace is a gift, and we are to live in it.
through whom we have obtained access to this grace in which we stand;
Grace is not a moment but a place where we stand. The access is “through” Christ: he is the door.
knowing that suffering produces endurance,
Paul does not boast of suffering for itself. He boasts because God can make it bear fruit.
and hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.
“God’s love” here means first God’s love for us, given and felt within. Christian hope rests on that gift, not on our own strength.
ch: The Catechism quotes Romans 5:5 when it teaches that God is love and that love is his first gift, containing all others, poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit (CCC 733). It also teaches that justification is the most excellent work of God’s love, given by grace through faith and Baptism, and that it truly makes us just from within (CCC 1987–1992, 1994). St Augustine returned to this verse again and again when he taught that grace is not only a law shown to us but love given to us (in substance, On the Spirit and the Letter).

r.h: The Spirit of truth will guide you
set: These verses come from Jesus’ farewell discourse at the Last Supper (John 13–17). In it he speaks five times of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete (14:16–17, 26; 15:26; 16:7–11, 12–15). This is the last of these sayings. The disciples are grieving because Jesus is going away (16:6); he tells them that the Spirit will lead them further into what he has given.
str: v. 12: many things you cannot bear now.
v. 13: the Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth; he speaks what he hears.
v. 14: he will glorify me, taking what is mine.
v. 15: all that the Father has is mine. ¶ The movement is from the Father to the Son to the Spirit to the disciples.
kw: To lead on the road, as a guide leads travellers (compare Psalm 25:5). The Spirit does not bring a new Gospel; he leads the Church deeper into the truth that is Jesus himself (14:6).
The verb is used three times in these verses. The Spirit announces, makes known, what he receives. He does not speak “on his own”.
In John truth is not only correct ideas; it is the reality of God made known in Jesus, who is “full of grace and truth” (1:14).
vv: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.
Jesus respects the slowness of his disciples. Understanding will grow after Easter and Pentecost.
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth;

The Second Vatican Council teaches that through the Holy Spirit the Tradition that comes from the apostles develops in the Church, as there is a growth in understanding of the realities and words handed down (Dei Verbum 8).
He will glorify me, because he will take what is mine and declare it to you.
The Spirit always points to Jesus. A spirituality that leads away from Christ is not from this Spirit.
All that the Father has is mine.
One of the clearest words in the Gospels on the unity of the Father and the Son. What the Spirit gives us comes from the Father, through the Son.
ch: The Fathers used this verse against those who denied that the Son is equal to the Father: if all that the Father has belongs to the Son, the Son is God with the Father. The Catechism teaches that the Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son; it explains that the Eastern tradition expresses this by saying he comes from the Father through the Son, and that, rightly understood, the two ways of speaking are complementary (CCC 246–248). St Ephrem compared the Trinity to the sun, its light and its warmth: distinct, yet one (in substance).

qa: Is the word “Trinity” in the Bible?

The word is not, but what it names is. The New Testament speaks of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as one God, as in the command to baptize “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19) and in Paul’s blessing (2 Corinthians 13:13). The Church, guided by the Spirit of truth, found the words to confess this faith at the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) (CCC 249–252).
Did Abraham see the Trinity at Mamre?

The text says that the Lord appeared and that Abraham saw three men. It does not teach the doctrine of the Trinity; that was revealed only in Christ (CCC 237). Some Fathers read the three as a sign of the Trinity, others as the Word of God with two angels. The Church allows both readings, and the icon of Rublev has made the first one beloved in East and West.
If God is three, how can he be one?

The Church does not say that God is one and three in the same respect. God is one in nature, one God, and three in Persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who are really distinct in their relations to one another (CCC 253–255). It is a mystery, not a contradiction: reason cannot discover it, but it can see that it is not absurd.
rite: In the Syro-Malabar calendar the feast of the Most Holy Trinity falls on the Second Sunday of the Apostles, one week after Pentecost, and the calendar gives the Sunday’s own readings as a second set. Our Holy Qurbana is soaked in the praise of the Trinity. In the Anaphora of the Apostles Mar Addai and Mar Mari, which we pray through this season, the great prayer opens by praising the adorable and glorious Name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, who created the world by his grace.

The Season of the Apostles began with the Spirit poured out on the Church. Today we see where that gift comes from: from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. Each time we make the sign of the Cross, or sing “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit”, we name the God into whose life we were baptized.
study: Abraham ran to welcome strangers. Whom can I welcome this week as if I were welcoming God?
Isaiah’s God says, “I teach you for your own good.” Where do I need God to teach and lead me now?
Paul says suffering can produce hope. Name one present trouble and ask: what might the Spirit be forming in me through it?
How can my family pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit, more consciously at home?

lead: The second week of the Season of the Apostles opens with two readings about the future God has prepared for our bodies. Paul tells the Philippians that their citizenship is in heaven and that Christ will transform the body of our humiliation to be like his glorious body. At Bethany, Jesus tells a grieving Martha, “I am the resurrection and the life,” and she answers with a full confession of faith.

r.h: Our citizenship is in heaven
set: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison; where he was held, whether in Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea, is still debated. Philippi was a Roman colony (Acts 16:12), and its people were proud to be citizens of Rome, far away. In chapter 3 Paul has warned against those who insisted on circumcision for Gentile believers, and he has told of counting all things loss for Christ (3:7–8). Now he warns against another danger: a life governed by appetite.
str: v. 16: hold fast to what you have attained.
