v. 17: imitate me, and watch those who live by our example.
vv. 18–19: with tears: enemies of the cross, whose god is the belly.
vv. 20–21: our citizenship is in heaven; the Saviour will transform our bodies.
kw: The word the people of a Roman colony would have used of their belonging to Rome. Christians belong to a homeland in heaven, and they live in this world as its citizens.
“Their god is the belly” describes people ruled by their appetites. Scholars debate whom Paul has in mind; what is clear is that he warns of a life without the cross.
The same root as in 3:10, “becoming like him in his death”. Those who share the form of Christ’s cross will share the form of his glory.
vv: Brothers and sisters, join in imitating me, and observe those who live according to the example you have in us.
Paul is not proud; he has just said he has not yet reached the goal (3:12). He offers himself as a model of one who runs toward Christ. Faith is learned by watching faithful people.
For many live as enemies of the cross of Christ; I have often told you of them, and now I tell you even with tears.
Paul’s warning comes with tears, not anger. He weeps for those who reject the cross.
But our citizenship is in heaven, and it is from there that we are expecting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.
In the Roman world “saviour” and “lord” were titles given to the emperor. Paul gives them to Jesus, who will come not from Rome but from heaven.
He will transform the body of our humiliation that it may be conformed to the body of his glory,
Not a “vile body”, as older translations put it, but a lowly body, weak and mortal. God does not throw away our bodies; he will glorify them.
ch: The early Letter to Diognetus describes Christians in Paul’s spirit: they live on earth, but they are citizens of heaven, and they obey the laws while surpassing them by their lives. The Catechism teaches that in the resurrection Christ will raise our bodies, transformed into the likeness of his glorious body (CCC 999–1000). The hope of heaven does not take us out of the world; the Second Vatican Council teaches that it should rather urge us to work for a better earth (Gaudium et Spes 39).

r.h: I am the resurrection and the life
set: Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Martha and Mary, was a friend Jesus loved (11:3, 5). Jesus delayed two days before going to Judea, where his life was in danger (11:6–8). Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, about three kilometres from Jerusalem; the Greek says fifteen stadia. The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest of the signs in John’s Gospel, and it leads the authorities to resolve to put Jesus to death (11:53).

The “Jews” who had come to console the sisters are their neighbours and friends from Jerusalem, carrying out the work of mercy of comforting mourners. In this chapter many of them come to believe (11:45).
str: vv. 17–19: four days in the tomb; many come to console.
vv. 20–22: Martha goes to meet Jesus: “Lord, if you had been here.”
vv. 23–24: “Your brother will rise again”; “on the last day”.
vv. 25–26: “I am the resurrection and the life… Do you believe this?”
v. 27: Martha’s confession: the Messiah, the Son of God.
kw: Lazarus has been dead four days. A later Jewish tradition held that the soul stayed near the body for three days; after four days death was beyond doubt. The sign will be undeniable.

Martha believes in the resurrection of the dead at the last day, as many Jews of her time did, especially the Pharisees (Acts 23:8). Jesus brings that hope into the present: the resurrection is a person, and he is here.
The fifth of the seven “I am” sayings with an image in John (bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine). It echoes the name of God revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14).
vv: When Jesus arrived, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.
Jesus seems to arrive too late. In John, God’s timing is never late; it serves a greater sign (11:4).
Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
Martha speaks with the honesty of a friend. Her grief and her faith stand side by side, and Jesus does not rebuke her.
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live,

Textual note: a few early witnesses, among them a papyrus of the third century, lack the words “and the life”. Nearly all manuscripts have them, and the Church reads them. Those who believe will die in body, yet live; and those who live in him will never die the death that separates from God.
Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.
Martha’s confession is as full as Peter’s at Caesarea Philippi (Matthew 16:16). It is almost the very confession for which John wrote his Gospel (20:31).
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it teaches that Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: “I am the resurrection and the life” (CCC 994). The Church reads this Gospel at funerals and prays in her liturgy that for the faithful life is changed, not ended. Martha, often remembered for being busy (Luke 10:40), is here the one who makes the great confession; the Church honours Martha, Mary and Lazarus together as saints (29 July in the Roman calendar).

qa: If Jesus is the resurrection, why do believers still die?

Jesus does not promise that believers will escape bodily death; Lazarus himself would die again. He promises that death no longer has the last word: those who believe in him, “even though they die, will live”. The Catechism teaches that for those who die in Christ’s grace, death is a participation in his death, so that they may also share his Resurrection (CCC 1006, 1010).
study: Paul says, “our citizenship is in heaven.” In what everyday choices does my true homeland show?
Martha brought both her grief and her faith to Jesus. What sorrow do I need to bring to him honestly today?

lead: Both readings are about belonging to Christ when it costs something. Paul has every right to be supported by the Corinthians, yet he gives up that right so that nothing may hinder the Gospel. In John, many disciples leave Jesus after his teaching on the bread of life, and Peter, speaking for the Twelve, stays: “Lord, to whom can we go?” In the Season of the Apostles the Church learns from both: an apostle holds his rights loosely and holds on to Christ.

r.h: Am I not an apostle?
set: Paul has just told the Corinthians to give up eating food offered to idols if it would make a weaker brother fall (8:13). Now he shows that he lives by the same rule. Some at Corinth questioned whether he was truly an apostle, perhaps because he worked with his hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) and refused their money. He answers that he has all the rights of an apostle, and has chosen not to use them.
str: vv. 1–2: Paul’s credentials: he has seen the Lord, and the Corinthians themselves are the seal of his apostleship.
vv. 3–6: the rights of an apostle: food and drink, a companion, freedom from manual work.
vv. 7–10: proofs from daily life (soldier, vinedresser, shepherd) and from the law of Moses.
vv. 11–12: the conclusion: he has the right, but he has not used it, for the sake of the Gospel.
kw: One who is sent with the authority of the sender. For Paul an apostle must have seen the Risen Lord (15:8) and been sent by him. That is why his first proof is: “Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?”
The mark pressed into wax to show that a document is genuine. The faith of the Corinthians is the Lord’s own stamp on Paul’s work.
The word runs through the whole chapter. Paul does not deny his rights; he shows that love may lay them down. The same freedom marks his Master, who “emptied himself” (Philippians 2:7).
vv: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?
Paul saw the Risen Lord on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3–6). His freedom is not freedom from service but freedom for it.
Do we not have the right to be accompanied by a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?

The Greek says literally “a sister, a wife”. Many read it of the apostles’ wives, and Peter was married (Mark 1:30). Some Fathers, among them St Jerome, read it of devout women who served the apostles, as women served Jesus (Luke 8:3). On “the brothers of the Lord”, see the question below.
You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.
Paul quotes Deuteronomy 25:4. The law that cared for the working ox teaches, all the more, care for the one who labours for the Gospel.
Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.
This is the heart of the passage. The Gospel must never seem to be for sale.
ch: The Church has always taught both halves of this reading: the faithful should support those who serve them in the Gospel (see Luke 10:7; Code of Canon Law, canon 222), and those who serve should not seek gain. The Second Vatican Council asks priests to use goods only for their right purposes and to embrace a voluntary poverty that makes them more like Christ (Presbyterorum Ordinis 17). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, praises Paul for going beyond what was commanded, taking no wages where he could have taken them (in substance, Homilies on 1 Corinthians).

r.h: To whom can we go?
set: The long discourse in the synagogue at Capernaum is over (6:59). Jesus has said that he is the bread of life and that his flesh must be eaten and his blood drunk. Many who followed him find it too hard (6:60). These verses tell the result: a great falling away, and a small, firm confession of faith from the Twelve. John’s Gospel has no scene at Caesarea Philippi; this is its counterpart, Peter’s confession.
str: vv. 64–65: Jesus knows who do not believe; no one comes unless the Father grants it.
v. 66: many disciples turn back.
v. 67: the question to the Twelve: “Do you also wish to go away?”
vv. 68–69: Peter’s answer: the words of eternal life; the Holy One of God.
vv. 70–71: yet one of the chosen Twelve will betray him.
kw: A rare title, used elsewhere by an unclean spirit who knows who Jesus is (Mark 1:24). Peter confesses that Jesus belongs wholly to God and comes from him.
we have come to believe and know
Both verbs are in the Greek perfect tense: a faith begun in the past that still stands. In John, believing and knowing go together; faith is a way of knowing.
Literally “slanderer, one who sets apart”. Jesus does not say Judas was created evil. He was chosen and loved, and he let the adversary enter his heart (13:2, 27).
vv: Because of this many of his disciples turned back and no longer went about with him.
It is worth noticing that Jesus does not run after them to soften his words. He does not trade the truth of the Eucharist for numbers.
So Jesus asked the twelve, “Do you also wish to go away?”
The question respects their freedom. Love that forces is not love.
Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.
Peter does not say he has understood everything. He says there is no one else. Trust comes before full understanding.
ch: The Catechism recalls this scene when it speaks of the Eucharist: the first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the Passion scandalized them, and the Lord’s question “Will you also go away?” echoes through the ages as an invitation to discover that only he has the words of eternal life, and that to receive the gift of his Eucharist in faith is to receive the Lord himself (CCC 1336). St Augustine, preaching on this passage, admires Peter’s answer: he speaks for the Twelve, and he puts believing before knowing; we believe so that we may know (in substance, Tractates on John 27).

qa: Paul speaks of “the brothers of the Lord”. Did Jesus have brothers?

The Church has always believed that Mary remained a virgin. In Hebrew and Aramaic, and in the Bible’s Greek, “brother” is used for close relatives such as cousins (in the Hebrew of Genesis 13:8 Abram calls his nephew Lot his brother; NRSV kindred). James and Joseph, called brothers of Jesus (Matthew 13:55), are sons of another Mary (Matthew 27:56). The Catechism explains that these are close relations of Jesus, according to an Old Testament way of speaking (CCC 500).
study: Paul gave up a right so that the Gospel would not be hindered. Is there a right or comfort I could lay down for the sake of someone’s faith?
When Christ’s teaching is hard for me, what helps me to say with Peter, “Lord, to whom can we go?”

lead: Both readings speak of belonging. Paul tells the Corinthians that their bodies belong to the Lord, bought at a price and made a temple of the Holy Spirit, and will be raised by God’s power. In John, Jesus promises that whoever the Father gives him he will never drive away, and that he will raise them up on the last day. The body that receives Christ is not a thing we may use as we like; it is held in the hands of the One who will raise it.

r.h: Your body is a temple
set: Corinth was a busy port city, known in the ancient world for loose living. Some Christians there seem to have taken Paul’s teaching on freedom from the Law and turned it into a slogan, “All things are lawful for me.” They may also have thought that what the body does does not touch the soul. Paul answers with the faith of the Church: the body belongs to the Lord, it will rise, and the Spirit dwells in it.
str: vv. 12–14: two Corinthian slogans answered: not all things are beneficial; the body is for the Lord, and God will raise it.
vv. 15–17: your bodies are members of Christ; union with a prostitute contradicts union with the Lord.
v. 18: shun fornication, a sin against one’s own body.
vv. 19–20: the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit; you were bought with a price; glorify God in your body.
¶ The NRSV prints the Corinthian slogans in quotation marks. Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks, but most scholars agree that Paul is quoting his readers here.
kw: For Paul the body is not a shell for the soul; it is the whole person in his visible, bodily life. That is why he can say that the body is “for the Lord” and will be raised.
The inner shrine where God dwells, not the whole temple area. Paul used the word for the whole community (3:16); here he uses it for each Christian’s body.
A word of the market place, used of buying a slave. Christians were bought at the price of Christ’s blood (1 Peter 1:18–19), and now belong to a new and loving Master.
vv: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are beneficial.
Paul does not deny Christian freedom. He asks what it is for. A freedom that makes us slaves of our appetites has destroyed itself.
And God raised the Lord and will also raise us by his power.
The resurrection of the body is the reason for Christian moral life. What God will raise must not be treated as worthless.
Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, which you have from God, and that you are not your own?
The Spirit is not a guest in the soul only. He dwells in the whole person, body included.
For you were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.
Chastity, care for health, modesty and work are all ways to glorify God in the body.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it teaches the resurrection of the body: the body is meant for the Lord, and the Lord for the body; your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit; you are not your own; so glorify God in your body (CCC 1004). It also teaches that the human body shares in the dignity of the image of God and is intended to become, in the Body of Christ, a temple of the Spirit (CCC 364). On this ground the Church teaches chastity for every state of life, married and unmarried, as the integration of sexuality within the person (CCC 2337, 2348).

r.h: I will never drive away
set: Jesus is speaking at Capernaum, the day after the feeding of the five thousand. The crowd has asked for a sign like the manna, and he has answered, “I am the bread of life” (6:35). Now he speaks of the Father’s will: that none whom the Father gives him should be lost. When some of the crowd grumble, he tells them that coming to him is itself the Father’s gift.
str: vv. 37–40: the Father’s will: all he gives will come; none will be lost; all who believe will be raised on the last day.
vv. 41–42: the crowd complains: is not this the son of Joseph?
vv. 43–44: no one can come unless drawn by the Father; and I will raise that person up.
kw: A strong double negative in Greek: I will surely not throw out. Whoever comes to Christ, however poor or sinful, is not turned away.
Words of the same root are used in the Greek Old Testament for Israel grumbling against Moses in the wilderness over food (Exodus 16:2, 7). The scene of the manna is being lived again.
A strong word, used for drawing a net full of fish (21:6, 11). The Father draws people to the Son, and the Son will draw all people to himself when he is lifted up (12:32).
vv: Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and anyone who comes to me I will never drive away
Two truths stand side by side: God’s gift and our coming. Grace does not cancel our freedom; it makes our coming possible.
And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.
Four times in this chapter Jesus promises to raise up on the last day (6:39, 40, 44, 54). Eternal life begins now in faith and reaches its fullness in the resurrection of the body.
No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me
The first step toward Christ is never only our own. Every desire for God is already God at work in us.
ch: St Augustine, commenting on verse 44, asks how anyone can be drawn if he comes of his own will, and answers that we are drawn not by force but by delight and love, as a sheep is drawn by a green branch held out to it (in substance, Tractates on John 26). The Catechism teaches that the preparation of man for grace is already a work of grace, and that God’s initiative calls for man’s response in freedom (CCC 2001–2002). John’s “the Jews” in verse 41 means here the Galilean crowd that questions Jesus, not the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus and his disciples were themselves Jews, and the Church warns against reading such words as blame on the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).

qa: If no one can come unless the Father draws him, are some people not drawn at all?

The Church teaches that God “desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4), and that Christ died for all without exception (CCC 605). The Father draws all; but his drawing is not force, and a person can resist it. Jesus’ words warn the grumblers not to trust in their own judgment, “whose father and mother we know”, but to let God teach them.
study: Paul says, “you are not your own.” How does this truth change the way I treat my body and the bodies of others?
Jesus says he will never drive away anyone who comes to him. Who in my family or parish needs to hear this today?

lead: On this Thursday, the day of the week of the Last Supper, the Church gives thanks for the gift of the Body and Blood of Christ, and the four readings walk through the whole history of that gift. In Genesis a mysterious priest-king, Melchizedek, brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram. Through Malachi, God rebukes priests who despise his table and foretells a pure offering made to his name in every place, among the nations. Paul hands on what he received from the Lord: on the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread and the cup and said, “This is my body,” “This cup is the new covenant in my blood.” And in John, Jesus says plainly that his flesh is true food and his blood true drink. Figure, prophecy, institution and teaching: the readings lead from the bread of Melchizedek to the altar of every Holy Qurbana.

r.h: Bread and wine from the priest of God Most High
set: Abram has just won a surprising victory. Four eastern kings, led by Chedorlaomer, had raided the cities of the plain and carried off Abram’s nephew Lot. With his household Abram pursued them, rescued Lot and brought back the captives and their goods (14:1–16). As he returns, two kings come out to meet him: the king of Sodom, and Melchizedek, king of Salem.

Melchizedek appears in the story without parents, ancestors or later history, and then disappears. Salem was understood in Israel as Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2). Psalm 110:4 speaks of a king who is “a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”, and the Letter to the Hebrews applies this to Christ, a priest not by descent from Aaron but by the power of an indestructible life (Hebrews 7:1–17).
str: v. 17: the king of Sodom comes out to meet the victorious Abram.
v. 18: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings out bread and wine.
vv. 19–20a: he blesses Abram and blesses God Most High.
v. 20b: Abram gives him a tenth of everything.

¶ After these verses the king of Sodom offers Abram the goods, and Abram refuses them (14:21–24). The contrast is deliberate: from Melchizedek Abram receives a blessing; from Sodom he will take nothing.
kw: The name means “my king is righteousness” or “king of righteousness”. Hebrews draws out both his name and his city: king of righteousness, and king of Salem, that is, king of peace (Hebrews 7:2).
A title of God found also in the Psalms (Psalm 78:35). Abram himself identifies God Most High with the Lord (14:22).
This is the first time the Bible uses the word “priest”. Long before the priesthood of Aaron, a priest appears who offers bread and wine and blesses.
vv: And King Melchizedek of Salem brought out bread and wine; he was priest of God Most High.

Some scholars read the bread and wine as royal hospitality for weary soldiers. The verse at once adds that he was a priest, and the Fathers saw in his gift an offering: a figure of the bread and wine that Christ, the true priest-king, would make his Body and Blood.
Blessed be Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth
The one who blesses is greater than the one blessed (Hebrews 7:7). The father of Israel, bearer of the promise, bows to receive a blessing.
And Abram gave him one-tenth of everything.
The tithe recognises Melchizedek as God’s priest. A tenth given to God says that all comes from him.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Church sees in the gesture of the priest-king Melchizedek, who brought out bread and wine, a prefiguring of her own offering (CCC 1333), and that Christ is the unique high priest after the order of Melchizedek (CCC 1544). St Cyprian of Carthage, writing about the cup of the Lord, says that in Melchizedek the sacrifice of the Lord was foreshown, since he offered bread and wine, and Christ offered the same, that is, his body and blood (in substance, Letter 63).

r.h: A pure offering in every place
set: Malachi is the last book of the prophets in our Bibles. The name means “my messenger” (3:1). He speaks after the return from exile, when the Temple had been rebuilt (it was dedicated about 515 BC) and worship had grown tired and careless. The Law required that animals offered to God be without blemish (Leviticus 22:20–22; Deuteronomy 15:21), but the priests were accepting the blind, the lame and the sick.
The book is built as a series of disputes. God makes a charge, the people answer “How have we…?”, and God replies. Today’s verses belong to the first charge against the priests (1:6–2:9).
str: v. 7: the charge: polluted food on my altar; you think the Lord’s table may be despised.
v. 8: the proof: blind, lame and sick animals; would your governor accept them?
vv. 9–10: an ironic call to pray, and a wish that someone would shut the temple doors.
v. 11: the great promise: from the rising of the sun to its setting, a pure offering among the nations.
v. 12: the contrast: but you profane it.
kw: Malachi calls the altar the Lord’s table (1:7, 12). Paul will speak of “the table of the Lord” at which Christians share (1 Corinthians 10:21).
A gift brought to God, often a grain offering of flour and oil (Leviticus 2). The word is used broadly here for every gift offered to God’s name.
Clean, fit for God, the opposite of the “polluted” food of verse 7. What God desires is not only an unblemished gift but a pure heart that offers it.
vv: By offering polluted food on my altar. And you say, “How have we polluted it?”
The priests do not see their own sin. Carelessness in worship begins in the heart that no longer honours God as Father (1:6).
Try presenting that to your governor; will he be pleased with you or show you favor?
A sharp, homely question. We take care over gifts for those we honour; God deserves our best, not our leftovers.
For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering
The Hebrew uses participles with no main verb, so the verse can be read as present or future. Either way it looks beyond the one Temple in Jerusalem to worship among all nations, in every place.
ch: The earliest Christians read verse 11 as a prophecy of the Eucharist. The Didache, a very early Christian writing, tells believers to gather on the Lord’s day, break bread and give thanks, after confessing their sins, so that their sacrifice may be pure, and it quotes Malachi’s words about a pure sacrifice in every place (in substance, Didache 14). St Justin Martyr also applies the verse to the bread and cup of the Eucharist offered by Christians in every place (in substance, Dialogue with Trypho 41). The Council of Trent teaches that the Eucharistic sacrifice is the clean oblation foretold by Malachi, which no unworthiness of those who offer it can defile (Session 22, chapter 1).

r.h: This is my body that is for you
set: Paul is writing to correct an abuse. When the Corinthians gathered for the Lord’s Supper, which was then joined to a common meal, the rich ate and drank first and the poor went hungry (11:17–22). Paul says that this is not really to eat the Lord’s Supper (11:20). To bring them back he reminds them of what the Supper is, in words he had received and already handed on to them.
This is the oldest written account of the institution of the Eucharist, set down about AD 54, before the Gospels were written. Its wording is very close to Luke’s (Luke 22:19–20).
str: v. 23a: Paul hands on what he received from the Lord.
vv. 23b–25: the institution: the bread, “This is my body that is for you”; the cup, “the new covenant in my blood”; twice, “Do this in remembrance of me.”
v. 26: every celebration proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes.
vv. 27–29: eating unworthily; examine yourselves; discern the body.
v. 30: a warning from their own community.
kw: Technical words for passing on a sacred tradition, as rabbis passed on teaching to their disciples. Paul uses the same pair for the Creed of the Resurrection (15:3). The Eucharist is not Paul’s invention; it is the Lord’s gift, handed down.
Not a mere thinking back. In the Bible, to remember before God is to make present and effective what God has done, as at the Passover meal (Exodus 12:14).
To distinguish, to judge rightly. To discern the body is to recognise that this bread is the Lord’s Body, and also to honour the body of Christ that is the community, especially its poor (12:27).
vv: the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread
Paul ties the Eucharist to history: a certain night, a betrayal. The gift was given at the very moment of rejection.
and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “This is my body that is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
“Given thanks” is eucharistēsas in Greek, from which the name Eucharist comes. The body is “for you”: given in sacrifice.
This cup is the new covenant in my blood.
The words recall the covenant at Sinai sealed with blood (Exodus 24:8) and the new covenant promised by Jeremiah (Jeremiah 31:31).
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
Every Holy Qurbana looks back to the Cross and forward to the Lord’s return. It stands between Calvary and the Second Coming.
For all who eat and drink without discerning the body, eat and drink judgment against themselves.
Paul is not frightening the humble away; he is calling the careless to faith and love.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the command “Do this in memory of me” is directed at the liturgical celebration, by the apostles and their successors, of the memorial of Christ, of his life, death, Resurrection and intercession with the Father (CCC 1341), and that in the liturgy this memorial makes the events of salvation present (CCC 1363). On verses 27–29 it teaches that anyone conscious of a grave sin must receive the sacrament of Reconciliation before coming to communion (CCC 1385). The Council of Trent teaches that in the Eucharist the body and blood of Christ, together with his soul and divinity, are truly, really and substantially contained (CCC 1374).

r.h: My flesh is true food
set: John does not tell the institution of the Eucharist at the Last Supper; there he tells of the washing of the feet (13:1–15). Instead he gives, in chapter 6, Jesus’ long teaching on the bread of life, spoken at Passover time (6:4) after the feeding of the five thousand. In these verses the teaching reaches its plainest and boldest words.

Until now Jesus has spoken of believing in him as the bread from heaven. From verse 51 he speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood. The hearers understand him literally, and he does not correct them; he says it again more strongly.
str: v. 51: I am the living bread; the bread I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.
v. 52: the dispute: how can this man give us his flesh to eat?
vv. 53–56: four sayings about eating his flesh and drinking his blood: life, eternal life, true food, abiding.
vv. 57–58: as I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me; not like the manna.
v. 59: the setting: the synagogue at Capernaum.
kw: The word of John 1:14, “the Word became flesh”. The flesh Jesus gives in the Eucharist is the flesh he took from Mary and offered on the Cross “for the life of the world”.
From verse 54 John changes from the ordinary verb for eating to trōgō, a very physical word, to chew or munch. The change makes it hard to read Jesus’ words as a mere figure of speech.
A favourite word of John (15:4–10). Communion is not a passing visit; it is a mutual dwelling: “they abide in me, and I in them.”
vv: I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever; and the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.
“For the life of the world”: the language of sacrifice. The Eucharist and the Cross are one gift.
So Jesus said to them, “Very truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.
Drinking blood was forbidden by the Law (Leviticus 17:10–14), because the life is in the blood. Jesus gives his own blood so that his life may be in us.
for my flesh is true food and my blood is true drink.
“True” here means real, genuine. The manna was a figure; this is the reality it pointed to.
Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.
The life that flows from the Father into the Son flows from the Son into those who receive him. Communion draws us into the life of the Trinity.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in the synagogue at Capernaum Jesus prepared for the institution of the Eucharist, calling himself the bread of life come down from heaven (CCC 1338), and it quotes verse 53 to show the urgency of his invitation to receive him (CCC 1384) and verse 56 to teach that communion deepens our union with Christ (CCC 1391). St Ignatius of Antioch, writing about AD 110, warns against those who stay away from the Eucharist because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins and which the Father raised up (in substance, To the Smyrnaeans 7). St Augustine, preaching on this chapter, cries out: O sacrament of devotion, O sign of unity, O bond of charity (Tractates on John 26; quoted in CCC 1398).

qa: Is the Eucharist only a symbol of Christ?

No. The Church believes that by the consecration the whole substance of the bread becomes the Body of Christ and the whole substance of the wine his Blood; the Council of Trent called this change transubstantiation (CCC 1376). Christ is present truly, really and substantially, not only as in a sign (CCC 1374). John 6 points the same way: when the hearers object, Jesus does not soften his words but repeats them more strongly, and lets many disciples go rather than turn the teaching into a figure of speech (6:66).
Who was Melchizedek, and why does he matter for the Eucharist?

Genesis tells only that he was king of Salem and priest of God Most High, that he brought out bread and wine, and that he blessed Abram. Psalm 110 and the Letter to the Hebrews make him a figure of Christ, an eternal priest who is also king. The Church sees in his offering of bread and wine a first sign of the Eucharist (CCC 1333).
Paul warns about receiving “in an unworthy manner”. Should I stay away if I feel unworthy?

No one is worthy of the Lord by his own merit; we receive him by grace. Paul is warning against careless and loveless reception, like the Corinthians who humiliated the poor at the Lord’s Supper. The Church teaches that anyone aware of a grave sin should first receive the sacrament of Reconciliation (CCC 1385). For everyone else, a humble sense of unworthiness is not a barrier but the right way to come.
rite: In our East Syriac tradition the Eucharist is called the Holy Qurbana, from a Syriac word meaning “offering”, the gift brought near to God. Malachi’s “pure offering” and Melchizedek’s bread and wine are fulfilled in it. The Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, which our Church prays, is among the oldest Eucharistic prayers still in use, and the most solemn form of our Qurbana is called the Raza, the Mystery.

Many Syro-Malabar families keep a home custom on Pesaha Thursday: the father of the family breaks the Pesaha bread and shares it with the household, in memory of the Lord’s Supper. Today’s Thursday feast can help families connect that home table with the altar, and to remember Paul’s warning: the Lord’s Body is not rightly received where the poor are forgotten.
study: Melchizedek blessed Abram before Abram gave him anything. How does the Holy Qurbana begin with God’s gift rather than with mine?
Malachi rebuked priests who brought God their leftovers. What would it mean for my family to bring God our best in worship: time, attention, preparation?
Paul says each Qurbana proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes. How can my communion today be both a memory of the Cross and a hope for his coming?
Jesus says, “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them.” Where in my week do I need to let him abide more deeply?

lead: Both readings ask where true wisdom comes from. Paul tells the Corinthians, proud of their favourite teachers, that the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God, and that all things are theirs only because they belong to Christ. In John, Jesus says that those who are taught by God come to him, because he alone has seen the Father and is himself the bread of life. True wisdom is not something we own; it is Someone we receive.

r.h: All things are yours
set: The Corinthian church was divided into groups: “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos”, “I belong to Cephas” (1:12). Each group boasted of its leader as if he were a school of wisdom. Paul has shown that the cross looks like foolishness to the world (1:18–25), and that teachers are only servants and fellow workers in God’s field (3:5–9). Now he draws his conclusion.
str: v. 18: do not deceive yourselves; become a fool in order to become wise.
vv. 19–20: two proofs from Scripture: God catches the wise in their craftiness (Job 5:13); the Lord knows their thoughts are futile (Psalm 94:11).
vv. 21–23: do not boast in human leaders: all things are yours, you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
kw: Not learning as such, which Paul himself had. It is a way of thinking that measures everything by success, status and cleverness, and so cannot understand a crucified Messiah.
A favourite word of Paul in this letter. The only right boast is in the Lord (1:31, quoting Jeremiah 9:24).
The Corinthians wanted to belong to one teacher. Paul turns it round: the teachers belong to them, and so does the whole world, life, death, present and future, because they belong to Christ.
vv: If you think that you are wise in this age, you should become fools so that you may become wise.
Humility is the door of wisdom. Whoever thinks he already knows cannot be taught.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.
Paul reverses the Corinthians’ scale of values. What the world calls foolish, the cross, is God’s wisdom (1:24).
whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future
A breathtaking list. Even death is “ours”, because in Christ it has become the way to life.
and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.
Christ “belongs to God” as the Son who receives everything from the Father and returns everything to him (15:28). The chain of belonging ends in the Father’s love.
ch: The Second Vatican Council closes its reflection on human activity spoiled by sin with these verses: all things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (Gaudium et Spes 37). The Christian does not despise the world or human wisdom; he receives them as gifts and orders them to Christ. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, notes that Paul humbles the proud teachers by making them belong to their hearers, and lifts the hearers up by giving them all things (in substance, Homilies on 1 Corinthians).

r.h: Taught by God
set: Jesus is still speaking in the synagogue at Capernaum. He has said that no one can come to him unless the Father draws him (6:44). Now he explains how the Father draws: by teaching. He quotes the prophets and then repeats, more plainly, the claim that gave offence: “I am the bread of life.”
str: v. 45: it is written, “they shall all be taught by God”; whoever has learned from the Father comes to me.
v. 46: only the one who is from God has seen the Father.
v. 47: whoever believes has eternal life.
vv. 48–50: I am the bread of life; your ancestors ate manna and died; this bread is for not dying.
kw: Jesus is quoting Isaiah 54:13, a promise for the restored Jerusalem: “All your children shall be taught by the Lord.” Jeremiah too promised a covenant in which God himself would teach every heart (Jeremiah 31:34).

In John, Jesus often says “I am” with an image: bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine. The words also echo the divine name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14), and sometimes stand alone (8:58).
The bread God gave Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16). It was a true gift of God, but it fed bodily life only. Jesus does not despise it; he says it pointed beyond itself.
vv: It is written in the prophets, ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me.
The Father’s drawing is not blind force; it is teaching that the heart can hear and accept. Every true seeker of God is on the way to Christ.
Not that anyone has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.
The Prologue said the same: “No one has ever seen God. It is God the only Son, who is close to the Father’s heart, who has made him known” (1:18).
Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.
Jesus speaks to his own people of “your ancestors”, as Moses and the prophets did. The point is not blame but contrast: the manna sustained them for a time; the bread he gives sustains for ever.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus, because he has seen the Father, is the only one who knows him and can reveal him (CCC 151, quoting 6:46), and that the Church sees in the manna in the desert a prefiguring of the Eucharist, the true bread from heaven (CCC 1094). St Augustine taught that Christ is the teacher within: human teachers speak to the ear, but it is Christ dwelling in the heart who teaches us to recognise the truth (in substance, The Teacher).

study: Paul says, “All things are yours… and you belong to Christ.” Which gifts in my life do I hold as if they were mine alone, rather than as gifts held in Christ?
Jesus says that all who are taught by God come to him. How do I let God teach me: in Scripture, in prayer, in the Church’s teaching, in the people he sends?

lead: The two readings meet at a table. Paul tells the Corinthians that the cup we bless and the bread we break are a sharing in the blood and body of Christ, and that because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. In John, Jesus takes five barley loaves, gives thanks, and feeds a great crowd, and nothing is lost. The bread that Christ gives makes the many one, and there is always enough.

r.h: One bread, one body
set: Corinth was full of temples, and much of the meat sold in the market had first been offered to the gods. Feasts in temple dining halls were a normal part of social life. Some Corinthian Christians thought that, since idols are nothing, they could join in such meals without scruple (8:1–10). Paul has warned them with the example of Israel in the wilderness (10:1–13). Now he speaks of the Lord’s Supper: those who share in Christ’s table cannot also share in the table of idols.
str: vv. 14–15: flee idolatry; judge for yourselves.
vv. 16–17: the cup and the bread are a sharing in Christ’s blood and body; one bread, one body.
v. 18: Israel’s sacrifices make those who eat them partners in the altar.
vv. 19–21: the idol is nothing, but pagan sacrifice is partnership with demons: you cannot share both tables.
v. 22: do not provoke the Lord to jealousy.
kw: A Jewish name for the cup of wine over which the blessing was said at a festive meal. Jesus took such a cup at the Last Supper, and the Church blesses it still.
Paul draws a conclusion from the single loaf broken at the Supper: many share one bread, and so they become one body. The Eucharist does not only express the Church’s unity; it makes it.
An echo of the Song of Moses, where Israel “made me jealous with what is no god” (Deuteronomy 32:21). God’s jealousy is the love of a husband who will not share his bride with idols.
vv: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?
Paul does not argue for the Real Presence; he takes it for granted, and builds his warning on it. Because the bread is truly a sharing in Christ’s body, eating it binds us to him.
Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
Communion is never private. To receive Christ’s body is to be joined to all who receive it, the poor and the stranger included.
You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.
Faith asks for an undivided heart. Today the “other table” may be money, power or superstition, wherever we seek what only God can give.
ch: The Catechism quotes verses 16–17 to teach that the Eucharist makes the Church: those who receive it are united more closely to Christ, and Christ unites them to all the faithful in one body (CCC 1396). It also quotes St Augustine’s words to the newly baptized: if you are the body and members of Christ, it is your own mystery that is placed on the Lord’s table; be what you see, and receive what you are (in substance, Sermon 272; CCC 1396).

r.h: Five barley loaves
set: This is the only miracle of Jesus’ public ministry, apart from the Resurrection, that all four Gospels tell. John sets it near Passover (6:4), the feast of the Exodus and the manna, and on a mountain, as Moses received the Law on a mountain. The scene opens the whole chapter on the bread of life, and the crowd’s reaction, wanting to make him king, shows how easily a sign can be misunderstood.
str: vv. 1–4: setting: across the sea, a large crowd, the mountain, Passover near.
vv. 5–9: Jesus tests Philip; Andrew finds a boy with five barley loaves and two fish.
vv. 10–11: the people sit on the grass; Jesus gives thanks and distributes.
vv. 12–13: “Gather up the fragments”: twelve baskets left over.
vv. 14–15: “This is indeed the prophet”; they want to make him king; he withdraws alone.
kw: John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs”: works that point beyond themselves to who he is. The feeding is a sign of the bread of life that he will explain in the synagogue.

The pieces broken from the loaves. Very early Christian prayer used the same word for the broken Eucharistic bread (Didache 9). “So that nothing may be lost” recalls the Father’s will that none be lost (6:39).
The crowd recalls Moses’ promise that God would raise up a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15). Moses gave manna; here is one who gives bread in the wilderness.
vv: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are they among so many people?”

Barley bread was the food of the poor. Only John mentions the boy and the barley, which recalls Elisha feeding a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, with some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). Christ begins with the little that someone is willing to give.
Then Jesus took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated
Took, gave thanks, distributed: the words of every Eucharist. John’s first readers would hear in them the Lord’s Supper.
When they were satisfied, he told his disciples, “Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.”
God’s abundance is never wasteful. Twelve baskets, a number that recalls the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles: enough for the whole people of God.
When Jesus realized that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, he withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
They want a king who will fill their stomachs. Jesus is King, but not in that way; his throne will be the Cross (19:19).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the miracles of the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord says the blessing, breaks and distributes the loaves through his disciples to feed the multitude, prefigure the superabundance of the unique bread of his Eucharist (CCC 1335). St Augustine remarks that God works greater wonders every day, when a few seeds multiply into whole harvests, but we no longer marvel at them; so in this miracle he did by his own hand what he does always in the fields, to awaken us to see him at work (in substance, Tractates on John 24).

qa: Why did Jesus withdraw when the crowd wanted to make him king?

He is King, but his kingdom is not of this world (18:36). The crowd wanted a ruler who would give bread and drive out the Romans. The Catechism notes that Jesus accepted the title of Messiah with reserve, because many of his contemporaries understood it in too human and political a sense (CCC 439). He would reveal his kingship on the Cross.
study: Paul says that because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. Whom do I find it hard to see as one body with me when we receive the Holy Qurbana together?
A boy gave five barley loaves, and Christ fed thousands. What small thing can I place in his hands today?

lead: This Sunday’s four readings move from a mountain to a roadside. In Deuteronomy, Moses recalls the Lord’s word at Horeb: “You have stayed long enough at this mountain”; the people must set out and take the land promised to their ancestors. In Isaiah, God grieves over a people wounded from head to foot, whose sores have not been bound up or softened with oil. Paul answers the Corinthians’ questions about marriage, teaching that husband and wife belong to each other in mutual self-giving. And in Luke, Jesus tells of a Samaritan who stops on the road, pours oil and wine on a stranger’s wounds and binds them up. The God who sends his people out from the mountain sends them to the wounded, and the love he asks of us begins at home and reaches to the stranger. In the Season of the Apostles, the Church hears again: go, and do likewise.

r.h: You have stayed long enough at this mountain
set: Deuteronomy is set in the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, in the fortieth year after the Exodus (1:3). Israel is about to enter the land, and Moses, who will not cross the Jordan with them, speaks his last words. The book is mostly made of his great speeches, in which he retells the journey and renews the covenant. Its name comes from the Greek for “second law”, because the Law of Sinai is here repeated and explained.

Deuteronomy calls the mountain of the covenant Horeb, the name it uses for Sinai. Israel had camped there for about a year (Numbers 10:11–12). Today’s verses are the start of Moses’ first speech: the journey begins with God’s command to leave.
str: v. 5: beyond the Jordan, in Moab, Moses begins to explain the law.
v. 6: God’s word at Horeb: you have stayed long enough at this mountain.
v. 7: resume your journey: the regions of the land, as far as the Euphrates.
v. 8: see, I have set the land before you; go in and take possession, as I swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
kw: The verb bē’ēr means to make plain, to explain clearly. Deuteronomy is the Law not only given but taught, so that each generation may understand and love it.
Literally “much for you is the dwelling”: enough sitting still. Sinai was the place of covenant, but it was not the goal. God’s people are a pilgrim people.
To inherit, to occupy. The land is a gift sworn to the patriarchs, yet Israel must walk into it. God’s gifts are received by those who set out.
vv: Beyond the Jordan in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to expound this law as follows:
Before the people enter the land, they are taught. Faith that will last in a new place needs a clear understanding of God’s word.
The Lord our God spoke to us at Horeb, saying, “You have stayed long enough at this mountain.
It was good to be at the mountain where God spoke, but God does not let his people settle there. The experience of God is meant to send us out.
See, I have set the land before you; go in and take possession of the land that I swore to your ancestors, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob
The promise to the patriarchs (Genesis 12:7; 26:3; 28:13) is about to be fulfilled. God keeps his word across centuries.
ch: The Second Vatican Council calls the Church a pilgrim people, on the way to the heavenly homeland (Lumen Gentium 48–50). Pope Francis recalls that this dynamic of “going forth” runs through the whole word of God, from Abraham and Moses to the apostles, and that today all of us are called to go forth from our comfort zone to reach the peripheries (Evangelii Gaudium 20). St Gregory of Nyssa, in his Life of Moses, taught that the soul that truly seeks God never stands still, but always goes on to more (in substance).

r.h: No soundness in it
set: Isaiah son of Amoz preached in Jerusalem in the eighth century before Christ, from the time of King Uzziah to that of Hezekiah (about 740 to 700 BC). Verse 1 is the heading for the whole book. The chapter then opens like a court case: heaven and earth are called as witnesses, as in the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:1), and God sets out his complaint against his children.

The picture of a land burned and occupied, with Jerusalem left alone like a hut in a field (vv. 7–8), fits the invasion of the Assyrian king Sennacherib in 701 BC, when many towns of Judah were taken and Jerusalem alone survived. Many scholars date this passage to that time.
str: v. 1: the heading: Isaiah’s vision in the days of four kings of Judah.
vv. 2–3: the charge: I reared children, and they rebelled; even the ox and the donkey know better.
v. 4: a lament over a sinful nation that has forsaken the Holy One of Israel.
vv. 5–6: the people as a body beaten from head to foot, its wounds untended.
vv. 7–9: the land devastated; Zion left like a hut; only a few survivors kept by the Lord.
kw: The word for what a prophet sees and hears from God. It covers the whole book: Isaiah’s message is not his own opinion but what God showed him.

Isaiah’s own title for God, used about twenty-five times in the book and rarely elsewhere. It goes back to his vision in the Temple: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts” (6:3). The Holy One has bound himself to Israel.
Those left after disaster. The thought of a faithful remnant, kept by God, runs through Isaiah (10:20–22). Paul quotes verse 9 to speak of God’s mercy in keeping a remnant (Romans 9:29).
vv: I reared children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against me.
God speaks first as a father, not as a judge. The sin is painful because the love was great.
The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s crib; but Israel does not know, my people do not understand.
Christian art and preaching placed the ox and the donkey at the manger in Bethlehem, drawing on this verse: the animals knew their Lord when many did not.
they have not been drained, or bound up, or softened with oil.
Oil was the ancient medicine for wounds. The people lie wounded and no one tends them. Today’s Gospel answers this verse: the Samaritan pours oil on the wounds and binds them up (Luke 10:34).
If the Lord of hosts had not left us a few survivors, we would have been like Sodom, and become like Gomorrah.
Even in judgment God does not let his people be wiped out. The remnant is a sign that his mercy is greater than their sin.
ch: The Church has always read the prophets’ rebukes as addressed first to herself, not to others: whenever God’s people forget him, the warning applies. The Catechism teaches that the prophets formed God’s people in the hope of salvation and that the poor and humble of the Lord, the remnant, would bear that hope (CCC 64). St Paul takes up verse 9 to show that God’s faithfulness to Israel has never failed, because he has always kept a remnant chosen by grace (Romans 9:29; 11:5).

r.h: Husband and wife belong to each other
set: Here a new section of the letter begins. The Corinthians had written to Paul with questions, and he takes them up one by one, each time with “Now concerning” (7:1, 25; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1). The first is about marriage and sexual life.

Some at Corinth had gone to the opposite extreme from the ones Paul rebuked in chapter 6. Thinking the body unimportant or unspiritual, they said, “It is well for a man not to touch a woman,” and some married couples seem to have stopped living together as husband and wife. Paul answers that marriage is good, that husband and wife owe each other their love, and that any abstaining must be by agreement, for a time, for prayer.
str: v. 1: the Corinthian slogan: it is well for a man not to touch a woman.
v. 2: Paul’s answer: each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.
vv. 3–4: mutual duty and mutual belonging of husband and wife.
v. 5: abstain only by agreement, for a set time, for prayer, then come together again.
vv. 6–7: a concession, not a command; Paul wishes all were as he is, but each has his own gift from God.
kw: Translated “conjugal rights”. Literally a debt. Paul uses the language of mutual obligation for love: each spouse owes the other himself or herself.
From the word for harmony, “sounding together”. Even a holy reason such as prayer must be decided together, not imposed by one on the other.
Paul calls both marriage and celibacy a gift of God (v. 7). Neither is a lower road; each is a calling.
vv: Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is well for a man not to touch a woman.”
The NRSV rightly prints the second half as the Corinthians’ own words. Paul quotes the slogan in order to correct it.
The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.
Paul begins with the husband’s duty to his wife, and then states the same for the wife. In the ancient world this equal language was striking.
For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.
The sentence is perfectly balanced. Each belongs to the other. This is not domination but mutual gift, the opposite of “All things are lawful for me.”
Do not deprive one another except perhaps by agreement for a set time, to devote yourselves to prayer, and then come together again
Prayer and married love are not rivals. Paul knows that times of fasting and prayer belong to Christian life, and also that the union of husband and wife is holy and protects their faithfulness.
I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has a particular gift from God
Paul was unmarried, and he valued that freedom for the Gospel (7:32–35). But he does not make his own path the rule for all.
ch: The Catechism teaches that both the sacrament of Matrimony and virginity for the Kingdom of God come from the Lord himself, and that esteem for virginity and the Christian understanding of marriage support each other (CCC 1620). Quoting the Second Vatican Council, it teaches that the acts by which spouses are intimately united are noble and honourable, and express and foster their mutual self-giving (CCC 2362; Gaudium et Spes 49). Pope St John Paul II wrote that virginity and marriage are two ways of expressing and living the one mystery of the covenant of God with his people (Familiaris Consortio 16).

r.h: Go and do likewise
set: Jesus has set his face toward Jerusalem (9:51), and just before this a Samaritan village refused to receive him (9:52–53). James and John wanted to call down fire; Jesus rebuked them. Now, on the same road, Jesus tells a story in which a Samaritan is the hero.

Samaritans lived in the hill country between Judea and Galilee. They worshipped the God of Israel and kept the five books of Moses, but on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem (John 4:20). For centuries there was bitterness on both sides, so much that John can say Jews and Samaritans did not share things in common (John 4:9). The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops about a thousand metres through lonely desert country, and was known for robbers.
str: vv. 25–28: the lawyer’s question about eternal life; the two great commandments; “do this, and you will live.”
v. 29: the second question: “And who is my neighbor?”
vv. 30–35: the parable: the man attacked; the priest and the Levite pass by; the Samaritan is moved with pity and cares for him.
vv. 36–37: Jesus’ question turned round: who became a neighbour? “Go and do likewise.”
kw: Not a lawyer of the courts, but an expert in the Law of Moses. He answers well, joining Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18, the same two commandments Jesus names elsewhere (Mark 12:29–31).
Literally “the one near”. The lawyer asks whom he must count as near. Jesus answers by asking who came near to the wounded man.

A strong word for compassion felt in the depths of the body. Luke uses it of Jesus at the widow’s funeral at Nain (7:13) and of the father who sees his lost son (15:20). The Samaritan feels as God feels.
vv: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.
The lawyer quotes his own Scriptures, and Jesus praises the answer. The commandment of love is not new to the Gospel; it is the heart of the Law given to Israel.
But wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?”
The question looks for a limit: whom may I leave out? The parable will remove the limit.
But a Samaritan while traveling came near him; and when he saw him, he was moved with pity.
The priest and the Levite saw him and passed by; the Samaritan saw him and came near. The difference is not in the seeing but in the heart.
He went to him and bandaged his wounds, having poured oil and wine on them.
Wine to clean, oil to soothe: the ordinary medicine of the time. Then the Samaritan gives his animal, his time and his money, and promises to return.
He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”
The lawyer does not say “the Samaritan”, perhaps unwilling to name him, but he gives the right answer. Jesus ends not with a definition but with a mission.
ch: Origen records an interpretation he received from an elder: the wounded man is Adam, Jerusalem is paradise and Jericho the world, the robbers are hostile powers, the priest and Levite stand for the Law and the prophets, the Samaritan is Christ, the inn is the Church, and the Samaritan’s promise to return is the Second Coming (in substance, Homilies on Luke 34). The Church has kept both readings together: Christ is the Good Samaritan who has come near to our wounds, and he sends us to do likewise. Pope St John Paul II called the parable the heart of the Gospel’s teaching on suffering: we are not allowed to pass by on the other side (in substance, Salvifici Doloris 28–30). Pope Francis built a whole chapter of Fratelli Tutti (2020) on this parable.

qa: Why did the priest and the Levite pass by?

The parable does not say. Some suggest they feared becoming ritually unclean by touching a body that might be dead (Leviticus 21:1), but they were going down from Jerusalem, and the story gives no reason. Jesus is not accusing priests or Levites as a group, nor the Jewish people; he and his hearers were Jews, and the lawyer’s own answer comes from the Law. The parable warns every religious person, ourselves first, that worship and duty do not excuse us from mercy.
Who were the Samaritans, and why does it matter that the hero is one?

They were a people of the old northern kingdom’s land who worshipped the God of Israel on Mount Gerizim and kept the books of Moses. Between them and the Jews of Judea there was long mistrust (John 4:9). By making a Samaritan the one who shows mercy, Jesus breaks down the walls we build between “our people” and “others”. Luke shows the same openness when Jesus heals ten lepers and only the Samaritan returns to give thanks (17:16).
Does Paul look down on marriage in 1 Corinthians 7?

No. He corrects those who did. He insists that husband and wife give themselves to each other, calls any abstaining a matter of mutual agreement for a short time, and names both marriage and celibacy as gifts of God (7:7). The Church teaches that Matrimony is a sacrament and that virginity and marriage support each other (CCC 1620).
rite: In the Season of the Apostles our Church remembers how the Gospel went out from Jerusalem to the nations, and how Mar Thoma Shleeha brought it to our land. Moses’ words, “You have stayed long enough at this mountain,” speak to every Syro-Malabar parish and eparchy: the faith we received is meant to go out, and our missionaries in India and abroad carry it on. Every Holy Qurbana ends with a blessing that sends us back into the world; we leave the altar to find the wounded on the road.

Today’s readings also speak to our families. In the Syro-Malabar wedding the bridegroom ties the minnu and gives the manthrakodi, signs of the gift of himself to his bride and of the life they will share. Paul’s teaching that husband and wife belong to each other is lived in such homes. Our hospitals, palliative care and parish charities, and every family that takes in the sick and the old, continue the work of the Good Samaritan.
study: God said, “You have stayed long enough at this mountain.” Where in my faith have I settled down, and where is God asking me to set out?
Isaiah sees a people with wounds that no one has bound up. Whose wounds in my family or parish have been left untended?
Paul speaks of husband and wife belonging to each other by mutual agreement and gift. What would help married couples in my parish to live this more joyfully?
The Samaritan gave his oil, his wine, his animal, his money and his time. Which of these is hardest for me to give, and to whom is Christ sending me this Sunday?

lead: On the last day of May the Church remembers Mary’s visit to Elizabeth, and the two readings fit together closely. Paul gives the Romans a picture of genuine love: warm affection, zeal that does not lag, hospitality to strangers, joy with those who rejoice, and a heart that goes down to the lowly. In Luke, Mary lives that picture before it was written. Carrying the Son of God, she sets out with haste to serve her older kinswoman, and when she greets her, the child in Elizabeth’s womb leaps for joy. The same Greek word links the two readings: Paul’s “zeal” and Mary’s “haste” are both spoudē. Love that is real does not wait; it goes.

r.h: Let love be genuine
set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome from Corinth, about AD 57, before he had visited them. In chapters 1–11 he set out the Gospel: all have sinned, and all are justified by grace through faith in Christ. Chapter 12 turns to life. It begins, “present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (12:1), and speaks of the Church as one body with many gifts (12:4–8). Then comes a string of short, vivid commands, all describing love in practice.
str: v. 9: the heading: let love be genuine; hate evil, hold fast to good.
vv. 10–12: love among believers: affection, honour, zeal, ardour, hope, patience, prayer.
v. 13: love that gives: share with the saints in need; pursue hospitality.
vv. 14–16: love toward all: bless persecutors; rejoice and weep with others; live in harmony; associate with the lowly.
kw: Literally “without hypocrisy”, without a mask. The hypokritēs was an actor on the stage. Christian love is not a role played in church; it is the truth of the heart.
In verse 11 Paul says, “Do not lag in zeal.” Luke uses the same word when Mary goes “with haste” to Elizabeth (Luke 1:39). Christian zeal is the eagerness of love.

Literally “love of strangers”. Paul says to “pursue” it, the verb for running after something. Hospitality was essential for travelling missionaries and for the poor in the early Church (Hebrews 13:2).
vv: Let love be genuine; hate what is evil, hold fast to what is good
Love is not softness toward evil. Genuine love hates what destroys the beloved and clings to what is good for him.
Do not lag in zeal, be ardent in spirit, serve the Lord.
“Ardent” is literally “boiling”. The Spirit sets the heart on fire, and that fire shows itself in service.
Contribute to the needs of the saints; extend hospitality to strangers.
“The saints” are fellow Christians. Paul was then gathering a collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (15:25–26).
Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.
It is often easier to weep with others than to rejoice with them without envy. The Visitation is a meeting of shared joy.
do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly
The Greek can mean lowly people or lowly tasks. Both are true of Mary, who calls herself the Lord’s servant (Luke 1:38) and goes to serve.
ch: The Catechism, describing the new law of the Gospel, quotes these very verses as part of the moral teaching of the apostles: let love be genuine; hate what is evil; love one another with brotherly affection; rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer; contribute to the needs of the saints, practise hospitality (CCC 1971). It is a portrait of the Christian life lived by grace, and the Church sees it already drawn in Mary, who believed, hastened to serve, and rejoiced with her kinswoman.

r.h: The mother of my Lord
set: At the Annunciation the angel told Mary that her kinswoman Elizabeth, who had been called barren, was in her sixth month (1:36). Mary, having said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord” (1:38), sets out at once for the hill country of Judea. A tradition places Zechariah’s home at Ain Karim, west of Jerusalem, several days’ walk from Nazareth.

Luke tells the scene with echoes of the Ark of the Covenant being brought up to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). David asked, “How can the ark of the Lord come into my care?” (2 Samuel 6:9); Elizabeth asks, “Why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?” David danced before the ark (6:14); John leaps in the womb. The ark stayed three months in the house of Obed-edom (6:11); Mary stays with Elizabeth about three months (Luke 1:56).
str: vv. 39–40: Mary sets out with haste, enters Zechariah’s house and greets Elizabeth.
v. 41: at Mary’s greeting the child leaps; Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit.
vv. 42–43: Elizabeth’s loud cry: blessed are you among women; the mother of my Lord.
v. 44: the child leaped for joy.
v. 45: blessed is she who believed.
kw: Not nervous hurry but eager readiness. St Ambrose says that the grace of the Holy Spirit knows nothing of slow efforts (in substance, Exposition of Luke 2.19).

The word the Greek Old Testament uses for Jacob and Esau struggling in Rebekah’s womb (Genesis 25:22). Here it is a leap of joy: the unborn prophet greets his Lord, as the angel had said John would be filled with the Holy Spirit even before his birth (1:15).
In Luke “the Lord” is the name of God (1:6, 9, 11), and also of Jesus (2:11). Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, confesses that the child in Mary’s womb is her Lord.
vv: In those days Mary set out and went with haste to a Judean town in the hill country
Mary does not stay at home to keep her secret. The first thing she does after receiving Christ is to carry him to someone else.
When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the child leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit
It is through Mary’s greeting that Christ’s presence reaches John and the Spirit fills Elizabeth. Mary’s voice becomes the means of grace.
Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.
The Church joins these words to the angel’s greeting in the Hail Mary. Mary is blessed because of the fruit of her womb, and the two blessings belong together.
And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?
The older woman, wife of a priest, humbles herself before the young girl from Nazareth. Faith sees the greatness that the world does not.
And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.
A different word for “blessed” (makaria), the word of the Beatitudes. Mary is happy because she believed. Zechariah had doubted (1:20); Mary trusted.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Mary, called in the Gospels “the mother of Jesus”, is acclaimed by Elizabeth, at the prompting of the Spirit, even before the birth of her son, as “the mother of my Lord”; for this reason the Church confesses that Mary is truly the Mother of God, Theotokos (CCC 495). It sees in Mary the ark of the covenant, the place where the glory of the Lord dwells (CCC 2676), and in John, filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb, the forerunner who rejoices at Christ’s coming (CCC 717). It calls Mary the most perfect embodiment of the obedience of faith, and quotes Elizabeth’s words, “Blessed is she who believed” (CCC 148).

qa: How can the Church call Mary “Mother of God” from this Gospel?

Elizabeth calls Mary “the mother of my Lord”, using the title Luke gives to God. The child in Mary’s womb is one person, the eternal Son of God, who took flesh from her. A mother is mother of a person, not only of a body, so Mary is truly the Mother of God. The Council of Ephesus (431) proclaimed this faith, and the Church professes it in every age (CCC 466, 495).
Why did Mary go “with haste”? Was she anxious?

Luke does not say she was anxious, but that she went eagerly. The angel’s word had told her of Elizabeth’s need and joy, and Mary, who had just called herself the Lord’s servant, goes to serve. The World Youth Day held in Lisbon in 2023 took this verse as its theme, and Pope Francis spoke of Mary’s haste as the readiness of love, not anxious hurry. Paul’s word to the Romans, “Do not lag in zeal”, uses the same Greek word.
rite: In Kerala the month of May is kept as the month of Mary, with daily devotions in many Syro-Malabar parishes and homes, and today that month comes to its close with the Visitation. It falls this year in the Season of the Apostles, which suits it well: Mary is the first to carry Christ to another house, before any apostle was sent.

Families can make this day a small visitation of their own: a visit to a sick relative, an elderly neighbour, a mother expecting a child. As Mary’s greeting brought joy and the Spirit into Zechariah’s house, our visits, made with prayer, can bring Christ into the homes we enter. The Hail Mary we pray at home holds Elizabeth’s very words.
study: Paul says, “Let love be genuine.” Where might my love wear a mask, and what would make it more real?
Mary went “with haste” to serve. Is there a visit or a service I keep putting off that I can make soon?
Elizabeth recognised Christ hidden in Mary before he was born. How can I learn to recognise Christ hidden in others, especially the unborn, the sick and the lowly?
“Blessed is she who believed.” What promise of the Lord am I being asked to trust, though I cannot yet see it fulfilled?
